docs.title: Augmented Software Engineering
docs.text:
Build software. Use AI. Understand what you build.

A part-time program at Holberton School Albania. Learn the tools, the fundamentals and the full web stack, then build a portfolio with an AI assistant at your side.

Start here View roadmap

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
Four stages, each building on the one before, with career preparation running alongside the whole way.

  1. Tools

    60 h · 8 projects

    The shell, VS Code, Git, GitHub and an AI assistant, set up and used from day one.

    Explore

  2. Foundations

    88 h · 11 projects

    Python from first program to classes, inheritance, UML and design patterns.

    Explore

    228 h · 15 projects

    Databases and APIs, HTML and CSS, modern JavaScript and Node.js.

    Explore

  4. Portfolio

    400 h · 9 projects

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
The last stage is your portfolio: two tracks of work you can show to an employer.

  • AI-Augmented Builds

docs.title: How you will work
docs.text:
The Holberton way: you learn by building, with your peers, and you leave able to explain and present what you built.

  • Project-based learning

    You learn by doing. Every concept comes with a project that has to run, pass the checks and be pushed to GitHub.

  • Peer learning

    You learn with and from your cohort: pair programming, code reviews and explaining your solution to someone else.

  • AI as a pair, not a replacement

    You prompt, review and correct AI output. The assistant writes a draft; you are responsible for what gets merged.

  • Understand what you ship

    If you can't explain it, you don't commit it. Reading and debugging code matter as much as writing it.

  • Soft skills

    Communication, teamwork, giving and receiving feedback, and presenting your work clearly to technical and non-technical people.

  • Work like a professional

    Git, pull requests, deadlines and code review from day one, and mock interviews to prepare for the real thing.

Read the Holberton Way

docs.title: The Holberton Way
docs.text:
No lectures. Real projects. You own your learning.

Nobody will stand at a board and teach you here. You build, you get stuck, you get yourself unstuck, and that is the skill. Your peers help you think, and mentors help when you have really tried. This page is how it works, and what it asks of you.

When you're stuck See the roadmap

docs.title: Four ideas to remember
docs.text:
• You own your learning

    The projects, this handbook and the people around you are there to help. The learning itself is your work, every day.

  • Struggle is part of the work

    Being stuck is not a sign that something is wrong. Getting unstuck on your own is exactly what employers pay for.

  • Ask well, at the right time

    Not after two minutes, not after two days. Try for real first, then ask a clear question.

  • Explain what you ship

    If you cannot explain a line, it does not go in. Not from a peer, not from the internet, not from an AI.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
Learning here is a team effort, and everyone on the team has a different job.

  • You

    • Work on your projects every day
    • Read the task, the docs and the tutorials
    • Build, test, debug and commit
    • Try before you ask, then ask clearly
    • Explain your code to others

  • Your peers

    • Think through problems with you
    • Pair program and review your code
    • Ask you "why?" until it is clear
    • Learn from your solutions, as you learn from theirs

  • Your mentors

    • Unblock you when you are truly stuck
    • Challenge your approach and your design
    • Give feedback on your work
    • Prepare you for interviews and the job

Mentors are there for what is hard, not for what is new. A mentor session is most useful when you arrive with a specific problem you have already worked on:

Mentor sessions are for

  • A blocker you have tried to solve, and can describe
  • A design question: is there a better way to do this?
  • Feedback on code that already works
  • Questions about careers, interviews and how the industry works

Mentor sessions are not for

  • A topic you have not read about yet
  • A project you have not started
  • Writing your code, or checking every line of it
  • Questions that the task, the docs or a peer can answer in minutes

docs.title: How a project goes
docs.text:
Every project on the intranet follows the same path. This handbook covers the second step; the project is where you prove it.

The path of a project Six steps. Read the task and its learning objectives on the intranet. Learn the basics in this handbook. Build the solution and commit often. Check it with the Checker. Review it with peers. Explain every decision. The first step and the last four happen on the intranet project; the second happens in this handbook. INTRANETTHIS HANDBOOKINTRANET PROJECT 123456 ReadLearnBuildCheckReviewExplain the task andits objectives the basics,with practice your solution,commit often the Checkertests it peers readand question it you justifyevery decision next project
  • Read the task and its learning objectives before you write a line. They tell you what you will be asked to explain.
  • Learn the concepts here, and do the "Try it" exercises and the practice sets. They use different examples from your projects on purpose: the project is yours to solve.
  • Build your solution, and commit small steps as you go.
  • Check it with the Checker, fix, and check again.
  • Review it with peers, and review theirs.
  • Explain it: every line, every choice. That is what a review, a defense and a job interview will ask of you.

docs.title: When you're stuck
docs.text:
You will be stuck often. That is normal, and it is where most of the learning happens. What matters is how you get out. Climb the ladder one step at a time, and use your AI assistant alongside every step.

The ladder for getting unstuck Five steps that climb from left to right. One: re-read the task and the error message. Two: the docs and this handbook. Three: debug by printing, shrinking the problem and explaining it out loud. Four: ask your peers. Five: bring it to a mentor session. Along the bottom, under every step, runs your AI assistant and Clippy, which help you reason at every step but do not do the work for you. 12345 Re-readLook it upDebugAsk peersMentor the task andthe error the docs, manpages, thishandbook print, shrinkthe problem,explain itout loud in the room oron Slack, withwhat you tried in a mentorsession, with apreparedquestion after ~20 min of real trying Alongside every step: your AI assistant and Clippy to explain an error, suggest what to check, or quiz you on a concept. To help you reason, not to write it for you.
  1. Re-read. The task and the error message, slowly, word by word. Half of all problems are solved right here: a wrong file name, a missed requirement, an error that says exactly what is wrong.
  2. Look it up. The official docs, the man page, the tutorial in this handbook. Search for the exact error message.
  3. Debug. Print the values you think you know. Shrink the problem to the smallest piece of code that still fails. Explain it out loud, to a peer or to a rubber duck: saying it often shows you the mistake.
  4. Ask your peers. In the room or on Slack, with what you tried. Someone has often just solved the same problem, and explaining it helps them too.
  5. Mentor session. When you and your peers are still stuck, bring a prepared question to a mentor.

Your AI assistant works alongside every step, not only as a last resort: ask it what an error means, what to check next, or to quiz you on a concept. Your general assistant and Clippy, Holberton's assistant on the intranet, are both there for that. Clippy is built to guide you through the reasoning rather than hand you code; use your general assistant the same way.

How long before you ask?

Being stuck for twenty minutes is learning. Being stuck for two days is a waste. As a guide: give a problem around twenty minutes of real trying, with steps 1 to 3 and your assistant, before you go to your peers. If you are going in circles, ask sooner.

docs.title: Ask a good question
docs.text:
A good question gets a good answer fast, and writing it often solves the problem on its own. Use this template, on Slack or in a session:

A good question
What I'm trying to do:  ...
What I expected:        ...
What happened:          ... (the exact error, copied, not retyped)
What I've tried:        ...
The code:               ... (the smallest piece that shows the problem)

Hard to help

My SQL doesn't work, can someone help?

No task, no error, no code. Whoever answers has to ask five questions before they can start.

Easy to help

I'm counting loans per member with a LEFT JOIN. I expected Lea to have 0, but she has 1. I tried COUNT(*) and COUNT(member_id). Here is the query: ...

Anyone can see the problem in a minute, and you have probably spotted it yourself while writing.

Before a mentor session, check that you can tick all of these:

  • I have climbed steps 1 to 4 of the ladder
  • I can say what I am trying to do, in one sentence
  • I have the exact error, and the smallest code that shows it
  • I can say what I have already tried, and what happened
  • My latest code is pushed, so we can look at it together

docs.title: AI, the Holberton way
docs.text:
AI is your amplifier, not your replacement. You will use it every day, and these rules keep it working for you instead of against you:

  • Reason with it

    Ask it to explain errors, concepts and options. Ask it to quiz you. Use it to understand, not to skip understanding.

  • You are responsible

    It drafts; you decide. Whatever you commit is yours, including its mistakes.

  • Predict before you run

    Before you run code from an assistant, say what it should do. If the result surprises you, find out why.

  • Explain every line

    If you cannot explain a line it gave you, ask it to explain, then rewrite it in your own words, or leave it out.

AI in the loop

Set up your assistants, including Clippy, in the AI Assistant tutorial. Every tutorial in this handbook ends with an "AI in the loop" note like this one, about using AI well for that topic.

docs.title: Habits that work, habits that fail
docs.text:
Habits that work

  • Working a little every day
  • Reading the whole task before starting
  • Committing small steps, with clear messages
  • Asking after real trying, with a prepared question
  • Reading your peers' code, not only your own
  • Explaining your solution out loud before you submit it

Habits that fail

  • Leaving everything for the weekend before the deadline
  • Starting to code before reading the task
  • One huge push the night before
  • Asking after two minutes, or suffering alone for two days
  • Copying a solution you cannot explain
  • Letting an AI write what you have not understood

docs.title: My commitment
docs.text:
Read these, and tick the ones you are ready to commit to. Come back to them when a week goes badly.

  • I work on my projects every day, even when it is only a little
  • I read the task and try for real before I ask for help
  • I ask clear questions, and bring them prepared to mentor sessions
  • I review my peers' code and help them when I can
  • I use AI to understand, not to avoid understanding
  • I can explain every line I push

Start with Zero Day See the roadmap

docs.title: AI Assistant
docs.text:
40 min Tools Needs: VS Code connected to WSL, a GitHub account

You will use three assistants in this program, and each has a different job. This tutorial sets them up and shows you how to use them without letting them do your learning for you.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Professional developers use AI every day: to explain unfamiliar code, draft boilerplate, find bugs and write tests. You will too, from the first week.

AI can produce something that looks right very quickly. What it cannot do is check its own assumptions, know what your project actually needs, or take responsibility for the result. That part is yours. A project that passes the Checker but that you cannot explain will not survive a peer review, and it will not survive a job interview either.

docs.title: Three assistants, three jobs
docs.text:
The three assistants and when to use each GitHub Copilot lives in VS Code and helps while you write code, with suggestions and chat about your open files. Claude or ChatGPT live in the browser and help when you need to understand something, explaining concepts and errors and comparing approaches. Clippy lives on the intranet and helps when you are stuck on a task, guiding your reasoning step by step without giving you code. IN VS CODE GitHub Copilot Suggestions as you type, chat about your open files while you write code IN THE BROWSER Claude or ChatGPT Explains concepts and errors, compares approaches when you need to understand ON THE INTRANET Clippy Guides your reasoning step by step, never gives code when you are stuck on a task

Copilot sees the files you have open, so it is the fastest way to ask about your code. Claude or ChatGPT have more room for a conversation, so they are better for understanding a concept or an error properly. Clippy knows Holberton's projects and is built to make you think: it asks questions and gives you the next step, not the answer.

docs.title: How to use any of them
docs.text:
Whichever assistant you open, the same loop applies.

The verify loop Ask with context, read the draft, test it yourself, and only then commit, and only what you can explain. If the test fails or you cannot explain it, go back and revise your question. Ask with context Read every line of the draft Test run it yourself Commit if you can explain it fails, or you cannot explain it: revise

The step people skip is Read. If you cannot say what a line does, you are not ready to test it, and you are certainly not ready to commit it.

docs.title: Step 1: Switch on GitHub Copilot in VS Code
docs.text:
Copilot is built into VS Code. You only need to sign in.

  1. Open VS Code connected to WSL, so the bottom left says WSL: Ubuntu.
  2. Hover over the Copilot icon in the status bar and choose Use AI Features.
  3. Sign in with your GitHub account and approve the request in the browser.

If your account has no Copilot plan, it is enrolled in Copilot Free automatically, which gives you a monthly allowance of suggestions and chat. If you are a student, you can also apply through GitHub Education for the free student plan. Plans and limits change often, so check the current details there.

Two shortcuts to learn now:

Keys What it opens Ctrl+Alt+I Chat view: a conversation about your project Ctrl+I Inline chat: ask about, or change, the selected code

Consider turning off inline suggestions while you learn the basics

Grey suggestions that appear as you type are useful once you know the language. In your first weeks they type the answer before you have thought of it, and you learn the syntax much more slowly. Hover over the Copilot icon in the status bar to switch code completions off. Chat keeps working, so you can still ask questions.

docs.title: Step 2: Set up a browser assistant
docs.text:
Create a free account on Claude or ChatGPT. One is enough; pick whichever you prefer. Keep it pinned in your browser next to the intranet.

Use it for the bigger questions:

  • Explain a concept from your project in plain language.
  • Read an error message with you and say what it means.
  • Compare two ways of solving something and their trade-offs.

docs.title: Step 3: Meet Clippy
docs.text:
Clippy lives on the intranet, on your project pages. It knows what each task asks for and is built to coach you rather than solve it.

Tell Clippy what you are trying to do, what you have tried and where you are stuck. It answers with questions and the next step of reasoning, not with code. That is deliberate. Use it when you are stuck on how to think about a task, before you go looking for code anywhere else.

docs.title: Ask well
docs.text:
A vague question gets a vague answer. A good prompt gives the assistant four things: what you are working on, what you tried, what happened, and what kind of help you want.

Explain an error

I'm writing a Python script on Ubuntu for a beginner project.
Running `python3 0-add.py` gives this error:

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

Explain what the error means and where to look in my code.
Don't rewrite the code for me.

Ask for a hint, not the answer

My task: write a function that returns the largest number in a list
without using max(). I tried looping over the list, but I don't know
what to compare each number against. Give me a hint for the next
step, not the solution.

Review code you wrote

Here is my solution to a task. It passes, but review it like a
senior developer: is anything unclear, fragile or unnecessary?
Explain each point. Don't give me a rewritten version.

[paste your code]

Notice the last line of each prompt. Saying what you do not want is the easiest way to keep the learning on your side.

docs.title: Rules for Holberton projects
docs.text:
• Do

    • Ask it to explain concepts, docs and error messages
    • Ask for a hint when you are stuck
    • Ask it to review code you wrote yourself
    • Ask it for test cases you had not thought of
    • Check what it says against the docs or by running it

  • Don't

    • Paste a task and submit whatever comes back
    • Commit a line you cannot explain
    • Paste passwords, tokens or .env files into any assistant
    • Paste a classmate's code without asking them
    • Trust a confident answer you have not tested

Your peers and mentors will ask you to explain your code. "The AI wrote it" is not an explanation.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
There is no Copilot icon in the status bar

Update VS Code with Help > Check for Updates, then restart it. If the icon is still missing, press Ctrl+Shift+P and run Chat: Open Chat, which also offers the sign-in.

Copilot says I have reached my limit

The free plan has a monthly allowance. Use the browser assistant or Clippy until it resets, or apply for the student plan through GitHub Education.

The answer looks right but the code fails

That happens often. Assistants guess at versions, file names and what your task requires. Paste the exact error back and say what you expected, or read the docs for the function it used.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. The Copilot icon in the status bar shows you are signed in.
  2. Open hello.py, select the print line, press Ctrl+I and ask explain this line. Read the answer.
  3. In Claude or ChatGPT, ask: What is the difference between running python3 hello.py and ./hello.py on Linux? Then try both in your terminal and see whether the answer was right.
  4. Open any project on the intranet and ask Clippy how to start the first task. Notice that it asks you questions back.

docs.title: Git & GitHub
docs.text:
75 min Tools Needs: Shell Basics, a GitHub account

Git saves snapshots of your work. GitHub stores those snapshots online so you do not lose them and other people can see them. In this tutorial you set both up, push your first repository, then learn to branch, merge, resolve a conflict and undo a mistake.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
You will write a lot of code in this program. Some of it will work and then stop working, and you will want yesterday's version back. Git gives you that.

There is a second reason. When you apply for a job, your GitHub profile is one of the first things a hiring manager opens. Every project you finish here ends up there, and the Checker reads your work from it. Start building that history on day one.

docs.title: How Git works
docs.text:
Four places hold your work. Three are on your laptop, one is on GitHub. Each command moves your work from one place to the next.

How work moves through Git Your working directory, then the staging area using git add, then the local repository history using git commit, then GitHub using git push. The git pull command brings work back from GitHub to your working directory. Working directory files you edit Staging area picked to save Local history commits on your laptop GitHub online, shareable git add git commit git push git pull

Keep this picture in your head. Most Git confusion comes from not knowing which of the four boxes your work is sitting in right now.

docs.title: Step 1: Tell Git who you are
docs.text:
Git writes your name on every commit. Set it once, in the Ubuntu terminal:

git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

Use the same email address as your GitHub account. If the two do not match, your commits show up on GitHub without your profile attached. The last line makes every new repository start on a branch called main, the same name GitHub uses.

Nothing prints when this works. Check it:

git config --global --list

docs.title: Step 2: Let your laptop talk to GitHub
docs.text:
GitHub does not accept your account password in the terminal. You authenticate with a Personal Access Token instead: a long random string that works like a password, but only for what you allow and only until it expires.

Personal access tokenGitHub CLI
  1. On GitHub, open Settings, then Developer settings, then Personal access tokens, then Fine-grained tokens.
  2. Click Generate new token. Give it a name and an expiry of 90 days.
  3. Under Repository access, choose All repositories. Under Permissions, set Contents to Read and write.
  4. Click Generate token and copy it. GitHub shows it once and never again, so store it in a password manager now.

Then tell Git to remember it:

git config --global credential.helper store

The first time you push, Git asks for a username and a password. Type your GitHub username, then paste the token as the password. Git saves it and stops asking.

The gh tool creates and stores a token for you through the browser.

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y gh
gh auth login

Choose GitHub.com, HTTPS, yes to authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials, then login with a web browser. Copy the one-time code, press Enter and finish in the browser.

Check it worked with gh auth status.

Never put your token in a URL or a file you commit

You will find advice online to clone with https://username:token@github.com/.... It works, and it leaks. Git writes that URL into .git/config, your shell saves it in its history, and one screenshot in Slack gives someone else access to your account. If a token ever leaks, delete it on GitHub straight away and make a new one.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a repository on GitHub
docs.text:
A repository, or repo, is a project folder that Git tracks. It is easiest to create it on GitHub and copy it down.

  1. On GitHub, click the green New button.
  2. Name it git-practice.
  3. Leave it public, and leave Add a README file unchecked.
  4. Click Create repository.

docs.title: Step 4: Clone it to your laptop
docs.text:
Cloning downloads the repo and connects your local folder to GitHub. That connection is called a remote, and Git names it origin.

cd ~/holberton
git clone https://github.com/your-username/git-practice.git
cd git-practice
git remote -v

You should see the clone warn that the repository is empty, and two origin lines pointing at GitHub. The warning is fine.

docs.title: Step 5: The everyday loop
docs.text:
Make a change, check it, stage it, commit it, push it. You will run this loop hundreds of times.

echo "# Git practice" > README.md
git status

git status is the most useful command in Git. Run it whenever you are unsure where things stand. Right now it lists README.md as untracked: Git sees the file but is not saving it yet.

git add README.md                 # stage it
git commit -m "Add README"        # save a snapshot locally
git push -u origin main           # send it to GitHub

The -u links your local main to GitHub's main, so from now on git push and git pull are enough. Refresh the repo page in your browser. Your file is there.

To see what you have saved so far:

git log --oneline

Write commit messages in the imperative

Write "Add login form", not "Added login form". Git's own messages read that way, so your history stays consistent. If a message needs the word and, you are probably saving two changes at once. Make two commits.

docs.title: Step 6: Ignore what does not belong
docs.text:
Some files should never be committed: caches, editor settings, dependencies you can reinstall, and above all secrets. List them in a file called .gitignore at the root of the repo.

.gitignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/

# JavaScript
node_modules/

# Secrets and local settings
.env
.vscode/

git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"
git push

Now create a file called .env and run git status. Git does not list it. Ignored files stay on your laptop and never reach GitHub.

.gitignore does not untrack files already committed

If you committed a file before ignoring it, Git keeps tracking it. Stop tracking it with git rm --cached filename, then commit. If it was a secret, treat it as leaked: it is still in the history.

docs.title: Step 7: Work on a branch
docs.text:
A branch is a separate line of commits. You make one for each change, work there without touching main, and merge it back when it is ready.

A feature branch merged back into main The main branch has two commits. A feature branch starts from the second, with git switch -c, and gets two commits of its own. It is then merged back into main with git merge, creating a merge commit. main feature/greeting git switch -c git merge your commits, isolated 
git switch -c feature/greeting      # create the branch and move to it
echo "Hello from a branch" > greeting.txt
git add greeting.txt
git commit -m "Add greeting"
git push -u origin feature/greeting

git branch lists your branches and marks the current one with *. git switch main moves back. Notice that greeting.txt disappears from your folder on main: it only exists on the branch so far.

docs.title: Step 8: Merge, and resolve a conflict
docs.text:
To bring the branch into main, switch to main and merge:

git switch main
git merge feature/greeting
git push

Most merges finish by themselves. A conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines, and Git cannot know which version you want. Make one on purpose so you know what it looks like:

git switch -c feature/title
echo "# Git practice, branch version" > README.md
git commit -am "Change title on branch"

git switch main
echo "# Git practice, main version" > README.md
git commit -am "Change title on main"

git merge feature/title

Git stops and reports a conflict in README.md. Open the file:

<<<<<<< HEAD
# Git practice, main version
=======
# Git practice, branch version
>>>>>>> feature/title

The part above ======= is what main has. The part below is what the branch has. Edit the file so it says what it should, delete all three marker lines, then finish the merge:

git add README.md
git commit -m "Merge feature/title"
git push

VS Code highlights conflicts and offers Accept Current, Accept Incoming and Accept Both buttons above each one. They do the same editing for you, but read the result before you commit.

docs.title: Step 9: Undo a mistake
docs.text:
Git has two main ways to undo a commit. The difference is whether you rewrite history or add to it.

git reset compared with git revert With git reset, commit C is removed and the branch points back at B: history is rewritten, so use it only for commits you have not pushed. With git revert, a new commit, C prime, is added that undoes C: history is kept, so it is safe on shared branches. git reset --hard HEAD~1 A B C main C is gone; main points at B Rewrites history. Only for commits you have not pushed yet. git revert C A B C C' C' is a new commit that undoes C Keeps history. Safe on shared branches.

git revert adds a new commit that does the opposite of an old one. Nothing disappears, so it is safe on any branch other people use, including main after you have pushed.

git log --oneline          # find the commit's short hash, e.g. a1b2c3d
git revert a1b2c3d         # Git opens an editor for the message; save and close
git push

git reset moves the branch back to an earlier commit, as if the later ones never happened. Use it only on commits you have not pushed, because it rewrites history that others may already have.

Command Commit removed? Your changes git reset --soft HEAD~1 Yes Kept, and still staged git reset HEAD~1 Yes Kept in your files, unstaged git reset --hard HEAD~1 Yes Deleted. There is no undo button

HEAD~1 means "one commit before the current one". The safe default when you are unsure is git revert.

AI in the loop

Paste the output of git status or a conflict into Copilot Chat and ask what state your repository is in and what your options are. Assistants are good at reading Git output. Ask for an explanation rather than a command, and never run reset --hard or a force push because an assistant suggested it until you know what it deletes.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
fatal: not a git repository

You are not inside the repo folder. Run pwd, then cd into the folder you cloned.

Authentication failed when you push

The token is wrong or expired, or you typed your GitHub password instead of the token. Make a new token, run rm ~/.git-credentials, and push again. Or run gh auth login.

Updates were rejected because the remote contains work

Someone pushed to GitHub after you last pulled. Run git pull, resolve any conflicts, then push again.

Please tell me who you are

You skipped Step 1. Set your name and email, then commit again.

I committed to main instead of a branch

If you have not pushed yet: git switch -c feature/name to keep the commit on a new branch, then git switch main and git reset --hard origin/main to put main back the way GitHub has it.

docs.text:
• How to configure Git with your name and email
  • How to create a repository on GitHub and clone it locally
  • What the working directory, staging area and history are, and which command moves work between them
  • What .gitignore is for, and what belongs in it
  • How to push and pull, and how a Personal Access Token is used
  • What a branch is, and how to create and switch between them
  • How to merge a branch, and how to resolve a conflict
  • The difference between git reset and git revert, and when to use each

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command What it does git status Show what changed and what is staged git add file / git add . Stage one file / everything git commit -m "message" Save a snapshot locally git push / git pull Send commits to GitHub / bring them down git log --oneline List commits, one per line git switch -c name Create a branch and move to it git switch name Move to an existing branch git merge name Merge a branch into the current one git revert hash Undo a commit with a new commit git reset HEAD~1 Remove the last local commit, keep the changes git rm --cached file Stop tracking a file without deleting it

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You can track your own work. Next, work with other people.

GitHub Flow

Want to go deeper: the Pro Git book is free and thorough, and Learn Git Branching lets you practise branching visually.

docs.title: GitHub Flow
docs.text:
75 min Tools Needs: Git & GitHub, a partner from your cohort

GitHub Flow is the simple way most teams work together on one codebase: every change lives on its own branch, goes through a pull request, gets reviewed, and is merged into main only when it is ready. This tutorial walks through the whole cycle, from forking a repository to tagging a release.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
On your own, Git is a safety net. In a team, it is how work gets reviewed, discussed and shipped without people overwriting each other. The team projects later in the program use this flow, and so does almost every company you will apply to.

Do this tutorial with a partner. Reviewing someone else's pull request teaches you as much as opening your own.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
GitHub Flow in six steps Branch from main. Commit small, clear changes. Push the branch to GitHub. Open a pull request. A teammate reviews it, and you update it until it is approved. Merge it into main, then delete the branch. Branch Commit Push Pull request Review Merge off main small, clear to GitHub describe it until approved into main changes requested: commit again on the same branch

main is always working code. Nobody commits to it directly; changes reach it only through a reviewed pull request.

docs.title: Step 1: Fork and set up remotes
docs.text:
When you do not have write access to a repository, for example an open source project or a repo your partner owns, you fork it: GitHub makes a copy under your account. You work on your fork and propose changes back to the original.

Upstream, your fork and your laptop The original repository, called upstream, is forked into your account on GitHub, called origin. You clone origin to your laptop and push your branches back to it. You open a pull request from origin to upstream. To stay up to date you fetch from upstream directly. upstream the original repo, on GitHub origin your fork, on GitHub your laptop where you work 1. Fork 4. Pull request 2. clone 3. push your branch fetch upstream

One partner creates a repo called flow-practice with a README. The other forks it with the Fork button on GitHub, then clones the fork:

cd ~/holberton
git clone https://github.com/your-username/flow-practice.git
cd flow-practice
git remote add upstream https://github.com/partner-username/flow-practice.git
git remote -v

You now have two remotes. origin is your fork, where you push. upstream is the original, where you get other people's changes.

Before starting any new piece of work, bring main up to date:

git switch main
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
git push origin main

Working in the same repo instead

If your partner adds you as a collaborator instead, you skip the fork: clone their repo directly and there is only origin. Every other step is the same.

docs.title: Step 2: Create a branch with a clear name
docs.text:
Name branches by the kind of change and what it does, in lowercase with hyphens.

Prefix For Example feature/ New functionality feature/user-login fix/ Bug fixes fix/empty-cart-crash docs/ Documentation only docs/setup-instructions refactor/ Restructuring with no behaviour change refactor/split-utils chore/ Tooling, config, dependencies chore/add-gitignore 
git switch -c docs/add-contributors

docs.title: Step 3: Make meaningful commits
docs.text:
A good commit does one thing and says what it does. Many teams also start the message with a type, a convention called Conventional Commits:

git commit -m "docs: add contributors section to README"
git commit -m "fix: handle empty input in parser"
git commit -m "feat: add login form"

The types line up with branch prefixes and with version numbers later in this tutorial. Whatever convention your team picks, keep messages in the imperative and keep each commit small.

Push the branch to your fork:

git push -u origin docs/add-contributors

docs.title: Step 4: Open a pull request
docs.text:
A pull request, or PR, asks the repository's owners to review your branch and merge it. After you push, GitHub shows a Compare & pull request button. Click it, check that the base is main on the original repo and the head is your branch, then write a description.

A good description answers three questions:

Pull request description
## What
Adds a Contributors section to the README listing both partners.

## Why
New team members could not tell who to ask about the project.

## How to test
Open README.md on this branch and check the section renders.

Closes #3

Closes #3 links the PR to issue number 3 and closes the issue when the PR is merged. Keep the PR small: a reviewer can read 100 lines carefully, but skims 1,000.

You can also open it from the terminal with gh pr create, which asks for the title and description.

AI in the loop

Copilot can draft a PR description from your changes. Use it as a first draft, then edit it until every sentence is true and specific. It can also do a first review pass, but it does not replace your teammate. It cannot know what the team agreed or why the change was needed.

docs.title: Step 5: Review, and respond to review
docs.text:
Swap roles. Open your partner's PR, go to Files changed, and read every line.

  • Click the + next to a line to leave a comment on it.
  • Use Insert a suggestion to propose an exact change they can accept with one click.
  • When you are done, click Review changes and choose one of: Comment (no verdict), Request changes (must be fixed before merging) or Approve.

Good review comments are specific and kind. "This loop runs twice for the same item, could we break after the first match?" helps. "This is wrong" does not. Ask questions when you do not understand something: often the code is the thing that needs to change.

When you receive comments, fix them on the same branch and push again. The PR updates by itself; there is no need to open a new one. Reply to each comment so the reviewer knows it is handled.

docs.title: Step 6: Resolve conflicts in a pull request
docs.text:
If main changed while your PR was open, GitHub may say This branch has conflicts that must be resolved. Bring the latest main into your branch and resolve them locally:

git switch docs/add-contributors
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main          # use origin/main if you have no fork
# fix the conflict markers, as in the Git tutorial
git add README.md
git commit -m "Merge main into docs/add-contributors"
git push

The PR updates, the conflict warning disappears, and the reviewer can approve.

docs.title: Step 7: Merge and clean up
docs.text:
Once the PR is approved, the repo owner clicks Merge pull request. GitHub offers three ways; teams usually pick one and stick to it.

Option Result on main Create a merge commit All your commits, plus one merge commit Squash and merge Your commits combined into one Rebase and merge Your commits replayed on top, no merge commit

Then delete the branch. It has done its job, and old branches pile up fast.

git switch main
git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main
git branch -d docs/add-contributors              # delete it locally
git push origin --delete docs/add-contributors   # delete it on your fork
git fetch --prune                                # forget remote branches that are gone

GitHub also shows a Delete branch button right after merging.

docs.title: Step 8: Tag a release with SemVer
docs.text:
When main reaches a state worth naming, you tag it with a version number. Semantic Versioning, or SemVer, uses three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

Change Bump Example Breaks something people relied on MAJOR 1.4.2 → 2.0.0 Adds a feature, nothing breaks MINOR 1.4.2 → 1.5.0 Fixes a bug, nothing new PATCH 1.4.2 → 1.4.3

Versions below 1.0.0 mean "still being built, anything may change". A first public release is 1.0.0.

git switch main && git pull
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release"
git push origin v1.0.0

On GitHub, open Releases, then Draft a new release, pick the tag and paste the notes from your changelog.

docs.title: Step 9: Keep a CHANGELOG
docs.text:
A CHANGELOG.md at the root of the repo tells people what changed in each version, in words rather than commits. A widely used format is Keep a Changelog:

CHANGELOG.md
# Changelog

## [Unreleased]

## [1.0.0] - 2026-10-20
### Added
- Contributors section in the README.
- Setup instructions for WSL.

### Fixed
- Broken link to the project board.

Collect changes under Unreleased as PRs are merged. When you tag a release, rename that section to the new version and date, and start a new empty Unreleased above it. Use the headings Added, Changed, Fixed and Removed.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
I committed to main on my fork

Move the work to a branch and reset main: git switch -c feature/name, then git switch main and git reset --hard upstream/main, then git push --force origin main. Force-pushing is acceptable here only because it is your own fork's main. Never force-push a shared branch.

My fork is far behind the original

git switch main, git fetch upstream, git merge upstream/main, git push origin main. GitHub's Sync fork button on your fork's page does the same.

fatal: 'upstream' does not appear to be a git repository

You have not added the upstream remote yet. Run git remote add upstream <url of the original repo>.

The PR shows commits I did not make

Your branch started from an old main. Update main from upstream, then merge main into your branch, as in Step 6.

docs.title: Explain it to someone
docs.text:
• The steps of GitHub Flow, and why main is never committed to directly
  • What a fork is, and the difference between origin and upstream
  • How to name a branch, and why naming conventions help a team
  • What makes a commit message meaningful
  • How to open a pull request and what its description should say
  • How to comment, request changes and approve in a review
  • How to resolve a conflict that appears in a pull request
  • How SemVer numbers change for a breaking change, a feature and a fix
  • What goes in a CHANGELOG and when it is updated
  • How to clean up branches after a merge

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command What it does git remote add upstream url Connect your clone to the original repo git fetch upstream Download upstream's latest commits git merge upstream/main Bring them into your current branch git switch -c type/short-name Start a new branch git push -u origin branch Publish a branch to your fork gh pr create Open a pull request from the terminal git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "msg" Tag a release git push origin v1.0.0 Publish the tag git branch -d branch Delete a merged branch locally git push origin --delete branch Delete it on GitHub git fetch --prune Forget remote branches that were deleted

docs.text:
Your tools are ready: a Linux machine, an editor, AI assistants, the shell and Git. Time to write real programs.

docs.title: Shell Permissions
docs.text:
45 min Tools Needs: Shell Basics

Linux is a multi-user system. Every file has an owner, a group, and a set of rules about who may read it, change it or run it. In this tutorial you learn to read those rules, change them, and act as another user when you need to.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Permission denied is one of the first errors you will meet, and one of the most common on servers. Most of the time the fix is one command, but only if you understand what the system is protecting.

Permissions also matter for safety. A web server that can write to its own code, or a secrets file that every user can read, is how systems get broken into.

docs.title: Read the permissions
docs.text:
Run ls -l on a file:

-rwxr-xr-- 1 you developers 512 Oct 20 10:04 deploy.sh

The first ten characters are the permissions. Read them in four parts.

Reading -rwxr-xr-- as 754 The first character is the file type: a dash for a regular file, d for a directory. The next three, r w x, are the owner's permissions, 4 plus 2 plus 1 equals 7. The next three, r dash x, are the group's, 4 plus 0 plus 1 equals 5. The last three, r dash dash, are everyone else's, 4 plus 0 plus 0 equals 4. Together they make 754. - r w x r - x r - - type - file, d dir owner (u) group (g) others (o) 4 + 2 + 1 4 + 0 + 1 4 + 0 + 0 7 5 4 chmod 754 deploy.sh r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, - = 0
  1. Type. - for a regular file, d for a directory, l for a link.
  2. Owner (u, for user). Here rwx: the owner can read, write and execute.
  3. Group (g). Here r-x: members of the developers group can read and execute, but not change it.
  4. Others (o). Here r--: everyone else can only read it.

The two names after the permissions, you and developers, are the file's owner and group.

docs.title: What r, w and x mean
docs.text:
The letters mean slightly different things on files and on directories.

On a file On a directory r read See the contents List the names inside (ls) w write Change the contents Create, rename or delete files inside x execute Run it as a program Enter it (cd) and reach files inside

docs.title: Each set as one digit
docs.text:
Each letter has a value: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Add up the letters in a set and you get one digit from 0 to 7. Three sets make three digits.

Digit Letters Typical use 7 rwx Owner of a script or directory 6 rw- Owner of a normal file 5 r-x Others may run or enter, not change 4 r-- Read only 0 --- No access

So 755 is rwxr-xr-x, the usual setting for scripts and directories, and 644 is rw-r--r--, the usual setting for normal files. 600 (rw-------) is for files only you should read, such as keys.

docs.title: Change permissions with chmod
docs.text:
chmod changes the permissions. You can give it the three digits, or describe the change with letters.

chmod 755 deploy.sh      # set exactly rwxr-xr-x
chmod u+x deploy.sh      # add execute for the owner
chmod g-w notes.txt      # remove write from the group
chmod o=r notes.txt      # set others to exactly read
chmod a+r notes.txt      # add read for all three (a = all)
chmod ug+rw,o-rwx data/  # combine changes with commas

Digits are quicker when you know the result you want. Letters are safer when you only want to change one thing and leave the rest alone.

Only the file's owner, or root, can change its permissions.

Never fix an error with chmod 777

777 gives everyone permission to read, change and run the file. It makes the error go away and opens a hole anyone on the machine can use. Work out who actually needs access, and grant exactly that.

docs.title: Users and groups
docs.text:
Every user has a name and a number, the user ID or UID. Every user also belongs to one or more groups, each with a group ID or GID.

whoami          # your effective user name
id              # your user ID, group ID and every group you are in
id -u           # just your effective user ID, as a number
groups          # the groups you are in
groups alex     # the groups another user is in

Usually your real ID (who you logged in as) and your effective ID (who the system treats you as right now) are the same. They differ when you run something as another user, which is the next section.

docs.title: Create users and groups
docs.text:
These commands need root privileges, so they start with sudo. They are safe to try on your own WSL machine.

sudo adduser alex                # create user alex, with a home folder
sudo groupadd developers         # create a group
sudo usermod -aG developers alex # add alex to the group
groups alex                      # check

adduser is Ubuntu's friendly version and asks you questions. The lower-level useradd does the same job with flags, and it is what man pages and scripts often use. Clean up afterwards with sudo deluser alex and sudo groupdel developers.

docs.title: Change owner and group
docs.text:
chown changes a file's owner, and optionally its group. chgrp changes only the group.

sudo chown alex report.txt              # owner becomes alex
sudo chown alex:developers report.txt   # owner and group
sudo chgrp developers report.txt        # group only
sudo chown -R alex project/             # a folder and everything in it

Why does chown need sudo? If normal users could give their files away, they could create a file and make it look as though someone else wrote it, or push their files onto another user's disk quota. Only root can change who owns a file. You can change the group of a file you own, but only to a group you belong to.

docs.title: Act as root, or as another user
docs.text:
root is the administrator account, with user ID 0. It can do anything, which is why you avoid working as root all the time.

  • sudo runs one command as root

    sudo apt update
sudo !!

    It asks for your password, runs that one command with root privileges, and records it in a log. Your user must be allowed to use sudo, which the first user on Ubuntu is.

  • su switches to another user

    su alex      # become alex
sudo su -    # become root
exit         # back to yourself

    su asks for the target user's password and opens a shell as them. The prompt changes to show who you are. The - also loads their environment and takes you to their home folder.

Use sudo for single commands. Use su when you really need to work as another user for a while, and type exit as soon as you are done.

AI in the loop

Assistants often suggest commands that start with sudo. Before you run one, ask what each part does and what it changes. A command you do not understand, run as root, is the fastest way to break your system or open it up to someone else.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Permission denied

Run ls -l on the file and on the folder it is in. Work out which of the three sets applies to you (are you the owner, in the group, or other?) and which letter is missing. Then grant only that.

Operation not permitted with chown or chgrp

Changing an owner needs root. Run it again with sudo.

you is not in the sudoers file

Your user is not allowed to use sudo. On your own WSL machine the first user always is. On a shared machine, ask the administrator.

su: Authentication failure

su wants the password of the user you are switching to, not your own. To become root on Ubuntu, use sudo su - with your own password instead.

docs.title: Explain it to someone
docs.text:
• What chmod, sudo, su, chown and chgrp do
  • How to read Linux permissions from ls -l
  • How to write each set of permissions as one digit
  • How to change the permissions, owner and group of a file
  • Why a normal user cannot chown a file
  • How to run one command with root privileges
  • How to switch to another user, or become root
  • How to create a user and a group
  • How to print real and effective user and group IDs
  • How to print the groups a user is in
  • How to print your effective user ID

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command What it does ls -l file Show permissions, owner and group chmod 755 file Set permissions with digits chmod u+x file Change one permission with letters sudo chown user:group file Change owner and group sudo chgrp group file Change group only whoami / id -u Effective user name / effective user ID id Real and effective user and group IDs, and groups groups user Groups a user belongs to sudo adduser name / sudo groupadd name Create a user / a group sudo command Run one command as root su user / exit Become another user / go back

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You can move around and control who may touch what. Now start tracking your work.

Git & GitHub

docs.title: Shell Basics
docs.text:
50 min Tools Needs: Ubuntu in WSL, or a Mac or Linux terminal

The shell is the program that reads what you type in the terminal and makes it happen. In this tutorial you learn what it is, how to move around the filesystem with it, and how to find answers on your own.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Servers have no mouse. When you deploy code, debug a container or fix something on a remote machine, the shell is all you get. Holberton's Checker also runs everything from a shell, so the faster you are here, the faster every project goes.

It is also simpler than it looks. A dozen commands cover most of what you will do in a day.

docs.title: Terminal, shell and prompt
docs.text:
People use terminal and shell as if they mean the same thing. They do not.

Terminal, shell and the system The terminal is the window: it shows text and sends your keystrokes. The shell, usually bash, reads each command and runs it. The system underneath holds the programs and files that the command uses, such as ls, python3 and your folders. THE WINDOW Terminal shows text, sends keystrokes THE INTERPRETER Shell (bash) reads a command, runs it THE SYSTEM Programs and files ls, python3, your folders you type it runs
  • The terminal is the window. It draws text and passes your keys along. Windows Terminal and the VS Code panel are both terminals.
  • The shell is the program inside it that reads a command, works out what you meant and runs it. On Ubuntu the default shell is bash. You can check yours with echo $SHELL.
  • The prompt is the text the shell prints when it is ready for your next command.
yourname@LAPTOP:~/holberton$
Part Meaning yourname the user you are logged in as LAPTOP the name of the machine ~/holberton your current folder, the working directory $ you are a normal user. It becomes # when you are root

docs.title: RTFM: read the manual
docs.text:
RTFM stands for "read the fine manual", and it is the first advice any experienced developer gives. Almost every command ships with its own documentation, written by the people who built it.

man ls

This opens the manual page for ls. Inside it:

Key What it does Space / B Page down / page up / then a word Search. N jumps to the next match Q Quit

Some commands are not separate programs but are built into the shell itself, such as cd. Those use help:

type cd        # cd is a shell builtin
help cd
type ls        # ls is /usr/bin/ls

For a quick summary of any program, try ls --help.

AI in the loop

An assistant is a fast way to understand a command: ask "what does ls -la do, flag by flag?". But assistants sometimes invent flags that do not exist. Treat the answer as a lead, then confirm it with man. The manual describes the version actually installed on your machine.

docs.title: The filesystem is a tree
docs.text:
Linux keeps every file in a single tree. There are no drive letters. The top of the tree is the root directory, written /.

The Linux directory tree The root directory, slash, sits at the top. Below it are bin, etc, home, root, tmp and usr. Slash home contains your home folder, which contains holberton. Slash root, a different directory, is the home folder of the root user. / the root directory bin etc home root tmp usr you holberton /home/you your home directory, also ~ ~/holberton /root home of the root user

Three places on that tree matter most:

  • / is the root directory, the top of everything.
  • /home/you is your home directory, written ~ for short. Your files and settings live here.
  • /root is the home directory of the user called root, the administrator account. It is just one folder inside /, not the top of the tree. The names are confusing; the picture is not.

Every file has a path that says where it sits in the tree:

  • An absolute path starts at the root: /home/you/holberton.
  • A relative path starts from where you are now: holberton, or ../tmp.

docs.title: Move around
docs.text:
You are always in one directory, called the working directory. Three commands are enough to move around.

Where am I? pwd prints the working directory.

pwd

/home/you

What is here? ls lists the contents.

ls            # names only
ls -l         # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -la        # long format, including hidden files
ls /etc       # list another directory without going there

Go somewhere. cd changes the working directory.

cd holberton          # relative: into holberton, below where you are
cd /tmp               # absolute: straight to /tmp
cd ..                 # up one level
cd                    # home, from anywhere (same as cd ~)
cd -                  # back to the previous directory, and print it

cd - is the one people forget. It flips between your last two locations, which is handy when you are working in two folders at once.

docs.title: ., .. and hidden files
docs.text:
Run ls -la in your home folder:

drwxr-x--- 5 you you 4096 Oct 20 09:12 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Oct 19 18:40 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you  220 Oct 19 18:40 .bash_logout
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 3771 Oct 19 18:40 .bashrc
drwxr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Oct 20 09:12 holberton
  • . is the directory you are in. ./script.sh means "the script.sh in this folder".
  • .. is the directory above it. cd .. goes up one level.
  • Hidden files are any files whose name starts with a dot, such as .bashrc. Plain ls skips them; ls -a shows them. They usually hold settings, which is why they are kept out of the way.

There is nothing secret about a hidden file. The dot only changes whether ls shows it by default.

docs.title: Use the history
docs.text:
The shell remembers what you typed.

Do this What happens Up / Down Walk back and forward through previous commands history List recent commands, numbered !42 Run command number 42 from that list again !! Run the last command again. sudo !! reruns it as root Ctrl+R then type Search backwards for a command containing that text

Ctrl+R saves more time than anything else on this page. Try it now: press it, type cd, and press Ctrl+R again to see older matches.

docs.title: Write your first script
docs.text:
A shell script is a text file of commands that run one after the other. The first line is the shebang: #! followed by the path to the program that should run the file.

hello_shell
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello from the shell"

The shebang tells Linux to run this file with /bin/bash. Without it, Linux has to guess, and Holberton's checkers will reject the file.

Create it, make it executable, and run it:

cd ~/holberton
code hello_shell        # write the two lines and save
chmod u+x hello_shell
./hello_shell

chmod u+x gives you, the owner, permission to execute the file. You learn exactly how that works in Shell Permissions. The ./ says "the file in this folder", because the shell does not look in the current folder for programs unless you tell it to.

Holberton script conventions

Projects usually ask for the shebang #!/bin/bash on the first line, a final newline at the end of the file, and nothing else on the first line. The VS Code settings from the VS Code tutorial add the final newline for you.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Permission denied when running a script

The file is not executable. Run chmod u+x filename, then try ./filename again.

command not found

Check the spelling first. If you are running your own script, add ./ in front of the name. If it is a program, it may not be installed: sudo apt install name usually fixes it.

No such file or directory

The path is wrong relative to where you are. Run pwd to see where you are and ls to see what is actually there. Remember that names are case sensitive: Holberton and holberton are different.

I am stuck inside a manual page

Press Q. The same works for less and most other full-screen viewers.

docs.title: Explain it to someone
docs.text:
The project asks you to explain each of these without looking anything up. Tick them off when you can.

  • What RTFM means, and how to open a manual page
  • What a shebang is, and why the first line of a script needs one
  • What the shell is, and how it differs from a terminal
  • What the prompt shows
  • How to reuse previous commands with the history
  • What cd, pwd and ls do
  • What . and .. are
  • What the working directory is, how to print it and how to change it
  • What the root directory is, and what the home directory is
  • The difference between / and /root
  • What makes a file hidden, and how to list hidden files
  • What cd - does

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command What it does pwd Print the working directory ls -la List everything here, hidden files included, in long format cd path Change to path cd or cd ~ Go to your home directory cd .. / cd - Up one level / back to the previous directory man command Read the manual for a command help builtin Read the help for a shell builtin such as cd type command Say whether a command is a builtin or a program history List recent commands echo $SHELL Show which shell you are using

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You can move around. Now learn who is allowed to do what.

Shell Permissions

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
30 min Tools Needs: WSL set up

VS Code is the editor you will use for every project in this program: Python, SQL, HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It installs on Windows and works inside Ubuntu, so you get a familiar window and a Linux machine underneath it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A good editor does a lot of quiet work. It catches typos before the Checker does, keeps your formatting consistent, and puts a terminal, Git and an AI assistant in the same window as your code. Set it up properly once and you stop thinking about it.

docs.title: The window at a glance
docs.text:
The five parts of the VS Code window 1, the activity bar down the far left. 2, the side bar with the file explorer. 3, the editor in the middle, where you write code. 4, the panel at the bottom with the terminal. 5, the status bar along the bottom edge, whose left corner shows WSL: Ubuntu when VS Code is connected to Linux. EXPLORER ▾ holberton hello.py README.md 1 print("Hello, Holberton") 2 TERMINAL you@laptop:~/holberton$ python3 hello.py Hello, Holberton WSL: Ubuntu main Ln 1, Col 1 Python 1 2 3 4 5
  1. Activity bar. Switches the side bar between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions and Copilot Chat.
  2. Side bar. Shows whatever the activity bar picked. Most of the time, the files in your project.
  3. Editor. Where you write code. You can split it to see two files at once.
  4. Panel. The terminal lives here. It is a real Ubuntu terminal, the same one you used in the WSL tutorial.
  5. Status bar. The bottom left corner must say WSL: Ubuntu. That label tells you your code runs on Linux. Check it whenever something behaves strangely.

docs.title: Step 1: Install VS Code on Windows
docs.text:
Download it from code.visualstudio.com and run the installer. Tick these boxes when offered:

  • Add "Open with Code" action to the file context menu
  • Add "Open with Code" action to the directory context menu
  • Add to PATH

The last one lets you type code . in a terminal to open the current folder. You will use it constantly.

Install VS Code on Windows only. Do not install it inside Ubuntu.

docs.title: Step 2: Install the WSL extension
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code and press Ctrl+Shift+X to open Extensions.
  2. Search for WSL, published by Microsoft, and click Install.

docs.title: Step 3: Open your projects folder from Ubuntu
docs.text:
Open the Ubuntu terminal and run:

cd ~/holberton
code .

The first time, Ubuntu downloads a small helper called the VS Code Server. Give it a minute. A VS Code window opens with your holberton folder in the Explorer.

Look at the bottom left corner. It should say WSL: Ubuntu. Open the terminal with Ctrl+` (the key above Tab). The prompt looks like this:

yourname@LAPTOP:~/holberton$

That is Linux. Everything you type there runs on Ubuntu.

docs.title: Step 4: Install extensions on the Linux side
docs.text:
Extensions install separately on each side. Having one on Windows does not mean it works in the WSL window.

Open Extensions with Ctrl+Shift+X in the WSL window and install these. Each one shows an Install in WSL: Ubuntu button.

Extension Publisher What it gives you Python Microsoft Highlighting, error hints and the Python interpreter ESLint Microsoft Flags JavaScript mistakes as you type

Later modules add a few more. Keep the list short: every extension slows the editor down a little.

docs.title: Step 5: Settings that keep the Checker happy
docs.text:
Holberton's style checkers reject lines longer than 79 characters, spaces at the end of a line, and files without a final newline. VS Code can handle all three for you.

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON), and add these lines inside the curly braces:

{
  "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
  "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "editor.rulers": [79],
  "editor.renderWhitespace": "trailing",
  "[python]": { "editor.tabSize": 4 },
  "[javascript]": { "editor.tabSize": 2 }
}

If the file already has settings, add the new lines among them and separate each line with a comma. Save with Ctrl+S.

The ruler draws a thin line at column 79. Keep your code to the left of it.

docs.title: Step 6: Run your first file
docs.text:
In the Explorer, click the new-file icon and create hello.py:

print("Hello, Holberton")

Run it in the terminal:

python3 hello.py

The output appears right below. The Checker runs your files from a terminal exactly like this, so get used to running them the same way rather than with a Run button.

AI in the loop

VS Code has GitHub Copilot built in. You switch it on in the next tutorial, together with a browser assistant and Clippy, and learn when to use which.

docs.title: Shortcuts worth knowing
docs.text: Keys What it does Ctrl+Shift+P Command palette. Everything VS Code can do is in here Ctrl+P Jump to a file by typing part of its name Ctrl+` Show or hide the terminal Ctrl+B Show or hide the side bar Ctrl+Shift+E File explorer Ctrl+/ Comment or uncomment the selected lines Alt+Up / Alt+Down Move the current line up or down Ctrl+D Select the next match of the selected word

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
code: command not found in Ubuntu

Close and reopen the Ubuntu terminal. If it still fails, reinstall VS Code on Windows and make sure Add to PATH is ticked, then restart the laptop.

The status bar does not say WSL: Ubuntu

You opened the folder from Windows. Close the window, open the Ubuntu terminal, and run cd ~/holberton && code . again.

An extension is installed but does nothing

It is installed on the Windows side only. Open Extensions in the WSL window and click Install in WSL: Ubuntu.

Everything is slow, and Git takes seconds

Your project is under /mnt/c. Move it into ~/holberton, as in the WSL tutorial.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. The bottom left corner says WSL: Ubuntu.
  2. In the VS Code terminal, pwd prints /home/yourname/holberton.
  3. python3 hello.py prints Hello, Holberton.
  4. Type a line longer than the ruler in hello.py. You can see where it crosses column 79.
  5. Add a few spaces at the end of a line and save. They disappear.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You have an editor running on Linux. Now bring in the assistants.

Set up your AI assistant

Official guide if you want more: Developing in WSL.

docs.title: WSL
docs.text:
35 min Tools Needs: Windows 10 (2004+) or 11, admin rights

WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, runs a real Ubuntu inside Windows. Every project in this program is written, run and checked on Linux, so this is where your code will live.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Almost every server, cloud machine and container you will deploy to runs Linux. Holberton projects are tested on Ubuntu too, so code that works on Windows can still fail the Checker because of a path, a line ending or a missing command.

WSL removes that gap. You keep the Windows you are used to for your browser, Slack and VS Code. Your code runs on Linux, and the two share files. This setup is required for the program.

On a Mac or Linux?

You do not need WSL. macOS and Linux already have a Unix terminal. Go straight to VS Code and use your normal terminal wherever these tutorials say Ubuntu terminal.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
Windows and Ubuntu side by side with WSL On the Windows side you have your apps, such as VS Code and the browser, and your Windows files. On the Ubuntu side, inside WSL, your code runs with Python, Node.js and Git, and your projects live in a folder in your Linux home. VS Code connects to Ubuntu through the WSL extension. Windows files are reachable from Ubuntu under slash mnt slash c. WINDOWS VS Code, browser, Slack what you look at and type in Your Windows files C:\Users\you\Documents UBUNTU, INSIDE WSL Python, Node.js, Git where the code actually runs Your projects ~/holberton WSL extension /mnt/c

One thing to hold on to: the window is Windows, the code is Linux.

docs.title: Step 1: Check your Windows
docs.text:
Press Win+R, type winver and press Enter. You need Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or later. If you are on an older version, run Windows Update first.

Then open Task Manager with Ctrl+Shift+Esc, go to Performance, then CPU, and find the line Virtualization. It should say Enabled. If it says disabled, see When something goes wrong before you continue.

docs.title: Step 2: Install WSL
docs.text:
Right-click the Start button and choose Terminal (Admin). On Windows 10 this may be called Windows PowerShell (Admin). Then run:

wsl --install

This turns on the Windows features WSL needs, downloads the Linux kernel and installs Ubuntu. It takes a few minutes. Restart when it asks.

docs.title: Step 3: Create your Linux user
docs.text:
After the restart, Ubuntu opens by itself and asks for a username and a password.

  • Username: lowercase, no spaces. It does not have to match your Windows name.
  • Password: pick one you will remember. You type it every time you run a command with sudo.

Linux shows nothing while you type a password, not even dots. That is normal. Type it and press Enter.

Check it worked. Back in the Windows terminal, run:

wsl --list --verbose

You want to see Ubuntu with version 2:

  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2

docs.title: Step 4: Update Ubuntu and install the basics
docs.text:
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. Everything from here on runs in the Ubuntu terminal, not in PowerShell.

Update the package lists and upgrade what is installed:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Then install the tools the first projects need:

sudo apt install -y build-essential git curl python3 python3-pip python3-venv

Check them:

python3 --version
git --version

You should see Python 3.10 or later, and any recent Git version.

AI in the loop

When an install fails, copy the full error message into Claude or ChatGPT and ask what it means and what each suggested fix does. Run a fix only once you understand what it changes. Pasting commands you do not understand into a terminal with sudo is how people break their setup.

docs.title: Step 5: Make your projects folder
docs.text:
This is the one WSL rule worth memorising.

Keep your projects in your Linux home folder. Files there live on the Linux filesystem and are fast. Files under /mnt/c live on the Windows filesystem, and every read crosses a bridge. Git and Python become noticeably slow, and file permissions behave strangely.

mkdir -p ~/holberton
cd ~/holberton
pwd

You should see /home/yourname/holberton. That is where every project in this program goes.

To look at the folder in Windows Explorer, run:

explorer.exe .

The dot means this folder. Explorer opens it under Linux in the sidebar.

Make Ubuntu your default terminal

In Windows Terminal, open Settings, set Default profile to Ubuntu and save. Every new terminal tab then opens straight into Linux.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
wsl --install fails, or Virtualization says disabled

Virtualisation is turned off in your BIOS. Restart, enter the BIOS setup (usually F2, F10 or Del while the laptop starts), and enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V, sometimes called SVM. Save, restart and run wsl --install again.

wsl --list --verbose shows version 1

Run wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2 in PowerShell and wait. It can take a few minutes. Then run wsl --set-default-version 2 so future installs use version 2.

Ubuntu opens and closes straight away

Run wsl --update in PowerShell, restart the laptop and open Ubuntu again.

I forgot my Linux password

In PowerShell, run wsl -u root to open Ubuntu as the administrator account. Then run passwd yourname, set a new password, and type exit.

Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock

Another update is running in the background. Wait a minute and run your apt command again.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. In PowerShell, wsl --list --verbose shows Ubuntu with version 2.
  2. In the Ubuntu terminal, cd ~/holberton && pwd prints /home/yourname/holberton, not a /mnt/c path.
  3. python3 --version prints 3.10 or later.
  4. git --version prints a version number.
  5. explorer.exe . opens your holberton folder in Windows Explorer.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command Where What it does wsl --install PowerShell (Admin) Installs WSL and Ubuntu wsl --list --verbose PowerShell Shows installed Linux versions wsl --update PowerShell Updates WSL itself sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y Ubuntu Updates Ubuntu's packages sudo apt install -y name Ubuntu Installs a package cd ~/holberton Ubuntu Goes to your projects folder explorer.exe . Ubuntu Opens the current folder in Windows Explorer

docs.text:
Linux is running. Now connect an editor to it.

Set up VS Code

Official guide if you want more: Install WSL.

docs.title: Zero Day
docs.text:
30 min Tools Needs: the email Holberton sent you

Before you write any code, you need your accounts working and you need to know how learning works here. This page covers both. Do it before your first day, not during it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Holberton works differently from a classroom. Nobody lectures you through the material, and nobody hands you the answer. If you start expecting that, the first weeks feel confusing. If you know the method, they feel fast.

The accounts matter for a plainer reason: they are how your work gets seen and checked. A broken login in week one turns into a missing submission in week two.

docs.title: How learning works at Holberton
docs.text:
You learn by building. Every concept arrives as a project with a deadline, and you work out how to solve it with your peers, the documentation and your AI tools. The project is the lesson. The Holberton Way page explains the method in full: who does what, and what to do when you are stuck.

The Holberton learning loop Four steps repeat for every project. Build: you write the code yourself. Check: the Checker tests it instantly. Review: peers read and question it. Explain: you justify every decision. Then the next project starts the loop again. 1 Build you write the code 2 Check the Checker tests it 3 Review peers question it 4 Explain you justify it next project

Build. You write the solution yourself. Searching, reading docs and asking for help are all part of the work; copying a finished answer is not.

Check. The Checker runs your code against the project's tests and tells you straight away what passes and what fails. Fix, push, check again.

Review. Your peers read your code and ask why it works the way it does. You do the same for them, and you learn as much from reading their solutions as from writing yours.

Explain. You should be able to justify every line you submit. That is the skill employers test in interviews, and it is the skill AI makes more valuable, not less.

docs.title: Your week
docs.text:
• Work every day

    A little every day beats a long weekend session. Projects have deadlines and build on each other, so falling behind compounds.

  • Peer learning days

    You work through problems with your cohort, review each other's code and explain your solutions out loud.

  • Mentor days

    Time with mentors to unblock hard problems, get feedback on your approach and prepare for interviews.

AI in the loop

AI is a collaborator here, not a shortcut. It drafts quickly, but it cannot check its own assumptions or take responsibility for the result. You can, and that is the job. On the intranet you also have Clippy, Holberton's own assistant. It helps you reason through a task step by step instead of giving you the code. You set up all of your assistants in the AI Assistant tutorial.

docs.title: The platforms
docs.text:
The platforms you need The intranet for projects, the Checker and Clippy. Slack for communication, with the same login as the intranet. GitHub for your code and portfolio, on your own separate account. Your laptop, running Ubuntu inside WSL, which you set up in the next tutorial. Intranet Projects, the Checker, Clippy, your scores intranet.hbtn.io Slack Questions, announcements, your cohort same login as the intranet GitHub Your code, and your public portfolio your own separate account Your laptop Ubuntu inside WSL, where your code runs next tutorial

The intranet and Slack share one login. GitHub is your own account, and it is the one that follows you after you finish the program.

docs.title: Step 1: Set up the intranet
docs.text:
Go to intranet.hbtn.io and log in with the credentials from your welcome email. Bookmark the page. You will open it every day.

Then finish your profile:

  1. Click your profile icon in the bottom left corner.
  2. Fill in every field marked with an asterisk.
  3. Add a photo. A plain head and shoulders shot is fine. This is the photo your mentors and future employers will see.
  4. Save.

Do not change your password yet

Slack reads your account from the intranet. Change the password now and you may lock yourself out of Slack before it has synced. Wait until everything on this page works.

docs.title: Step 2: Join Slack
docs.text:
Open the intranet and find the Slack link in the left navigation panel. Log in with the same credentials.

You are added to your cohort channel automatically. Install the desktop or phone app as well. The browser tab is easy to forget, and Slack is where schedule changes get announced.

docs.title: Step 3: Create your GitHub account
docs.text:
Already have one you use professionally? Use it and skip to Step 4.

Otherwise go to github.com/signup. Two choices matter here.

The email. Use one you will still read in five years. Not a work or school address that gets shut off when you leave.

The username. It becomes part of your professional identity and appears in every project link you send to an employer. Something close to your real name works well. Something you thought was funny at nineteen does not.

When you have it, go back to your intranet profile and add the username there. The Checker uses it to find your repositories, so a typo means your projects do not get checked.

docs.title: Step 4: Get your laptop ready
docs.text:
You write and run all your code on your own laptop, inside Ubuntu Linux. On Windows that means WSL, which is required for this program. You set it up in the next tutorial. Before then, check two things:

  • You can install software on the laptop. You need administrator rights.
  • Windows is up to date: Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or later.

On a Mac or Linux?

You already have a Unix terminal. Skip the WSL tutorial and go straight to VS Code.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Five minutes, and it proves everything works.

  1. Log in to the intranet and confirm your profile shows your photo and your GitHub username.
  2. Post a short hello in your cohort channel on Slack.
  3. Open your GitHub profile page and check the username reads the way you want an employer to read it.
  4. Open any project on the intranet and find Clippy.

If any of these fails, ask in Slack now. That is exactly what the channel is for.

docs.text: Platform Where What it is for Login Intranet intranet.hbtn.io Projects, deadlines, the Checker The one from your email Clippy Inside the intranet Reasoning through a task, step by step Same as intranet Slack Link inside the intranet Questions and announcements Same as intranet GitHub github.com Your code and portfolio Your own account

Programming in Python, from a first script to object-oriented design.

Stage 2 88 h 11 projects
