docs.title: Object-Oriented Design
docs.text:
Model problems with classes: bundle data with the rules that protect it, build families of related types, and describe your design with UML and design patterns. Five projects, one running example.

Foundations 40 h 5 projects Needs: Python Fundamentals

Tutorials published5 of 5

docs.title: One example, five projects
docs.text:
Every tutorial in this module builds on the same small digital wallet. You start with a single Account class and finish with a family of account types, a design you can draw in UML, and the patterns that keep it easy to change.

How the wallet grows across the module Version 1, Classes: the Account class: ready. Version 2, Inheritance: savings and checking accounts: ready. Version 3, Abstract classes: contracts and mixins: ready. Version 4, UML: drawing the design: ready. Version 5, Patterns: Factory, Observer and Decorator: ready. v1 · READY Classes Account v2 · READY Inheritance savings, checking v3 · READY Abstract contracts, mixins v4 · READY UML draw the design v5 · READY Patterns three patterns

Companion repository

The code for each stage is in evisp/oop-wallet, saved under a Git tag per tutorial: v1-classes, v2-inheritance, and so on. Write each version yourself first, then compare it with the tag.

docs.title: Build with objects
docs.text:
• 1 · Classes & Object Model

    Classes and instances, __init__, validation, properties and string representations.

    Ready 8 h

    Start

  • 2 · Inheritance & Polymorphism

    Subclasses that extend and override, and one method call that works across types.

    Ready 8 h

    Start

  • 3 · Abstract Classes & Interfaces

    Contracts with ABC, duck typing, extending built-ins, and mixins.

    Ready 8 h

    Start

docs.title: Design with objects
docs.text:
• 4 · Introduction to UML Modeling

    Draw the wallet as class diagrams: attributes, methods, inheritance, relationships, multiplicity, and sequence diagrams in Mermaid.

    Ready 8 h

    Start

  • 5 · Introduction to Design Patterns

    Reshape the wallet with three proven solutions: Factory, Observer and Decorator.

    Ready 8 h

    Start

AI in the loop

Object-oriented code is where assistants are most tempting: ask for a class and you get fifty tidy lines. Write your own design first, from the description in each tutorial, then ask an assistant to review it: what could put the object into an invalid state, which names are unclear, what would be hard to change. You learn design by making the decisions, not by reading someone else's.

docs.title: Abstract Classes & Interfaces
docs.text:
90 min Object-Oriented Design Needs: Inheritance & Polymorphism

Inheritance lets classes share code. This tutorial is about sharing promises: what every class of a kind must be able to do. You turn Account into an abstract contract, let gift cards pay alongside accounts, give the wallet a transaction log that behaves like a list, and add reusable behaviour with mixins. By the end, the wallet's design is something you could hand to another developer and they would know exactly what each class guarantees.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Version 2 works, but it relies on good behaviour. Nothing stops someone creating a plain Account, which has no real end-of-month rule, or adding a new account type and forgetting month_end. The mistake shows up much later, as a wrong balance.

Large codebases, frameworks and libraries all deal with this the same way: they define contracts that classes must fulfil, and check them as early as possible. Knowing how to read and write those contracts is what lets you plug your code into someone else's.

docs.title: Where we left off
docs.text:
How the wallet grows across the module Version 1, Classes: the Account class: done. Version 2, Inheritance: savings and checking accounts: done. Version 3, Abstract classes: contracts and mixins: this page. Version 4, UML: drawing the design: coming next. Version 5, Patterns: Factory, Observer and Decorator: coming next. v1 · DONE Classes Account v2 · DONE Inheritance savings, checking v3 · THIS PAGE Abstract contracts, mixins v4 UML draw the design v5 Patterns three patterns

Start from version 2, or the tag v2-inheritance: an Account base class with SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount below it. The wallet now has three new requirements:

  1. There is no such thing as a plain account. Every account type must define its own end-of-month rule.
  2. Customers can also pay with gift cards. A gift card has a code and a value, but it is not an account.
  3. Accounts and gift cards keep a history of every transaction, and can be exported as JSON for other systems.

This is where the design is heading:

The wallet design at version 3 Payer is an interface with one method, pay. Account is an abstract class that implements Payer and declares the abstract method month_end. GiftCard also implements Payer but is not an account. Both Account and GiftCard mix in HistoryMixin and JSONMixin. SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount inherit from Account and implement month_end. Every history is a TransactionLog, which extends the built-in list. «interface» Payer pay(amount) «abstract» Account month_end() abstract + HistoryMixin, JSONMixin GiftCard pay(amount) + HistoryMixin, JSONMixin implements implements SavingsAccount month_end() CheckingAccount month_end() TransactionLog extends list · every history is one history

Dashed outlines mark contracts, italic names mark abstract parts, and the hollow arrowheads point from a class to what it inherits from or implements. You will meet this notation properly in the UML project.

docs.title: Step 1: Abstract classes and @abstractmethod
docs.text:
An abstract class is a class that is not meant to be used on its own. It holds the code its subclasses share, and declares the methods each subclass must provide. Python's abc module provides the tools: inherit from ABC, and mark the required methods with @abstractmethod.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Account(ABC):
    """Abstract base for wallet accounts holding money, in whole lek."""

    # __init__, owner, balance, deposit, withdraw, __str__, __repr__
    # stay exactly as in version 2

    @abstractmethod
    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance."""

The body of month_end is now just a docstring. It says what the method must do, not how. Python then enforces the contract in two places.

You cannot create the abstract class itself:

Account("Ada", 500)
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Account without an
# implementation for abstract method 'month_end'

You cannot create a subclass that forgets the method:

class BusinessAccount(Account):
    pass


BusinessAccount("Acme", 10)
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class BusinessAccount without an
# implementation for abstract method 'month_end'

The error comes when the object is created, not when month_end is finally called at the end of the month. That is the whole point: the mistake surfaces at once, on the line that caused it.

SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount already define month_end, so they satisfy the contract and work unchanged. Define it in BusinessAccount and that works too:

class BusinessAccount(Account):
    def month_end(self):
        return self._balance


acme = BusinessAccount("Acme", 10)
acme.deposit(5)          # 15: deposit is inherited, as before

Notice what an abstract class is not: it is not empty. Account still contains all of its working code, deposit, withdraw, the properties and the string methods. An abstract class is a partly built class: shared code, plus clearly marked gaps that every subclass must fill.

In version 2, the plain Account.month_end did nothing. That was a hint. A method that "does nothing, override me" is a missing contract.

docs.title: Step 2: Interfaces
docs.text:
An abstract class that contains only abstract methods, and no code at all, describes pure capability: what an object can do, and nothing about how. Other languages call that an interface and have a keyword for it. Python models it with the same tool, an ABC.

Both accounts and gift cards can pay. That shared capability becomes an interface:

class Payer(ABC):
    """Interface: anything that can pay an amount."""

    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, or raise ValueError; return what is left."""

Account now implements Payer. Paying from an account means withdrawing, so pay simply calls withdraw:

class Account(Payer):
    ...

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from this account; return the new balance."""
        return self.withdraw(amount)

Because Payer inherits from ABC, Account is still abstract, with two methods in its contract: pay, which it implements, and month_end, which it leaves to its subclasses. Thanks to polymorphism, linus.pay(300) runs the checking version of withdraw, overdraft and all.

A GiftCard is not an account, so it must not inherit from Account. But it can pay, so it implements the same interface:

class GiftCard(Payer):
    """A prepaid card with a fixed value. It is not an account."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, code, value):
        """Create a gift card with a code and a starting value."""
        if not isinstance(code, str) or not code.strip():
            raise ValueError("code must be a non-empty string")
        _check_amount(value)
        self._code = code.strip()
        self._value = value

    @property
    def value(self):
        """What is left on the card."""
        return self._value

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from the card; return the value left."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._value:
            raise ValueError("not enough value on the card")
        self._value -= amount
        return self._value

docs.title: One change to version 2
docs.text:
Gift cards need the same amount check as accounts. In version 2 it was a method, Account._check_amount, which a gift card cannot reach. It now moves out of the class to a plain module-level function, _check_amount(amount), and every call to self._check_amount(amount) becomes _check_amount(amount). Shared code belongs where everyone who needs it can reach it, and a function does not force a gift card to pretend to be an account.

Now code that takes payments can accept any Payer:

def checkout(payer, amount):
    """Charge amount to anything that can pay; return what it returns."""
    return payer.pay(amount)


checkout(linus, 300)      # -300: a checking account, in its overdraft
checkout(card, 120)       # 180: what is left on the gift card
isinstance(card, Payer)   # True
isinstance(card, Account) # False

docs.title: Step 3: Duck typing
docs.text:
Look at checkout again. It never checks that payer is a Payer. It just calls pay. That works for any object that has a pay method, whether or not it inherits from Payer:

class FakePayer:
    """Records payments instead of making them. Useful in tests."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.paid = []

    def pay(self, amount):
        self.paid.append(amount)
        return 0


fake = FakePayer()
checkout(fake, 50)        # 0
fake.paid                 # [50]
isinstance(fake, Payer)   # False, and checkout did not care

This is duck typing, from the saying "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". Python cares what an object can do, not what it is. An object that cannot do it fails at the moment it is asked:

checkout("Ada", 50)
# AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'pay'
checkout works with anything that has a pay method checkout calls payer.pay. A CheckingAccount and a GiftCard both implement the Payer interface and pay. A FakePayer is not a Payer but has a pay method, so it pays too. A string has no pay method, so checkout fails with an AttributeError. checkout(payer, 50) payer.pay(50) CheckingAccount a Payer pays ✓ GiftCard a Payer pays ✓ FakePayer not a Payer, has pay() pays ✓ "Ada" no pay() AttributeError

docs.title: ABC or duck typing?
docs.text:
They are two answers to the same question, and Python uses both.

Formal interface (ABC) Duck typing A class opts in by inheriting from the interface having the right methods A missing method is caught when the object is created when the method is called Works with classes you did not write only if they inherit from it yes Best for your own families of classes, frameworks functions that accept "anything that can..."

The wallet uses both: Payer documents and enforces the contract for its own classes, and checkout stays open to anything that can pay, including test doubles like FakePayer.

typing.Protocol

Modern Python can also describe a duck type for tools such as type checkers and editors, with typing.Protocol. A protocol class lists the methods, like an interface, but classes do not need to inherit from it. You will meet it when you start using type hints.

docs.title: Step 4: Extend a built-in class
docs.text:
Every transaction should be recorded as a (kind, amount) tuple, such as ("deposit", 200). A plain list would accept anything, including "junk". Built-in types are classes too, so you can subclass list and keep everything it does, while adding your own checks and methods:

class TransactionLog(list):
    """A list that only accepts (kind, amount) transaction entries."""

    KINDS = ("deposit", "withdraw", "payment", "interest", "fee")

    def __init__(self, entries=()):
        super().__init__()
        self.extend(entries)

    def append(self, entry):
        """Add one entry, after checking it."""
        self._check(entry)
        super().append(entry)

    def extend(self, entries):
        """Add several entries; check them all before adding any."""
        entries = list(entries)
        for entry in entries:
            self._check(entry)
        super().extend(entries)

    def total(self, kind):
        """Return the sum of all amounts of one kind."""
        return sum(amount for k, amount in self if k == kind)

    def _check(self, entry):
        if not isinstance(entry, tuple) or len(entry) != 2:
            raise TypeError("entry must be a (kind, amount) tuple")
        kind, amount = entry
        if kind not in self.KINDS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown kind: {kind!r}")
        _check_amount(amount)

Preserve the built-in's behaviour. Each override does its extra work, then calls the real list method through super(). So a TransactionLog still is a list in every way that matters:

log = TransactionLog()
log.append(("deposit", 200))
log.append(("withdraw", 50))

log                      # [('deposit', 200), ('withdraw', 50)]
len(log)                 # 2
log[0]                   # ('deposit', 200)
for kind, amount in log: # iteration works
    ...
isinstance(log, list)    # True
log.total("deposit")     # 200: the one new method

And bad entries are refused:

log.append("junk")                          -> TypeError: entry must be a (kind, amount) tuple
log.append(("gift", 10))                    -> ValueError: unknown kind: 'gift'
log.append(("deposit", -5))                 -> ValueError: amount must be positive
log.extend([("fee", 100), ("deposit", 0)])  -> ValueError: amount must be positive

After that failed extend, the log is unchanged: neither entry was added, because extend checks everything before adding anything. An operation that fails halfway and leaves half its work done is one of the hardest bugs to track down.

The trap: list has many doors

list is written in C, and its methods do not call each other. So overriding append does not guard the other ways in. Even the constructor needed its own override above, because list([...]) never calls append. In this class, these still skip the checks:

log.insert(0, "junk")     # accepted
log += ["more junk"]      # accepted
log[0] = 42               # accepted

And slicing or + gives back a plain list, not a TransactionLog. Subclass a built-in when you want all of its behaviour plus a little more, and accept that you guard only the doors you override. When every change must be checked, hold a list inside your class instead of being one: that is the "has a" choice from the last tutorial.

The wallet is safe with this design because no outside code writes to a history directly. Accounts keep their log in _history, and the public history property hands out a copy.

docs.title: Step 5: Multiple inheritance and the MRO
docs.text:
A class can inherit from more than one parent. Python then needs a single, predictable order in which to look for methods. That order is the method resolution order, which you met in the last tutorial, and with several parents it matters more:

class GiftCard(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    ...


GiftCard.mro()
# [GiftCard, HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer, ABC, object]

Python builds this order by three rules: a class comes before its parents, parents keep the left-to-right order you wrote them in, and every class appears exactly once. That last rule matters when two parents share an ancestor, the so-called diamond: every class here eventually inherits from object, yet object appears once, at the end. If the rules cannot all be satisfied, Python refuses to create the class:

class Broken(ABC, Payer):    # ABC listed before its own subclass
    pass
# TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO)
# for bases ABC, Payer

Multiple inheritance between full, independent class hierarchies gets confusing fast. In practice it is used almost entirely for one job: mixins.

docs.title: Step 6: Mixins
docs.text:
A mixin is a small class that adds one piece of behaviour to any class that lists it as a parent. It is not meant to be used on its own, and it is not an "is a" relationship. A gift card is not a history; it has the history behaviour mixed in.

The wallet needs two pieces of behaviour that both accounts and gift cards share, and that have nothing to do with money rules: keeping a history, and turning into JSON.

class HistoryMixin:
    """Give a class a transaction history."""

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Add one entry to this object's history."""
        if "_history" not in vars(self):
            self._history = TransactionLog()
        self._history.append((kind, amount))

    @property
    def history(self):
        """A copy of the transaction history."""
        return TransactionLog(vars(self).get("_history", ()))


class JSONMixin:
    """Give a class a dictionary and JSON form of its simple attributes."""

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the type and simple attributes as a dictionary."""
        data = {"type": type(self).__name__}
        for name, value in vars(self).items():
            if isinstance(value, (str, int, float, bool)):
                data[name.lstrip("_")] = value
        return data

    def to_json(self):
        """Return to_dict() as a JSON string."""
        return json.dumps(self.to_dict())

Mix them in by listing them first, before the main base class:

class Account(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    ...


class GiftCard(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    ...

Then each method that moves money records it with one line, for example self._record("deposit", amount) in deposit, self._record("payment", amount) in GiftCard.pay, and self._record("fee", self.fee) when a checking account is charged. Notice the overrides from the last tutorial: CheckingAccount.withdraw replaces the parent's method entirely, so it must record the withdrawal itself. Keeping the parent's promises includes this one.

Both families now get both behaviours, written once:

linus.history       # [('withdraw', 300), ('fee', 100)]
grace.to_dict()     # {'type': 'SavingsAccount', 'owner': 'Grace', 'balance': 1020, 'rate': 2}
card.to_json()      # '{"type": "GiftCard", "code": "HB-2026", "value": 180}'

to_dict keeps only simple values, so the history log is left out, and strips the leading underscore, so _owner becomes owner.

Good mixins follow a few rules:

  • One job each. A mixin's name says what it adds: HistoryMixin, JSONMixin.
  • No __init__ of its own, if possible. HistoryMixin creates its log the first time it is needed, so it does not have to take part in the classes' constructors.
  • Mixins first, main base last, as in class GiftCard(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer). Python searches left to right, so the mixins' methods are found first and the main base class sits at the end.
  • Ask whether it is really shared. If only one class needs the behaviour, put it in that class.

docs.title: The code so far
docs.text:
This is version 3 of the wallet, tagged v3-abstract in the companion repository. It has grown, so read it top to bottom once: the helpers and mixins first, then the interface, the abstract Account with its two subclasses, the gift card, and checkout.

wallet.py · version 3 wallet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small digital wallet, built up across the OOP tutorials.

Version 3: Abstract Classes & Interfaces.
"""
import json
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


def _check_amount(amount):
    """Raise if amount is not a positive whole number."""
    if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
        raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")


class TransactionLog(list):
    """A list that only accepts (kind, amount) transaction entries."""

    KINDS = ("deposit", "withdraw", "payment", "interest", "fee")

    def __init__(self, entries=()):
        super().__init__()
        self.extend(entries)

    def append(self, entry):
        """Add one entry, after checking it."""
        self._check(entry)
        super().append(entry)

    def extend(self, entries):
        """Add several entries; check them all before adding any."""
        entries = list(entries)
        for entry in entries:
            self._check(entry)
        super().extend(entries)

    def total(self, kind):
        """Return the sum of all amounts of one kind."""
        return sum(amount for k, amount in self if k == kind)

    def _check(self, entry):
        if not isinstance(entry, tuple) or len(entry) != 2:
            raise TypeError("entry must be a (kind, amount) tuple")
        kind, amount = entry
        if kind not in self.KINDS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown kind: {kind!r}")
        _check_amount(amount)


class HistoryMixin:
    """Give a class a transaction history."""

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Add one entry to this object's history."""
        if "_history" not in vars(self):
            self._history = TransactionLog()
        self._history.append((kind, amount))

    @property
    def history(self):
        """A copy of the transaction history."""
        return TransactionLog(vars(self).get("_history", ()))


class JSONMixin:
    """Give a class a dictionary and JSON form of its simple attributes."""

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the type and simple attributes as a dictionary."""
        data = {"type": type(self).__name__}
        for name, value in vars(self).items():
            if isinstance(value, (str, int, float, bool)):
                data[name.lstrip("_")] = value
        return data

    def to_json(self):
        """Return to_dict() as a JSON string."""
        return json.dumps(self.to_dict())


class Payer(ABC):
    """Interface: anything that can pay an amount."""

    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, or raise ValueError; return what is left."""


class Account(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """Abstract base for wallet accounts holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        """Create an account for owner with an opening balance."""
        self.owner = owner
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self._balance = balance
        if balance:
            self._record("deposit", balance)

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        """Add amount to the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        self._balance += amount
        self._record("deposit", amount)
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount from the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from this account; return the new balance."""
        return self.withdraw(amount)

    @abstractmethod
    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance."""

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance})")


class SavingsAccount(Account):
    """An account that earns interest every month."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=1):
        """Create a savings account; rate is monthly interest in percent."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(rate, bool) or not isinstance(rate, int):
            raise TypeError("rate must be an integer")
        if not 0 <= rate <= 10:
            raise ValueError("rate must be between 0 and 10")
        self._rate = rate

    @property
    def rate(self):
        """Monthly interest rate, in whole percent."""
        return self._rate

    def add_interest(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the amount added."""
        interest = self._balance * self._rate // 100
        if interest > 0:
            self._balance += interest
            self._record("interest", interest)
        return interest

    def month_end(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the new balance."""
        self.add_interest()
        return self._balance

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, rate={self.rate})")


class CheckingAccount(Account):
    """An everyday account that may go below zero, up to a limit."""

    fee = 100

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft=0):
        """Create a checking account with an overdraft limit."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(overdraft, bool) or not isinstance(overdraft, int):
            raise TypeError("overdraft must be an integer")
        if overdraft < 0:
            raise ValueError("overdraft must not be negative")
        self._overdraft = overdraft

    @property
    def overdraft(self):
        """How far below zero the balance may go."""
        return self._overdraft

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount out, letting the balance go down to -overdraft."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if self._balance - amount < -self._overdraft:
            raise ValueError("overdraft limit exceeded")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def month_end(self):
        """Charge the monthly fee if overdrawn; return the new balance."""
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
            self._record("fee", self.fee)
        return self._balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{super().__str__()} (overdraft {self.overdraft})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, overdraft={self.overdraft})")


class GiftCard(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """A prepaid card with a fixed value. It is not an account."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, code, value):
        """Create a gift card with a code and a starting value."""
        if not isinstance(code, str) or not code.strip():
            raise ValueError("code must be a non-empty string")
        _check_amount(value)
        self._code = code.strip()
        self._value = value

    @property
    def value(self):
        """What is left on the card."""
        return self._value

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from the card; return the value left."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._value:
            raise ValueError("not enough value on the card")
        self._value -= amount
        self._record("payment", amount)
        return self._value

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Gift card {self._code}: {self.value} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"GiftCard(code={self._code!r}, value={self.value})"


def checkout(payer, amount):
    """Charge amount to anything that can pay; return what it returns."""
    return payer.pay(amount)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    grace = SavingsAccount("Grace", 1000, rate=2)
    linus = CheckingAccount("Linus", overdraft=500)
    card = GiftCard("HB-2026", 300)

    checkout(linus, 300)
    checkout(card, 120)
    for account in (grace, linus):
        account.month_end()

    for item in (grace, linus, card):
        print(item)
    print(linus.history)
    print(card.to_json())

./wallet.py

Grace: 1020 ALL
Linus: -400 ALL (overdraft 500)
Gift card HB-2026: 180 ALL
[('withdraw', 300), ('fee', 100)]
{"type": "GiftCard", "code": "HB-2026", "value": 180}

AI in the loop

Give an assistant the Payer interface and ask it to design, not write, a new payer: "Propose a Voucher class that fits this wallet. Should it implement Payer, inherit from Account or GiftCard, and which mixins should it use? Explain each choice." Compare its reasoning with the rules on this page. Then write the class yourself and run it through checkout.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... without an implementation for abstract method ...

You created an abstract class, or a subclass that does not define every abstract method. Add the method named in the message, with exactly that name. A typo such as month_End leaves the real one still missing.

My abstract class can be created, and it should not

The method is missing its @abstractmethod decorator, or the class does not inherit from ABC, directly or through a parent such as Payer.

AttributeError: '...' object has no attribute 'pay'

Duck typing at work: the object passed in cannot do what the function asks. Either pass an object that has the method, or check the caller.

TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO)

The parent classes are listed in an order Python cannot satisfy, usually a class placed before one of its own subclasses. Put mixins first and the main base class last.

My list subclass accepted something it should have refused

It came in through a door you did not override, such as insert, +=, item assignment or the constructor. Override that method too, or hold a list inside the class instead of subclassing it.

docs.text: Code What it does class Base(ABC): Make a class that can hold abstract methods @abstractmethod Require subclasses to define this method Class.__abstractmethods__ The abstract methods still missing class Thing(Interface): Implement an interface obj.method() with no type check Duck typing class Log(list): + super().append(x) Extend a built-in, keep its behaviour class C(MixinA, MixinB, Base): Mix behaviour in: mixins first, base last Class.mro() The order Python searches for methods

The wallet now has eight classes, two functions and several kinds of relationship between them. Next you learn to draw that design as a UML class diagram, so you can plan and discuss a design before writing it.

Introduction to UML Modeling

docs.title: Classes & Object Model
docs.text:
75 min Object-Oriented Design Needs: Exception Handling

Until now your data and the functions that work on it have lived apart: a balance in one variable, a deposit function somewhere else. A class puts them together. In this tutorial you build the first piece of a small digital wallet, an Account that holds money, refuses bad input and protects its own balance. The rest of the module keeps building on it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Programs model things: users, orders, accounts, bookings. Each thing has data (an account has an owner and a balance) and rules (the balance can never go below zero). Without classes, nothing stops some other part of the program from breaking those rules. With a class, the data and the rules travel together, and the object itself refuses to get into an invalid state.

Almost every framework you will use later, from web back-ends to the HBnB portfolio project, is built from classes. Reading and designing them is a core skill.

docs.title: Step 1: Design before you type
docs.text:
Start from a description of what the program must do, in plain words:

A customer has an account with a balance, in lek. They can deposit and withdraw money. The balance can never go below zero, and nobody may change it directly.

Read it and sort the words. Nouns that have their own data become classes and attributes. Verbs become methods. Rules become validation.

In the description Becomes In code account a class Account customer, balance attributes owner, balance deposit, withdraw methods deposit(), withdraw() never below zero a check that raises ValueError("insufficient funds") nobody changes it directly protected state a read-only balance

Five minutes on this table saves an hour of rewriting. You will draw the same design formally in the UML project.

docs.title: Step 2: Class and instance
docs.text:
A class is a blueprint: it describes what every account has and can do. An instance, or object, is one account built from that blueprint, with its own data.

One class, three instances The Account class lists the attributes every account has, owner and balance, the shared class attribute currency, and the methods deposit and withdraw. Three instances are built from it: ada with balance 600, linus with balance 0 and grace with balance 1200. Each instance has its own owner and balance, and all of them share the methods. CLASS · THE BLUEPRINT Account owner balance currency = "ALL" deposit(amount) withdraw(amount) data behaviour INSTANCES · ONE PER ACCOUNT ada owner='Ada' balance=600 linus owner='Linus' balance=0 grace owner='Grace' balance=1200 Account(...)

The smallest possible class has no body at all:

class Account:
    pass


ada = Account()
linus = Account()
print(type(ada))      # <class '__main__.Account'>
print(ada is linus)   # False: two separate objects

Calling the class, Account(), builds a new instance. ada and linus come from the same blueprint, but they are two separate objects. That is the whole idea: one class, as many instances as you need, each with its own state.

Class names use CapitalisedWords. Function, method and variable names stay in lower_case, as before.

docs.title: Step 3: __init__ and self
docs.text:
An empty account is not much use. Every account should start with an owner and a balance. The special method __init__ runs automatically each time an instance is created, and it sets up that instance's attributes:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance


ada = Account("Ada", 500)
linus = Account("Linus")
print(ada.owner, ada.balance)      # Ada 500
print(linus.owner, linus.balance)  # Linus 0

self is the instance being built. When you write Account("Ada", 500), Python creates an empty object, then calls __init__ with that object as self, "Ada" as owner and 500 as balance. self.owner = owner stores the name on that object, which is why ada and linus each keep their own.

You can see an instance's own attributes with vars:

vars(ada)    # {'owner': 'Ada', 'balance': 500}

__init__ is called the initialiser. It never returns a value; its only job is to put the new object into a sensible starting state.

docs.title: Step 4: Methods that work on the object's state
docs.text:
A method is a function defined inside a class. Its first parameter is always self, so it can read and change the instance it was called on.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance


ada = Account("Ada", 500)
ada.deposit(200)     # 700
ada.withdraw(100)    # 600

ada.deposit(200) is shorthand. Python turns it into Account.deposit(ada, 200): it looks up deposit on the class and passes ada in as self. Try both; they do exactly the same thing. That is the entire mystery of self: it is the object before the dot.

Notice that the methods return the new balance, as you learned in Functions & Modularity. They do not print. Whoever uses the class decides what to show.

docs.title: Step 5: Validate input when constructing objects
docs.text:
The class works, and it is already broken. Try these:

ada.withdraw(10_000)        # -9350: the balance is now negative
ada.deposit(-500)           # a "deposit" that removes money
bad = Account("", "lots")   # an account with no owner and a text balance
ada.balance = 1_000_000     # anyone can set any balance

Every line breaks a rule from the description in Step 1, and Python accepts all of them. The class must enforce its own rules. The approach is the one from Exception Handling: check the input and raise a specific exception.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        if not isinstance(owner, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not owner.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self.owner = owner.strip()
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self._check_amount(amount)
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        self._check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance

    def _check_amount(self, amount):
        if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
            raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")

Now the broken calls fail loudly and clearly:

Account("", 100)         -> ValueError: owner must not be empty
Account(42)              -> TypeError: owner must be a string
Account("Ada", -5)       -> ValueError: balance must not be negative
Account("Ada", "lots")   -> TypeError: balance must be an integer
ada.withdraw(10_000)     -> ValueError: insufficient funds
ada.deposit(-500)        -> ValueError: amount must be positive
ada.deposit(2.5)         -> TypeError: amount must be an integer

Three design points are worth noticing:

  • Validate in __init__. If the constructor checks everything, an invalid Account can never exist. Every other method can then trust the object's state.
  • One helper, used twice. deposit and withdraw both need the same amount check, so it lives in one method, _check_amount. The leading underscore says it is for the class's own use, not for callers. More on that in the next step.
  • Why the bool check? In Python, True passes isinstance(True, int), and True + 1 is 2. Without the extra check, ada.deposit(True) would quietly add 1 lek. The reason is that bool is a subclass of int, which is exactly what the next tutorial is about.

Amounts are whole numbers of lek on purpose. Floating-point numbers cannot store most decimal fractions exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3. Real financial software stores money as whole units for the same reason.

docs.title: Step 6: Control access to internal attributes
docs.text:
One line from Step 5 still works: ada.balance = 1_000_000. The validation in deposit and withdraw means nothing if anyone can write to balance directly. This is what encapsulation is about: the object keeps its data behind a small set of methods, and those methods are the only way in.

Outside code reaches internal state only through the public interface Outside code calls ada.deposit(200), which goes through the public deposit method, checks the amount, and updates the internal _balance. Reading ada.balance goes through a read-only property. Assigning ada.balance equals 0 is rejected at the interface with an AttributeError, because the property has no setter. OUTSIDE CODE PUBLIC INTERFACE INTERNAL STATE ada.deposit(200) ada.balance ada.balance = 0 deposit() checks the amount first balance read-only property no setter AttributeError _owner = 'Ada' _balance = 700 changed only by methods

Python has no truly private attributes. Instead it uses naming conventions, and one tool, the property, that lets you control exactly how an attribute is read and written.

docs.title: _name: "internal, please do not touch"
docs.text: A single leading underscore marks an attribute or method as internal. Python does not stop anyone from using it, but every Python developer reads it as "not part of the public interface; may change without warning". You already used it for _check_amount.

docs.title: __name: name mangling
docs.text:
Two leading underscores make Python rename the attribute behind the scenes, which is called name mangling:

class Card:
    def __init__(self, pin):
        self.__pin = pin


card = Card(1234)
card.__pin           # AttributeError: 'Card' object has no attribute '__pin'
vars(card)           # {'_Card__pin': 1234}
card._Card__pin      # 1234

__pin was stored as _Card__pin. That protects it from accidental clashes, especially in subclasses, but it is not security: anyone who knows the rule can still reach it. In this wallet we use a single underscore, because the account types you build in the next tutorial will need to work with the balance too.

docs.title: @property: control reading and writing
docs.text:
A property looks like an attribute from outside, but runs a method when it is read or written. Store the real value in _balance, and expose a balance property with only a getter:

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

Reading works exactly as before, and writing is now refused:

ada.balance               # 700
ada.balance = 1_000_000   # AttributeError: property 'balance' of 'Account' object has no setter

For owner, renaming should be allowed but still validated. A property can have a setter as well, which runs on every assignment:

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

ada.owner = "  Ada Lovelace "   # stored as 'Ada Lovelace'
ada.owner = ""                  # ValueError: owner must not be empty

Here is the neat part: inside __init__, write self.owner = owner. That assignment goes through the setter too, so the owner checks live in one place and run both when the account is created and whenever it is renamed later.

docs.title: Step 7: String representations
docs.text:
Print an object with no string methods and you get its type and memory address, which tells you nothing:

print(ada)    # <__main__.Account object at 0x7f3ed9336cf0>

Two special methods fix this, each for a different reader:

  • __str__ is for people. print() and str() use it.
  • __repr__ is for developers. The interpreter, debuggers, and lists of objects use it. A good __repr__ looks like the code that would rebuild the object.
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Account(owner={self.owner!r}, balance={self.balance})"

print(ada)          # Ada: 600 ALL
repr(ada)           # "Account(owner='Ada', balance=600)"
print([ada, linus]) # [Account(owner='Ada', balance=600), Account(owner='Linus', balance=0)]
f"{ada} | {ada!r}"  # 'Ada: 600 ALL | Account(owner='Ada', balance=600)'

Notice the list: printing a list shows its items with __repr__, not __str__. If you only write one of the two, write __repr__; Python falls back to it when there is no __str__.

Both methods return a string. Neither prints.

docs.title: Step 8: Class attributes
docs.text:
Some data belongs to the class, not to any one account. Every account in this wallet uses the same currency, so it is defined once, directly in the class body:

class Account:
    """A wallet account holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

Account.currency            # 'ALL'
ada.currency                # 'ALL': found on the class
"currency" in vars(ada)     # False: ada does not store its own copy

When you read ada.currency, Python looks on the instance first, and then on the class. Change the class attribute and every instance sees the change. But assigning ada.currency = "USD" does not change the class: it creates a new attribute on ada alone, which then hides the class one. Use class attributes for values that really are shared, such as constants, and change them only through the class.

docs.title: The code so far
docs.text:
This is version 1 of the wallet. It is also tagged v1-classes in the companion repository.

wallet.py · version 1 wallet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small digital wallet, built up across the OOP tutorials.

Version 1: Classes & Object Model.
"""


class Account:
    """A wallet account holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        """Create an account for owner with an opening balance."""
        self.owner = owner
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self._balance = balance

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        """Add amount to the balance and return the new balance."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        self._balance += amount
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount from the balance and return the new balance."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount
        return self._balance

    def _check_amount(self, amount):
        """Raise if amount is not a positive whole number."""
        if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
            raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Account(owner={self.owner!r}, balance={self.balance})"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ada = Account("Ada", 500)
    ada.deposit(200)
    ada.withdraw(100)
    print(ada)
    print(repr(ada))

./wallet.py

Ada: 600 ALL
Account(owner='Ada', balance=600)

The file passes pycodestyle, and the demo runs only under if __name__ == "__main__":, so other files can import Account without printing anything.

AI in the loop

Paste your class into an assistant and ask it to attack it: "Find inputs or sequences of calls that put this Account into an invalid state. Don't fix anything, just list them." Then decide for each one whether your class should prevent it, and fix it yourself. Thinking like someone trying to break your object is the fastest way to learn what encapsulation is for.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
TypeError: Account.__init__() takes from 2 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

Python counts self as one of the arguments. Check the number of values you pass matches the parameters after self.

TypeError: Account.deposit() missing 1 required positional argument: 'amount'

Usually you called the method on the class, Account.deposit(200), instead of on an instance, ada.deposit(200). Or you forgot self as the first parameter of the method.

NameError: name '_balance' is not defined inside a method

Attributes always need self. in front: self._balance, not _balance.

RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded in a property

The property stores its value under its own name, for example self.owner = value inside the owner setter, so the setter calls itself forever. Store it under the underscore name: self._owner.

AttributeError: property 'balance' of 'Account' object has no setter

That is the class working as designed. Change the balance through deposit and withdraw.

docs.title: Introduction to Design Patterns
docs.text:
90 min Object-Oriented Design Needs: Introduction to UML Modeling

Some design problems come up in almost every program: creating the right object without knowing its class in advance, telling other parts of the system that something happened, adding optional features without a new subclass for every combination. Developers solved them long ago and gave the solutions names. Those are design patterns. In this last tutorial of the module you apply three of them to the wallet: Factory, Observer and Decorator.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A pattern is two things at once. It is a proven solution, so you do not have to invent one under deadline pressure. And it is a shared word: saying "the accounts publish events, the SMS service is an observer" explains a whole design in one sentence to anyone who knows the pattern.

You will meet these three everywhere. Web frameworks create objects through factories and registries. User interfaces, message queues and webhooks are observers. Python's own io module stacks decorators around files. Recognising the shape saves you hours reading someone else's code.
