Start from version 4, or the tag v4-uml: a customer with accounts and gift cards, a class diagram and two sequence diagrams. The wallet is now in use, and three requests have arrived:

  1. New account types keep being added, and accounts are created in many places: when a customer signs up, when data is imported from another system, in tests. Adding a type must not mean editing all of them.
  2. Other parts of the system need to react to transactions. An audit log must record everything, and customers can ask for a text message when they are charged a fee. Accounts must not need to know who is listening.
  3. Payments can get optional extras, in any combination: a spending limit, receipts, and rounding each payment up into savings.

Each request is the classic problem of one pattern.

docs.title: Step 1: What a design pattern is
docs.text:
A design pattern is a named, reusable strategy for a design problem that keeps coming back. The idea was popularised in 1994 by the book Design Patterns, written by four authors known ever since as the Gang of Four, which catalogued 23 of them.

The important word is strategy. A pattern is not code you copy. It describes roles and how they collaborate, and you write it fresh each time, shaped to your program. Every pattern description has the same four parts:

  • a name, so people can talk about it;
  • the problem it solves, and the signs that you have that problem;
  • the solution: the classes involved and what each one does;
  • the consequences: what you gain, and what it costs.

Patterns are grouped by the kind of problem they solve.

The three families of design patterns Creational patterns are about how objects are created: Factory, covered on this page, Builder and Singleton. Structural patterns are about how objects are combined: Decorator, covered on this page, Adapter and Facade. Behavioural patterns are about how objects communicate: Observer, covered on this page, Strategy and Command. Creational Structural Behavioural how objects are created how objects are combined how objects communicate Factory · this page Builder Singleton Decorator · this page Adapter Facade Observer · this page Strategy Command Family The question it answers Pattern on this page The problem it solves Creational How do I create objects without tying my code to their classes? Factory Code everywhere that names concrete classes to create them Structural How do I combine objects into bigger ones? Decorator Optional features that would need a subclass per combination Behavioural How do objects share work and tell each other things? Observer One object that must inform others it should not depend on

docs.title: The problem: creation scattered everywhere
docs.text:
Without a factory, every place that creates accounts must know every account class, and how to choose between them:

# in the sign-up code
if kind == "savings":
    account = SavingsAccount(name, rate=rate)
elif kind == "checking":
    account = CheckingAccount(name, overdraft=overdraft)
else:
    raise ValueError(f"unknown account kind: {kind!r}")

# in the import code: the same chain again
# in the tests: the same chain again

This is coupling: the sign-up code, the import code and the tests all depend directly on SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount. Add a business account and you must find and edit every chain. Miss one and that part of the program cannot create the new type.

docs.title: The solution: one place that knows the classes
docs.text:
A factory is an object whose job is to create other objects. The version here keeps a registry: a dictionary from a kind, such as "savings", to the class that creates it.

class AccountFactory:
    """Create accounts by kind, from a registry of account classes."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._registry = {}

    def register(self, kind, account_class):
        """Make kind create account_class, and return account_class."""
        if not isinstance(kind, str) or not kind.strip():
            raise ValueError("kind must be a non-empty string")
        if not (isinstance(account_class, type)
                and issubclass(account_class, Account)):
            raise TypeError("account_class must be a subclass of Account")
        self._registry[kind] = account_class
        return account_class

    def create(self, kind, owner, **options):
        """Create an account of a registered kind."""
        if kind not in self._registry:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown account kind: {kind!r}")
        return self._registry[kind](owner, **options)

    def kinds(self):
        """The registered kinds, sorted."""
        return sorted(self._registry)


account_factory = AccountFactory()
account_factory.register("savings", SavingsAccount)
account_factory.register("checking", CheckingAccount)

Two details make this work. Classes are objects in Python, so they can be stored in a dictionary as values and called later: self._registry[kind] is SavingsAccount, and adding (owner, **options) calls it. And **options passes any keyword arguments straight through, so the factory does not need to know which options each class takes.

Every caller now goes through one door. The customer gets a method for it:

    def open_account(self, kind, **options):
        """Open a new account of a registered kind, and return it."""
        account = account_factory.create(kind, self._name, **options)
        return self.add_account(account)

ada = Customer("Ada", "ada@example.com")
ada.open_account("savings", balance=1000, rate=2)
ada.open_account("checking", overdraft=500)
Before and after a factory Before: sign-up, import and tests each create SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount directly, giving six tangled dependencies. After: the three callers depend only on the factory, whose registry maps savings, checking and the newly added business kind to their classes. BEFORE · EVERY CALLER KNOWS EVERY CLASS AFTER · CALLERS KNOW ONE FACTORY sign-up import tests SavingsAccount CheckingAccount sign-up import tests account_factory registry "savings" "checking" "business" new

docs.title: Extend the registry without touching the creation logic
docs.text:
Now a business account arrives. It is a checking account with a higher fee. Write the class, register it, and use it:

class BusinessAccount(CheckingAccount):
    """A checking account for companies, with a higher monthly fee."""

    fee = 250


account_factory.register("business", BusinessAccount)

acme = Customer("Acme", "hello@acme.example")
acme.open_account("business", overdraft=2000)
# BusinessAccount(owner='Acme', balance=0, overdraft=2000)
account_factory.kinds()
# ['business', 'checking', 'savings']

create did not change, and neither did open_account, the import code or the tests. They all create business accounts already. This is the open/closed principle: a design should be open to extension, by adding a class and a registration, but closed to modification of code that already works.

The factory also makes it natural to create objects from data, where the kind is just a string, for example in a record read from a JSON file:

record = {"kind": "savings", "owner": "Ada", "balance": 500, "rate": 2}
account_factory.create(**record)
# SavingsAccount(owner='Ada', balance=500, rate=2)

And mistakes fail early, with clear messages:

account_factory.create("crypto", "Ada")      -> ValueError: unknown account kind: 'crypto'
account_factory.register("gift", GiftCard)   -> TypeError: account_class must be a subclass of Account

Consequences. The registry gives you one place to see every kind, and new types plug in without edits. The cost: kinds are strings, so a typo is only found when the code runs, and account_factory is shared state that every part of the program can change.

Factory Method

The Gang of Four describe a related pattern, Factory Method, in which subclasses decide which class to create by overriding a method. The registry version here is the one you will meet most in Python code. Both share the same goal: callers ask for a kind of object, not a specific class.

docs.title: The problem: an object that knows too much
docs.text:
The obvious way to add the audit log and the SMS alerts is to call them from the account:

    def month_end(self):
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
            audit_log.write(...)     # the account now depends on the audit log
            sms_service.send(...)    # ...and on the SMS service

Now CheckingAccount depends on two services it has nothing to do with. Every new listener means editing every account class, and you cannot test an account without an audit log and an SMS service present.

docs.title: The solution: publish events, let others subscribe
docs.text:
The Observer pattern has two roles. A subject publishes events. Observers subscribe to the subject, and are notified when events happen. The subject keeps a list of observers and calls one method on each, without knowing what they are.

In the wallet, the subject role is a mixin, since both accounts and gift cards play it. Events have a topic, which is the transaction kind, so observers can ask for only the topics they care about:

class ObservableMixin:
    """Let observers subscribe to this object's events, by topic."""

    def subscribe(self, observer, topics=None):
        """Send observer the events in topics, or every event if None."""
        if not callable(getattr(observer, "notify", None)):
            raise TypeError("observer must have a notify method")
        if isinstance(topics, str):
            topics = [topics]
        wanted = None if topics is None else frozenset(topics)
        if "_observers" not in vars(self):
            self._observers = []
        self._observers.append((observer, wanted))

    def unsubscribe(self, observer):
        """Stop sending events to observer."""
        observers = vars(self).get("_observers", [])
        observers[:] = [(o, t) for o, t in observers if o is not observer]

    def _publish(self, topic, amount):
        """Notify every observer that wants this topic."""
        for observer, wanted in list(vars(self).get("_observers", ())):
            if wanted is None or topic in wanted:
                observer.notify(self, topic, amount)

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Record the transaction, then publish it as an event."""
        super()._record(kind, amount)
        self._publish(kind, amount)

The subject relies on duck typing: an observer is anything with a notify(source, topic, amount) method. That is how it publishes events "without knowing the concrete type of every listener". It never imports, names or checks for AuditLog or SMSAlert.

The clever part is the last method. Accounts already call self._record(...) for every transaction. ObservableMixin overrides _record, lets the real one run through super(), then publishes. Put it first in the list of parents:

class Account(ObservableMixin, HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    ...

Account.mro()
# [Account, ObservableMixin, HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer, ABC, object]

super() inside ObservableMixin follows the MRO to the next class, HistoryMixin, not to ObservableMixin's own parent. This is the method resolution order from Abstract Classes doing real work: every account and gift card now publishes events, and not a single method in them changed.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
An observer is a small class with a notify method:

class AuditLog:
    """Observer: keep one line for every event it is sent."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.lines = []

    def notify(self, source, topic, amount):
        """Record the event."""
        self.lines.append(f"{type(source).__name__} {topic} {amount}")

To add a new observer and configure it for specific topics, write the class and pass topics when subscribing. The SMS alert only cares about fees:

class SMSAlert:
    """Observer: text a phone number about the events it is sent."""

    def __init__(self, phone):
        self.phone = phone
        self.sent = []

    def notify(self, source, topic, amount):
        """Send a short message about the event."""
        self.sent.append(f"To {self.phone}: {topic} of {amount} ALL")

checking = CheckingAccount("Ada", overdraft=500)
audit = AuditLog()
sms = SMSAlert("+355 69 000 0000")
checking.subscribe(audit)                  # every topic
checking.subscribe(sms, topics=["fee"])    # fees only

checking.withdraw(300)
checking.month_end()
checking.deposit(50)

audit.lines   # ['CheckingAccount withdraw 300', 'CheckingAccount fee 100', 'CheckingAccount deposit 50']
sms.sent      # ['To +355 69 000 0000: fee of 100 ALL']
One event, filtered by topic The checking account publishes a fee event of 100 lek. The audit log subscribed to every topic, so it is notified. The SMS alert subscribed to the fee topic, so it is notified. A second SMS alert that subscribed only to deposit is not notified. SUBJECT checking publishes every transaction "fee", 100 audit: AuditLog topics: all · notified sms: SMSAlert topics: fee · notified another SMSAlert topics: deposit · skipped ×

In a sequence diagram, a subject notifying its observers looks like this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as ada: Customer
    participant K as checking: CheckingAccount
    participant A as audit: AuditLog
    participant S as sms: SMSAlert
    C->>K: month_end()
    K->>K: _record("fee", 100)
    K->>K: _publish("fee", 100)
    K->>A: notify(checking, "fee", 100)
    K->>S: notify(checking, "fee", 100)
    K-->>C: -400

Consequences. Subjects and observers can change independently, and new listeners need no changes to existing classes. The costs: the flow of the program is harder to follow, because "who reacts to a fee?" is answered at run time, not in the code; observers run in the order they subscribed; an observer that raises an exception stops the ones after it; and an observer you forget to unsubscribe stays alive as long as the subject does.

docs.title: Step 4: Decorator
docs.text:
Not Python's @decorator

Python has a feature also called a decorator, the @name line above a function, which you met as @property and @abstractmethod. The Decorator pattern is a different, older idea: wrapping one object in another to add behaviour. They share a name because both "wrap" something, but they work differently.

docs.title: The problem: subclass explosion
docs.text:
Payments can have a spending limit, receipts and round-up savings, in any combination, on any kind of payer. With inheritance, each combination is a subclass:

Subclasses for every combination compared with stacked decorators With subclasses, every combination of features and payer type needs its own class, such as LimitedCheckingAccount, ReceiptCheckingAccount and LimitedReceiptRoundUpGiftCard, and the number keeps growing. With decorators, three small wrappers are stacked around any payer: RoundUp around Receipts around SpendingLimit around the checking account. A payment enters at the outer layer and passes inwards. WITH SUBCLASSES · ONE PER COMBINATION WITH DECORATORS · STACK WHAT YOU NEED LimitedCheckingAccount ReceiptCheckingAccount LimitedReceiptCheckingAccount RoundUpSavingsAccount LimitedRoundUpGiftCard LimitedReceiptRoundUpGiftCard 3 features × 3 payer types: up to 21 classes and every new feature doubles the count checkout(payer, 230) RoundUp saves the 70 lek spare Receipts writes a receipt SpendingLimit refuses over 500 checking the real payer

Three features on three kinds of payer is already up to 21 classes, and each new feature roughly doubles it. Worse, you cannot add a feature to an object that already exists: its class is fixed when it is created.

docs.title: The solution: wrap the object
docs.text:
A decorator is an object that has the same interface as the object it wraps. It adds its own behaviour, then passes the call on. Because the decorator is a Payer too, decorators can wrap each other, in any order and any number. This is composition, the "has a" from Inheritance & Polymorphism: each decorator has a payer inside it.

classDiagram
    class Payer {
        <<interface>>
        +pay(amount: int)* int
    }
    class PayerDecorator {
        #_wrapped: Payer
        +pay(amount: int) int
    }
    class SpendingLimit {
        #_limit: int
        +pay(amount: int) int
    }
    class Receipts {
        +receipts: list
        +pay(amount: int) int
    }
    class RoundUp {
        #_savings: Account
        +pay(amount: int) int
    }
    Payer <|.. Account
    Payer <|.. GiftCard
    Payer <|.. PayerDecorator
    PayerDecorator o-- "1" Payer : wraps
    PayerDecorator <|-- SpendingLimit
    PayerDecorator <|-- Receipts
    PayerDecorator <|-- RoundUp

Read the two lines between PayerDecorator and Payer together: a decorator implements Payer and wraps a Payer. That pair of lines is the signature of the pattern in any class diagram.

Start with a base class that only passes things on:

class PayerDecorator(Payer):
    """Wrap a payer to add behaviour to pay; forward everything else."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped):
        if not callable(getattr(wrapped, "pay", None)):
            raise TypeError("wrapped must have a pay method")
        self._wrapped = wrapped

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pass the payment on to the wrapped payer."""
        return self._wrapped.pay(amount)

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return getattr(self._wrapped, name)

    def __str__(self):
        return str(self._wrapped)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{type(self).__name__}({self._wrapped!r})"

__getattr__ is a special method Python calls only when normal lookup fails. Here it forwards anything the decorator does not have to the wrapped object, so payer.balance and payer.owner still work. Special methods such as __str__ are the exception: Python looks them up on the class directly, never through __getattr__, which is why __str__ is forwarded by hand. Without it, print(payer) would show <PayerDecorator object at 0x...>.

Each feature is now one small decorator that overrides pay:

class SpendingLimit(PayerDecorator):
    """Refuse any single payment above a limit."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped, limit):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        _check_amount(limit)
        self._limit = limit

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, unless it is over the limit."""
        if amount > self._limit:
            raise ValueError(f"payment over the limit of {self._limit}")
        return super().pay(amount)


class Receipts(PayerDecorator):
    """Keep a receipt for every payment that goes through."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        self.receipts = []

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, then write a receipt."""
        result = super().pay(amount)
        self.receipts.append(f"Paid {amount} ALL")
        return result

super().pay(amount) hands the payment to PayerDecorator.pay, which passes it to the wrapped object. A limit check happens before passing it on; a receipt is written after, so only payments that succeed get one.

docs.title: Add a new decorator that composes with the others
docs.text:
Round-up savings is the third feature: every payment is rounded up to the next 100 lek, and the difference goes into a savings account. Write it as a new decorator, without changing any existing class:

class RoundUp(PayerDecorator):
    """Round each payment up to the next 100 and save the difference."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped, savings):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        if not isinstance(savings, Account):
            raise TypeError("savings must be an Account")
        self._savings = savings

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, then move the round-up into savings if possible."""
        result = super().pay(amount)
        spare = -amount % 100
        if spare:
            try:
                result = super().pay(spare)
            except ValueError:
                return result
            self._savings.deposit(spare)
        return result

-amount % 100 is the distance to the next multiple of 100: for 230 it is 70. The round-up is a bonus, so if the payer cannot afford the extra 70, the original payment still stands and nothing is saved.

Now stack all three:

savings = SavingsAccount("Ada", 1000, rate=2)
checking = CheckingAccount("Ada", overdraft=500)

payer = RoundUp(Receipts(SpendingLimit(checking, limit=500)), savings)
checkout(payer, 230)

checking.balance   # -300: 230 paid, plus 70 rounded up
savings.balance    # 1070
payer.receipts     # ['Paid 230 ALL', 'Paid 70 ALL']
repr(payer)        # "RoundUp(Receipts(SpendingLimit(CheckingAccount(owner='Ada', balance=-300, overdraft=500))))"

checkout did not change: it still just calls pay. payer.receipts works even though RoundUp has no receipts, because __getattr__ passes the lookup inward to Receipts. And the same decorators wrap a gift card just as well: RoundUp(card, savings) works, because a card is a Payer too.

Order matters. The outermost decorator runs first. Move RoundUp inside the others and the result changes:

payer = Receipts(SpendingLimit(RoundUp(checking, savings), limit=500))
checkout(payer, 230)
payer.receipts     # ['Paid 230 ALL']

The same 300 lek leaves the account, but now the receipts only see the outer call, the 230. Neither order is wrong. They mean different things, and choosing the order is part of the design: here, should the limit and the receipts include the round-up or not?

Consequences. Features combine freely, at run time, and each one is a small class that is easy to test. The costs: a decorated payer is not the same object as the one inside it, so isinstance(payer, Account) is False and you cannot add it to a customer's accounts; and a deep stack of wrappers can be harder to debug than one class. That is why __repr__ shows the whole stack.

docs.title: Step 5: Use patterns, don't collect them
docs.text:
Patterns are tools for problems you already have. Adding one "just in case" makes code bigger and harder to follow, for no benefit.

You notice Consider The same if kind == ... creation chain in several places Factory An object that calls services it should not know about, to tell them something happened Observer Subclasses whose names list features: LimitedReceiptRoundUp... Decorator One object that must work with an interface it does not match Adapter A family of interchangeable algorithms chosen at run time Strategy

If you cannot point to the problem in the left column, you do not need the pattern yet.

docs.title: The code so far
docs.text:
This is version 5 of the wallet, tagged v5-patterns. The changes from version 4 are ObservableMixin, AccountFactory with Customer.open_account, the decorators, the two observers, and the demo.

wallet.py · version 5 wallet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small digital wallet, built up across the OOP tutorials.

Version 5: Introduction to Design Patterns.
"""
import json
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


def _check_amount(amount):
    """Raise if amount is not a positive whole number."""
    if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
        raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")


class TransactionLog(list):
    """A list that only accepts (kind, amount) transaction entries."""

    KINDS = ("deposit", "withdraw", "payment", "interest", "fee")

    def __init__(self, entries=()):
        super().__init__()
        self.extend(entries)

    def append(self, entry):
        """Add one entry, after checking it."""
        self._check(entry)
        super().append(entry)

    def extend(self, entries):
        """Add several entries; check them all before adding any."""
        entries = list(entries)
        for entry in entries:
            self._check(entry)
        super().extend(entries)

    def total(self, kind):
        """Return the sum of all amounts of one kind."""
        return sum(amount for k, amount in self if k == kind)

    def _check(self, entry):
        if not isinstance(entry, tuple) or len(entry) != 2:
            raise TypeError("entry must be a (kind, amount) tuple")
        kind, amount = entry
        if kind not in self.KINDS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown kind: {kind!r}")
        _check_amount(amount)


class HistoryMixin:
    """Give a class a transaction history."""

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Add one entry to this object's history."""
        if "_history" not in vars(self):
            self._history = TransactionLog()
        self._history.append((kind, amount))

    @property
    def history(self):
        """A copy of the transaction history."""
        return TransactionLog(vars(self).get("_history", ()))


class JSONMixin:
    """Give a class a dictionary and JSON form of its simple attributes."""

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the type and simple attributes as a dictionary."""
        data = {"type": type(self).__name__}
        for name, value in vars(self).items():
            if isinstance(value, (str, int, float, bool)):
                data[name.lstrip("_")] = value
        return data

    def to_json(self):
        """Return to_dict() as a JSON string."""
        return json.dumps(self.to_dict())


class ObservableMixin:
    """Let observers subscribe to this object's events, by topic.

    Every recorded transaction is published as an event whose topic is
    its kind: "deposit", "withdraw", "payment", "interest" or "fee".
    """

    def subscribe(self, observer, topics=None):
        """Send observer the events in topics, or every event if None."""
        if not callable(getattr(observer, "notify", None)):
            raise TypeError("observer must have a notify method")
        if isinstance(topics, str):
            topics = [topics]
        wanted = None if topics is None else frozenset(topics)
        if "_observers" not in vars(self):
            self._observers = []
        self._observers.append((observer, wanted))

    def unsubscribe(self, observer):
        """Stop sending events to observer."""
        observers = vars(self).get("_observers", [])
        observers[:] = [(o, t) for o, t in observers if o is not observer]

    def _publish(self, topic, amount):
        """Notify every observer that wants this topic."""
        for observer, wanted in list(vars(self).get("_observers", ())):
            if wanted is None or topic in wanted:
                observer.notify(self, topic, amount)

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Record the transaction, then publish it as an event."""
        super()._record(kind, amount)
        self._publish(kind, amount)


class Payer(ABC):
    """Interface: anything that can pay an amount."""

    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, or raise ValueError; return what is left."""


class Account(ObservableMixin, HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """Abstract base for wallet accounts holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        """Create an account for owner with an opening balance."""
        self.owner = owner
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self._balance = balance
        if balance:
            self._record("deposit", balance)

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        """Add amount to the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        self._balance += amount
        self._record("deposit", amount)
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount from the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from this account; return the new balance."""
        return self.withdraw(amount)

    @abstractmethod
    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance."""

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance})")


class SavingsAccount(Account):
    """An account that earns interest every month."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=1):
        """Create a savings account; rate is monthly interest in percent."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(rate, bool) or not isinstance(rate, int):
            raise TypeError("rate must be an integer")
        if not 0 <= rate <= 10:
            raise ValueError("rate must be between 0 and 10")
        self._rate = rate

    @property
    def rate(self):
        """Monthly interest rate, in whole percent."""
        return self._rate

    def add_interest(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the amount added."""
        interest = self._balance * self._rate // 100
        if interest > 0:
            self._balance += interest
            self._record("interest", interest)
        return interest

    def month_end(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the new balance."""
        self.add_interest()
        return self._balance

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, rate={self.rate})")


class CheckingAccount(Account):
    """An everyday account that may go below zero, up to a limit."""

    fee = 100

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft=0):
        """Create a checking account with an overdraft limit."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(overdraft, bool) or not isinstance(overdraft, int):
            raise TypeError("overdraft must be an integer")
        if overdraft < 0:
            raise ValueError("overdraft must not be negative")
        self._overdraft = overdraft

    @property
    def overdraft(self):
        """How far below zero the balance may go."""
        return self._overdraft

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount out, letting the balance go down to -overdraft."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if self._balance - amount < -self._overdraft:
            raise ValueError("overdraft limit exceeded")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def month_end(self):
        """Charge the monthly fee if overdrawn; return the new balance."""
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
            self._record("fee", self.fee)
        return self._balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{super().__str__()} (overdraft {self.overdraft})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, overdraft={self.overdraft})")


class GiftCard(ObservableMixin, HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """A prepaid card with a fixed value. It is not an account."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, code, value):
        """Create a gift card with a code and a starting value."""
        if not isinstance(code, str) or not code.strip():
            raise ValueError("code must be a non-empty string")
        _check_amount(value)
        self._code = code.strip()
        self._value = value
        self._holder = None

    @property
    def holder(self):
        """The customer holding this card, or None."""
        return self._holder

    @property
    def value(self):
        """What is left on the card."""
        return self._value

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from the card; return the value left."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._value:
            raise ValueError("not enough value on the card")
        self._value -= amount
        self._record("payment", amount)
        return self._value

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Gift card {self._code}: {self.value} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"GiftCard(code={self._code!r}, value={self.value})"


class AccountFactory:
    """Create accounts by kind, from a registry of account classes."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._registry = {}

    def register(self, kind, account_class):
        """Make kind create account_class, and return account_class."""
        if not isinstance(kind, str) or not kind.strip():
            raise ValueError("kind must be a non-empty string")
        if not (isinstance(account_class, type)
                and issubclass(account_class, Account)):
            raise TypeError("account_class must be a subclass of Account")
        self._registry[kind] = account_class
        return account_class

    def create(self, kind, owner, **options):
        """Create an account of a registered kind."""
        if kind not in self._registry:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown account kind: {kind!r}")
        return self._registry[kind](owner, **options)

    def kinds(self):
        """The registered kinds, sorted."""
        return sorted(self._registry)


account_factory = AccountFactory()
account_factory.register("savings", SavingsAccount)
account_factory.register("checking", CheckingAccount)


class Customer(JSONMixin):
    """A wallet customer, who can hold accounts and gift cards."""

    def __init__(self, name, email):
        """Create a customer with a name and an email address."""
        if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip():
            raise ValueError("name must be a non-empty string")
        if not isinstance(email, str) or "@" not in email:
            raise ValueError("email must contain @")
        self._name = name.strip()
        self._email = email.strip()
        self._accounts = []
        self._gift_cards = []

    @property
    def name(self):
        """The customer's name."""
        return self._name

    @property
    def email(self):
        """The customer's email address."""
        return self._email

    @property
    def accounts(self):
        """The customer's accounts, as a tuple."""
        return tuple(self._accounts)

    @property
    def gift_cards(self):
        """The customer's gift cards, as a tuple."""
        return tuple(self._gift_cards)

    def add_account(self, account):
        """Add an account this customer owns, and return it."""
        if not isinstance(account, Account):
            raise TypeError("account must be an Account")
        if account.owner != self._name:
            raise ValueError("account belongs to another customer")
        if account in self._accounts:
            raise ValueError("account already added")
        self._accounts.append(account)
        return account

    def open_account(self, kind, **options):
        """Open a new account of a registered kind, and return it."""
        account = account_factory.create(kind, self._name, **options)
        return self.add_account(account)

    def add_gift_card(self, card):
        """Give this customer a gift card nobody else holds; return it."""
        if not isinstance(card, GiftCard):
            raise TypeError("card must be a GiftCard")
        if card.holder is not None:
            raise ValueError("gift card already has a holder")
        card._holder = self
        self._gift_cards.append(card)
        return card

    def total_balance(self):
        """Return the sum of all account balances."""
        return sum(account.balance for account in self._accounts)

    def month_end(self):
        """Run the end-of-month rules on every account."""
        for account in self._accounts:
            account.month_end()

    def __str__(self):
        return (f"{self.name} <{self.email}>: "
                f"accounts: {len(self._accounts)}, "
                f"gift cards: {len(self._gift_cards)}")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Customer(name={self.name!r}, email={self.email!r})"


class PayerDecorator(Payer):
    """Wrap a payer to add behaviour to pay; forward everything else."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped):
        if not callable(getattr(wrapped, "pay", None)):
            raise TypeError("wrapped must have a pay method")
        self._wrapped = wrapped

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pass the payment on to the wrapped payer."""
        return self._wrapped.pay(amount)

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return getattr(self._wrapped, name)

    def __str__(self):
        return str(self._wrapped)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{type(self).__name__}({self._wrapped!r})"


class SpendingLimit(PayerDecorator):
    """Refuse any single payment above a limit."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped, limit):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        _check_amount(limit)
        self._limit = limit

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, unless it is over the limit."""
        if amount > self._limit:
            raise ValueError(f"payment over the limit of {self._limit}")
        return super().pay(amount)


class Receipts(PayerDecorator):
    """Keep a receipt for every payment that goes through."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        self.receipts = []

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, then write a receipt."""
        result = super().pay(amount)
        self.receipts.append(f"Paid {amount} ALL")
        return result


class RoundUp(PayerDecorator):
    """Round each payment up to the next 100 and save the difference."""

    def __init__(self, wrapped, savings):
        super().__init__(wrapped)
        if not isinstance(savings, Account):
            raise TypeError("savings must be an Account")
        self._savings = savings

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, then move the round-up into savings if possible."""
        result = super().pay(amount)
        spare = -amount % 100
        if spare:
            try:
                result = super().pay(spare)
            except ValueError:
                return result
            self._savings.deposit(spare)
        return result


class AuditLog:
    """Observer: keep one line for every event it is sent."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.lines = []

    def notify(self, source, topic, amount):
        """Record the event."""
        self.lines.append(f"{type(source).__name__} {topic} {amount}")


class SMSAlert:
    """Observer: text a phone number about the events it is sent."""

    def __init__(self, phone):
        self.phone = phone
        self.sent = []

    def notify(self, source, topic, amount):
        """Send a short message about the event."""
        self.sent.append(f"To {self.phone}: {topic} of {amount} ALL")


def checkout(payer, amount):
    """Charge amount to anything that can pay; return what it returns."""
    return payer.pay(amount)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ada = Customer("Ada", "ada@example.com")
    savings = ada.open_account("savings", balance=1000, rate=2)
    checking = ada.open_account("checking", overdraft=500)

    audit = AuditLog()
    sms = SMSAlert("+355 69 000 0000")
    for account in ada.accounts:
        account.subscribe(audit)
    checking.subscribe(sms, topics=["fee"])

    payer = RoundUp(Receipts(SpendingLimit(checking, limit=500)), savings)
    checkout(payer, 230)
    ada.month_end()

    for account in ada.accounts:
        print(account)
    print(*payer.receipts, sep="\n")
    print(*audit.lines, sep="\n")
    print(*sms.sent, sep="\n")

./wallet.py

Ada: 1091 ALL
Ada: -400 ALL (overdraft 500)
Paid 230 ALL
Paid 70 ALL
CheckingAccount withdraw 230
CheckingAccount withdraw 70
SavingsAccount deposit 70
SavingsAccount interest 21
CheckingAccount fee 100
To +355 69 000 0000: fee of 100 ALL

Read the last lines as a story: the payment of 230 and its 70 lek round-up leave the checking account, the 70 arrives in savings, the month ends with 21 lek of interest on the new balance and a 100 lek fee on the overdrawn account, and only the fee reaches Ada's phone.

Version Tutorial What it added v1 Classes & Object Model Account: validation, properties, string representations v2 Inheritance & Polymorphism SavingsAccount, CheckingAccount, one month_end call for all v3 Abstract Classes & Interfaces the Payer interface, abstract Account, GiftCard, TransactionLog, mixins v4 Introduction to UML Modeling Customer, multiplicities in code, class and sequence diagrams v5 Introduction to Design Patterns Factory, Observer and Decorator

The same few principles carried the whole way: an object protects its own state, shared promises become interfaces, "is a" becomes inheritance and "has a" becomes composition, and new behaviour arrives as new classes rather than edits to old ones.

AI in the loop

Patterns are where assistants over-engineer most. Ask one to "add a feature using best practices" and it may return three patterns you do not need. Ask instead: "Here is my code and the change I need. Which problem do I actually have, and is there a pattern that fits it? What would it cost?" Then compare its answer with the table in Step 5, and decide yourself.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
ValueError: unknown account kind: '...'

The kind was never registered, or is spelled differently. Check account_factory.kinds(), and make sure register runs before the first create, for example in the same module as the class.

My observer is never notified

Check the topic names it subscribed to: they must match the transaction kinds exactly. Passing a single topic as a string works, topics="fee", but a typo such as "fees" silently matches nothing.

AttributeError on a decorated payer

The attribute does not exist on the wrapped object either. __getattr__ forwards lookups inward, so the innermost object must have it. Also check that the decorator's own attributes are set before anything reads them in __init__.

print(payer) shows <... object at 0x...>

The decorator does not define __str__. Special methods are not forwarded by __getattr__, so each one must be passed on by hand.

A decorated payer is refused by add_account

A decorator is a Payer, not an Account. Keep the plain account in the customer's list, and wrap it only where you pay with it.

docs.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
docs.text:
75 min Object-Oriented Design Needs: Classes & Object Model

The wallet has one kind of account. A real wallet needs several: savings accounts that earn interest, checking accounts that may go below zero. They share almost everything an Account already does. Inheritance lets you write that shared part once and add only what is different. Polymorphism then lets the rest of your program treat every account the same way, even though each behaves in its own way.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Without inheritance you would copy Account into SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount, then fix every bug three times. With it, the validation, properties and string methods you wrote in the last tutorial are reused as they are, and each new class contains only the lines that make it different.

Polymorphism is the bigger idea. It is what lets you write account.month_end() without caring which kind of account it is, and add a fourth kind next year without touching the code that uses them. Frameworks are built on it, and so is the HBnB portfolio project.

You finished the last tutorial with an Account class that validates its input, protects its balance and prints itself clearly. Start from that file, or from the tag v1-classes.

The wallet now has a new requirement:

The wallet offers two more account types. A savings account earns interest every month. A checking account may go below zero, down to an agreed overdraft limit, and is charged a 100 lek fee for every month it ends overdrawn.

docs.title: Step 1: Parent and child classes
docs.text:
Both new accounts are accounts: they have an owner and a balance, and you can deposit into them. That "is a" relationship is what inheritance models.

Account and its two subclasses Account is the parent class, with owner, balance, deposit, withdraw and month_end. SavingsAccount inherits from it, adds rate and add_interest, and overrides month_end. CheckingAccount inherits from it, adds overdraft, overrides withdraw and month_end, and extends __str__ using super. + added ↻ overridden plain: inherited PARENT · BASE CLASS Account owner, balance deposit(), withdraw() month_end(), __str__() inherits from SavingsAccount CheckingAccount + rate + add_interest() ↻ month_end() + overdraft ↻ withdraw() ↻ month_end() ↻ __str__() via super()
  • The parent class, also called the base class or superclass, is Account.
  • The child classes, or subclasses, are SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount.
  • A child inherits every attribute and method of its parent. It can then add new ones and override inherited ones.

The syntax is one pair of brackets after the class name. A subclass with no body at all is already a working account:

class BusinessAccount(Account):
    pass


acme = BusinessAccount("Acme", 10)
acme.deposit(90)        # 100: deposit came from Account
print(acme)             # Acme: 100 ALL: __str__ came from Account

Every class has a parent, even when you do not write one. Account inherits from Python's built-in class object, which is where the default __str__ and __repr__ you saw printing <__main__.Account object at 0x...> came from.

docs.title: Step 2: Extend the constructor with super()
docs.text:
A savings account needs everything Account.__init__ already sets up, plus an interest rate. Do not copy the parent's checks. Call the parent's __init__ with super(), then add what is new:

class SavingsAccount(Account):
    """An account that earns interest every month."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=1):
        """Create a savings account; rate is monthly interest in percent."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(rate, bool) or not isinstance(rate, int):
            raise TypeError("rate must be an integer")
        if not 0 <= rate <= 10:
            raise ValueError("rate must be between 0 and 10")
        self._rate = rate

    @property
    def rate(self):
        """Monthly interest rate, in whole percent."""
        return self._rate

super() means "the parent class, for this object". The line super().__init__(owner, balance) runs all of Account's validation and sets _owner and _balance. The next lines handle only what is new. The validation from the last tutorial still protects every savings account:

SavingsAccount("", 100)              # ValueError: owner must not be empty
SavingsAccount("Ada", 100, rate=50)  # ValueError: rate must be between 0 and 10

Forget super().__init__ and the object is half built

If the subclass defines __init__ and never calls the parent's, Account.__init__ does not run. The object exists, but it has no _owner or _balance, and the first access fails with AttributeError: ... has no attribute '_balance'. When a subclass has its own __init__, its first line is almost always super().__init__(...).

docs.title: Step 3: Add new behaviour
docs.text:
A subclass can add methods the parent does not have. Savings accounts earn interest:

    def add_interest(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the amount added."""
        interest = self._balance * self._rate // 100
        self._balance += interest
        return interest

The rate is a whole percentage per month, and // keeps the interest in whole lek, the same reason the balance is an integer.

Everything else is inherited unchanged, including the rules:

grace = SavingsAccount("Grace", 1000, rate=2)
grace.deposit(100)      # 1100: inherited from Account
grace.add_interest()    # 22: new in SavingsAccount
grace.withdraw(5000)    # ValueError: insufficient funds, from Account

docs.title: Step 4: Override a method
docs.text:
A checking account must let the balance go below zero, up to its overdraft limit. Account.withdraw refuses that. So CheckingAccount defines its own withdraw, which overrides the parent's:

class CheckingAccount(Account):
    """An everyday account that may go below zero, up to a limit."""

    fee = 100

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft=0):
        """Create a checking account with an overdraft limit."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(overdraft, bool) or not isinstance(overdraft, int):
            raise TypeError("overdraft must be an integer")
        if overdraft < 0:
            raise ValueError("overdraft must not be negative")
        self._overdraft = overdraft

    @property
    def overdraft(self):
        """How far below zero the balance may go."""
        return self._overdraft

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount out, letting the balance go down to -overdraft."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        if self._balance - amount < -self._overdraft:
            raise ValueError("overdraft limit exceeded")
        self._balance -= amount
        return self._balance

linus = CheckingAccount("Linus", overdraft=500)
linus.withdraw(300)    # -300: allowed
linus.withdraw(300)    # ValueError: overdraft limit exceeded

Two details from the last tutorial pay off here. The new withdraw reuses the inherited _check_amount, so amounts are still validated in one place. And it can update self._balance directly, because we used a single underscore. Had we named it __balance, name mangling would have stored it as _Account__balance, and self.__balance inside CheckingAccount would have looked for _CheckingAccount__balance instead.

docs.title: How Python finds a method
docs.text:
When you call a method, Python searches for it starting at the object's own class, then moves up through the parents, and uses the first match it finds.

Method lookup goes from the object's class up to its parents For grace.deposit, Python checks SavingsAccount, which has no deposit, then Account, which has it, so Account's deposit runs. For linus.withdraw, Python checks CheckingAccount first, which has its own withdraw, so that one runs and Account is never checked. grace.deposit(100) linus.withdraw(300) grace SavingsAccount no deposit here Account found: this runs object linus CheckingAccount found: this runs Account never checked object

That search order is called the method resolution order, or MRO. You can print it:

SavingsAccount.mro()    # [SavingsAccount, Account, object]

This is also why overriding works: the child's version is found first, so the parent's is never reached.

docs.title: Step 5: Extend an inherited method with super()
docs.text:
Overriding replaces the parent's method. Sometimes you want to keep it and add to it. Call it through super() inside the override.

A checking account should print like any account, plus its overdraft:

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{super().__str__()} (overdraft {self.overdraft})"

print(linus)    # Linus: -300 ALL (overdraft 500)

super().__str__() runs Account.__str__ and returns Linus: -300 ALL. The override adds the rest. If the base format ever changes, the checking account follows automatically.

docs.title: One change to version 1
docs.text:
In version 1, __repr__ started with the class name written out: f"Account(owner=...". That is fine until a subclass inherits it: a BusinessAccount would then call itself Account(...) in every debugger and list, which is misleading. The fix is to ask the object for its real class name:

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance})")

type(self).__name__ is "Account" for an account and "BusinessAccount" for a business account. A parent class should not assume it is the only class that will use its methods. The two new classes override __repr__ anyway, to include their extra attribute:

repr(grace)    # "SavingsAccount(owner='Grace', balance=1122, rate=2)"
repr(linus)    # "CheckingAccount(owner='Linus', balance=-300, overdraft=500)"

docs.title: Step 6: Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours
docs.text:
Every account needs some work done at the end of each month, but the work is different: savings accounts earn interest, checking accounts may be charged a fee, plain accounts do nothing. Give the parent a month_end method that does nothing, and let each child override it:

# in Account
    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance.

        A plain account has none.
        """
        return self._balance

# in SavingsAccount
    def month_end(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the new balance."""
        self.add_interest()
        return self._balance

# in CheckingAccount
    def month_end(self):
        """Charge the monthly fee if overdrawn; return the new balance."""
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
        return self._balance

Now the code that closes the month does not need to know which kind of account it holds:

accounts = [
    Account("Ada", 500),
    SavingsAccount("Grace", 1000, rate=2),
    CheckingAccount("Linus", overdraft=500),
]
accounts[2].withdraw(300)
for account in accounts:
    account.month_end()
    print(account)

Ada: 500 ALL
Grace: 1020 ALL
Linus: -400 ALL (overdraft 500)
One call, three behaviours The loop calls account.month_end() on three objects. On the Account for Ada, nothing changes and the balance stays 500. On the SavingsAccount for Grace, 20 lek of interest is added, giving 1020. On the CheckingAccount for Linus, who is overdrawn, the 100 lek fee is charged, giving minus 400. Account Ada, 500 SavingsAccount Grace, 1000, rate 2 CheckingAccount Linus, -300 .month_end() the same call for each no change 500 +20 interest 1020 -100 fee -400

That is polymorphism: objects of different classes respond to the same method call, each in its own way. The loop only relies on one promise, every account has a month_end method, and each class keeps that promise differently.

Compare the version without it:

for account in accounts:                         # don't do this
    if isinstance(account, SavingsAccount):
        account.add_interest()
    elif isinstance(account, CheckingAccount):
        if account.balance < 0:
            ...                                  # charge the fee somehow

Every new account type would mean editing this loop, and every other loop like it. With polymorphism, a new type means one new class with its own month_end, and no existing code changes.

You have used polymorphism since your first week: print works on any object because every class has a __str__, and len works on strings, lists and dictionaries alike.

docs.title: Step 7: Check relationships with isinstance and issubclass
docs.text:
Sometimes you do need to ask what kind of object you have, or how two classes are related.

Expression Result Why isinstance(grace, SavingsAccount) True grace was built from it isinstance(grace, Account) True a savings account is an account isinstance(ada, SavingsAccount) False a plain account is not a savings account isinstance(grace, (SavingsAccount, CheckingAccount)) True a tuple means "any of these" type(grace) is SavingsAccount True its exact class type(grace) is Account False type ignores parents issubclass(SavingsAccount, Account) True the child inherits from the parent issubclass(Account, SavingsAccount) False not the other way round issubclass(SavingsAccount, object) True every class inherits from object

isinstance checks an object against a class, and counts parents. issubclass checks a class against a class. type(x) is Y checks the exact class only, ignoring inheritance, which is rarely what you want.

Now the puzzle from the last tutorial has an answer:

issubclass(bool, int)    # True
isinstance(True, int)    # True: a bool *is an* int
type(True) is int        # False: its exact class is bool

bool is a subclass of int, so every True passes an int check. That is why _check_amount tests for bool separately.

Use these checks at the edges of your program, for example to validate input, as the constructors do. Inside your own logic, prefer calling a method and letting polymorphism choose the behaviour.

docs.title: Step 8: Design simple hierarchies
docs.text:
A few rules keep inheritance helpful instead of tangled.

  • Inherit only for "is a". A savings account is an account. A customer has accounts but is not one, and a transaction belongs to an account but is not one. "Has a" relationships are modelled by storing one object inside another, which you will draw in the UML project.
  • Keep the parent's promises. Code written for Account must still work when given a CheckingAccount. Its withdraw still takes an amount, still validates it, still returns the new balance and still raises ValueError when refused. Only the limit changed. This rule has a name, the Liskov substitution principle, and breaking it is the most common inheritance bug.
  • Keep hierarchies shallow. One or two levels below the base class is plenty. If you find yourself five levels deep, some of those classes are probably "has a" in disguise.
  • Put shared code in the parent, differences in the children. If two children contain the same lines, move them up.

docs.title: The code so far
docs.text:
This is version 2 of the wallet, tagged v2-inheritance in the companion repository.

wallet.py · version 2 wallet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small digital wallet, built up across the OOP tutorials.

Version 2: Inheritance & Polymorphism.
"""


class Account:
    """A wallet account holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        """Create an account for owner with an opening balance."""
        self.owner = owner
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self._balance = balance

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        """Add amount to the balance and return the new balance."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        self._balance += amount
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount from the balance and return the new balance."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount
        return self._balance

    def _check_amount(self, amount):
        """Raise if amount is not a positive whole number."""
        if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
            raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must be positive")

    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance.

        A plain account has none.
        """
        return self._balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance})")


class SavingsAccount(Account):
    """An account that earns interest every month."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=1):
        """Create a savings account; rate is monthly interest in percent."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(rate, bool) or not isinstance(rate, int):
            raise TypeError("rate must be an integer")
        if not 0 <= rate <= 10:
            raise ValueError("rate must be between 0 and 10")
        self._rate = rate

    @property
    def rate(self):
        """Monthly interest rate, in whole percent."""
        return self._rate

    def add_interest(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the amount added."""
        interest = self._balance * self._rate // 100
        self._balance += interest
        return interest

    def month_end(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the new balance."""
        self.add_interest()
        return self._balance

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, rate={self.rate})")


class CheckingAccount(Account):
    """An everyday account that may go below zero, up to a limit."""

    fee = 100

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft=0):
        """Create a checking account with an overdraft limit."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(overdraft, bool) or not isinstance(overdraft, int):
            raise TypeError("overdraft must be an integer")
        if overdraft < 0:
            raise ValueError("overdraft must not be negative")
        self._overdraft = overdraft

    @property
    def overdraft(self):
        """How far below zero the balance may go."""
        return self._overdraft

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount out, letting the balance go down to -overdraft."""
        self._check_amount(amount)
        if self._balance - amount < -self._overdraft:
            raise ValueError("overdraft limit exceeded")
        self._balance -= amount
        return self._balance

    def month_end(self):
        """Charge the monthly fee if overdrawn; return the new balance."""
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
        return self._balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{super().__str__()} (overdraft {self.overdraft})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, overdraft={self.overdraft})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    accounts = [
        Account("Ada", 500),
        SavingsAccount("Grace", 1000, rate=2),
        CheckingAccount("Linus", overdraft=500),
    ]
    accounts[2].withdraw(300)
    for account in accounts:
        account.month_end()
        print(account)
    total = sum(account.balance for account in accounts)
    print(f"Total: {total} {Account.currency}")

./wallet.py

Ada: 500 ALL
Grace: 1020 ALL
Linus: -400 ALL (overdraft 500)
Total: 1120 ALL

AI in the loop

Before adding a class to a hierarchy, describe the new account type to an assistant and ask: "Should this inherit from Account, or hold an Account instead? What promises of Account would it break?" Then argue with the answer. Deciding is a versus has a is a design judgement, and it is exactly the kind of question your peers will ask in a code review.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
AttributeError: 'SavingsAccount' object has no attribute '_balance'

The subclass has its own __init__ and does not call super().__init__(...), so the parent never set _balance up. Add the call as the first line.

My override never runs; the parent's method runs instead

The names do not match exactly. A typo such as month_End creates a new, separate method, and Python keeps finding the parent's month_end. Copy the name from the parent.

TypeError: SavingsAccount.__init__() takes from 2 to 4 positional arguments but 5 were given

The subclass's __init__ has its own parameters. Check them, and pass extra values by name for clarity: SavingsAccount("Ada", 100, rate=2).

AttributeError: 'CheckingAccount' object has no attribute '_CheckingAccount__balance'

The parent stores the value with two underscores, so it is name-mangled to the parent's class. Use a single underscore for attributes subclasses need, as the wallet does.

RecursionError inside an overridden method

The override calls itself, for example self.withdraw(amount) inside withdraw. To reach the parent's version, call super().withdraw(amount).
