Account can still be created on its own, and nothing forces a new account type to define month_end. Next you turn the base class into a contract that every account type must fulfil.

Abstract Classes & Interfaces

docs.title: Introduction to UML Modeling
docs.text:
75 min Object-Oriented Design Needs: Abstract Classes & Interfaces

The wallet now has eight classes and several kinds of relationship between them. Reading 300 lines of Python is a slow way to understand that. UML, the Unified Modeling Language, is the standard way developers draw a design: boxes for classes, lines for relationships, numbers for how many of each. In this tutorial you draw the wallet, add the customer who owns it all, and write the diagrams as text with Mermaid, so they live next to your code.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A diagram is where design decisions are cheapest to change. Moving an arrow takes a second; moving a class hierarchy after the code is written takes a day. Teams sketch a design, discuss it in a pull request or on a whiteboard, and only then write it.

Diagrams are also how you will read other people's systems: the documentation of almost every framework, and the first phase of the HBnB portfolio project, start with a class diagram. This page uses only the parts of UML that working developers actually draw.

docs.title: Where we left off
docs.text:
How the wallet grows across the module Version 1, Classes: the Account class: done. Version 2, Inheritance: savings and checking accounts: done. Version 3, Abstract classes: contracts and mixins: done. Version 4, UML: drawing the design: this page. Version 5, Patterns: Factory, Observer and Decorator: coming next. v1 · DONE Classes Account v2 · DONE Inheritance savings, checking v3 · DONE Abstract contracts, mixins v4 · THIS PAGE UML draw the design v5 Patterns three patterns

Start from version 3, or the tag v3-abstract. The wallet has one requirement that is still missing: the customer. So far an account's owner is just a name. Here is the full description of the system as it should be at the end of this page:

A customer has a name and an email address. A customer can hold any number of accounts, and every account belongs to exactly one customer. An account is either a savings account, which earns monthly interest, or a checking account, which may go overdrawn up to a limit. Customers can also hold gift cards. A gift card can be sold before anyone holds it, but once it is given to a customer it belongs to that one customer only. Both accounts and gift cards can pay, and both keep a history of every transaction.

docs.title: Step 1: Extract classes, attributes and methods from text
docs.text:
You did a small version of this in the first tutorial. Now do it properly, on the full description. Read it once and mark three kinds of word:

  • Nouns are candidate classes or attributes.
  • Verbs are candidate methods.
  • Rules, especially ones with numbers or words like any, exactly or only, become multiplicities and checks.

Then decide what each candidate really is. Not every noun deserves a class.

Candidate Decision Why customer class Customer has its own data and behaviour name, email address attributes of Customer simple values, no behaviour of their own account abstract class Account "either a savings or a checking account": never a plain one savings account, checking account subclasses each is an account with its own rule gift card class GiftCard can pay, but is not an account pay interface Payer a capability shared by unrelated classes history class TransactionLog a collection with its own rules transaction a (kind, amount) tuple only data, no behaviour yet system, wallet not a class that is the whole program, not a thing inside it monthly interest, overdraft limit attributes rate, overdraft numbers that configure a class holds, belongs to relationships lines between classes, not classes

The last rows are the useful ones. A word like wallet names the system itself. Holds and belongs to are not things at all but connections, and they become the lines of the diagram.

docs.title: Step 2: Draw a class
docs.text:
A class in UML is a box with three compartments: the name, the attributes, and the methods. This is Account from version 3, written in Mermaid:

classDiagram
    class Account {
        <<abstract>>
        +currency: str$
        #_owner: str
        #_balance: int
        +owner: str
        +balance: int
        +deposit(amount: int) int
        +withdraw(amount: int) int
        +pay(amount: int) int
        +month_end()* int
    }

And this is what it draws:

classDiagram
    class Account {
        <<abstract>>
        +currency: str$
        #_owner: str
        #_balance: int
        +owner: str
        +balance: int
        +deposit(amount: int) int
        +withdraw(amount: int) int
        +pay(amount: int) int
        +month_end()* int
    }

Each line uses a small set of symbols:

Symbol Meaning In the wallet + public: part of the interface +deposit(...), +balance - private Python's __name; not used in the wallet # protected: for the class and its subclasses Python's _name, such as #_balance name: type an attribute and its type +owner: str method(params) type a method and what it returns +withdraw(amount: int) int $ at the end static: belongs to the class +currency: str$ * at the end abstract: subclasses must define it +month_end()* int <<...>> a stereotype: what kind of class <<abstract>>, <<interface>>

You do not have to show everything. A diagram for discussing the design usually shows only the public interface; a diagram for explaining the implementation may show internal attributes too. Choose for the reader.

docs.title: Step 3: Model relationships between classes
docs.text:
Classes rarely stand alone. UML has six kinds of line, and the wallet already uses all of them.

The six UML relationships, with wallet examples Inheritance: a solid line with a hollow triangle, SavingsAccount to Account, meaning is a. Realization: a dashed line with a hollow triangle, GiftCard to Payer, meaning implements. Association: a solid line with an open arrow, Customer to Account, meaning knows and uses. Aggregation: a solid line with a hollow diamond at Customer, to GiftCard, meaning has, and the part can exist alone. Composition: a solid line with a filled diamond at Account, to TransactionLog, meaning owns, and the part lives and dies with it. Dependency: a dashed line with an open arrow, checkout to Payer, meaning uses briefly. FROM LINE TO MEANING · MERMAID SavingsAccountAccount GiftCardPayer CustomerAccount CustomerGiftCard AccountTransactionLog checkoutPayer Inheritance: is a Realization: implements Association: knows, uses Aggregation: part can exist alone Composition: part dies with whole Dependency: uses briefly Account <|-- SavingsAccount Payer <|.. GiftCard Customer --> Account Customer o-- GiftCard Account *-- TransactionLog checkout ..> Payer

Inheritance and realization you already know: a solid line with a hollow triangle means "is a", a dashed one means "implements an interface". The triangle always points at the parent.

The other four are all forms of "has" or "uses", and the difference between them is about lifetime:

  • Association: one object keeps a reference to another and uses it. A customer knows their accounts.
  • Aggregation, a hollow diamond on the side of the whole: a "has a" where the part can exist on its own. A gift card exists in the shop before any customer holds it.
  • Composition, a filled diamond on the side of the whole: a "has a" where the part is created by the whole and goes with it. An account's history is created inside the account, and there is no history without its account.
  • Dependency, a dashed arrow: something uses another class briefly, for example as a parameter, without keeping it. checkout uses a Payer only while it runs.

When you are unsure between association, aggregation and composition, ask: if the whole disappears, does the part disappear too? Yes means composition. No means aggregation or association, and plain association is always a safe choice. The difference between those two is a matter of emphasis, and many teams only draw plain association.

docs.title: Step 4: Determine multiplicity from system rules
docs.text:
A line says two classes are related. Multiplicity says how many: a number, or a range, written at each end of the line.

Notation Means From a rule like 1 exactly one "belongs to exactly one customer" 0..1 zero or one "may have", "at most one" 0..* or * any number, including none "any number of", "can hold" 1..* at least one "one or more", "must have"

Read each relationship in both directions, one sentence per end. Take customers and accounts:

A customer can hold any number of accounts. → 0..* next to Account Every account belongs to exactly one customer. → 1 next to Customer

Then gift cards:

A customer can hold any number of gift cards. → 0..* next to GiftCard A gift card can be unsold, or held by one customer only. → 0..1 next to Customer

The trick is to put each number at the far end: it answers "for one of these, how many of those?" In Mermaid, the numbers go in quotes on either side of the line:

Customer "1" --> "0..*" Account : holds
Customer "0..1" o-- "0..*" GiftCard : holds

Multiplicity is the part of a diagram that turns most directly into code. Every 1 and 0..1 is a check something must perform, which you will write in Step 6.

docs.title: Step 5: Represent the system with class diagrams
docs.text:
Here is the whole domain, with the new Customer, every relationship and every multiplicity:

classDiagram
    direction TB
    class Customer {
        +name: str
        +email: str
        +accounts: tuple
        +gift_cards: tuple
        +add_account(account) Account
        +add_gift_card(card) GiftCard
        +total_balance() int
        +month_end()
    }
    class Payer {
        <<interface>>
        +pay(amount: int)* int
    }
    class Account {
        <<abstract>>
        +owner: str
        +balance: int
        +deposit(amount: int) int
        +withdraw(amount: int) int
        +month_end()* int
    }
    class SavingsAccount {
        +rate: int
        +add_interest() int
        +month_end() int
    }
    class CheckingAccount {
        +overdraft: int
        +fee: int$
        +withdraw(amount: int) int
        +month_end() int
    }
    class GiftCard {
        +value: int
        +holder: Customer
        +pay(amount: int) int
    }
    class TransactionLog {
        +total(kind: str) int
    }
    Payer <|.. Account
    Payer <|.. GiftCard
    Account <|-- SavingsAccount
    Account <|-- CheckingAccount
    Customer "1" --> "0..*" Account : holds
    Customer "0..1" o-- "0..*" GiftCard : holds
    Account "1" *-- "1" TransactionLog : history
    GiftCard "1" *-- "1" TransactionLog : history

This diagram leaves out the mixins on purpose. They are about how the code shares behaviour, not about what the wallet models, and adding them would double the number of lines. They get a small diagram of their own:

classDiagram
    class HistoryMixin {
        <<mixin>>
        +history: TransactionLog
        #_record(kind, amount)
    }
    class JSONMixin {
        <<mixin>>
        +to_dict() dict
        +to_json() str
    }
    class list {
        <<built-in>>
    }
    HistoryMixin <|-- Account
    JSONMixin <|-- Account
    HistoryMixin <|-- GiftCard
    JSONMixin <|-- GiftCard
    JSONMixin <|-- Customer
    list <|-- TransactionLog
    HistoryMixin ..> TransactionLog : creates

That is a habit worth keeping: one diagram per question. "What does the system model?" and "how is the code organised?" are different questions, and a single diagram that answers both is hard to read.

docs.title: Step 6: From the diagram to code
docs.text:
The diagram has one class that does not exist yet. Write Customer from it: the attributes and methods come straight from its box, and each multiplicity becomes a rule.

class Customer(JSONMixin):
    """A wallet customer, who can hold accounts and gift cards."""

    def __init__(self, name, email):
        """Create a customer with a name and an email address."""
        if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip():
            raise ValueError("name must be a non-empty string")
        if not isinstance(email, str) or "@" not in email:
            raise ValueError("email must contain @")
        self._name = name.strip()
        self._email = email.strip()
        self._accounts = []
        self._gift_cards = []

    @property
    def accounts(self):
        """The customer's accounts, as a tuple."""
        return tuple(self._accounts)

    def add_account(self, account):
        """Add an account this customer owns, and return it."""
        if not isinstance(account, Account):
            raise TypeError("account must be an Account")
        if account.owner != self._name:
            raise ValueError("account belongs to another customer")
        if account in self._accounts:
            raise ValueError("account already added")
        self._accounts.append(account)
        return account

    def add_gift_card(self, card):
        """Give this customer a gift card nobody else holds; return it."""
        if not isinstance(card, GiftCard):
            raise TypeError("card must be a GiftCard")
        if card.holder is not None:
            raise ValueError("gift card already has a holder")
        card._holder = self
        self._gift_cards.append(card)
        return card

    # name, email, gift_cards, total_balance, month_end,
    # __str__ and __repr__ are in the full code below

Trace each piece back to the diagram:

In the diagram In the code Customer "1" --> "0..*" Account a list, _accounts, that can hold any number, exposed as a tuple so nobody edits it from outside the 1 next to Customer add_account refuses an account whose owner is someone else Customer "0..1" o-- "0..*" GiftCard a list, _gift_cards the 0..1 next to Customer each card stores its holder; a card that already has one is refused +holder: Customer in GiftCard a new read-only property, set only by add_gift_card

The 0..1 needed a change to GiftCard: to know whether it already has a holder, the card must remember who that is. A relationship that has to be checked from both ends usually needs a reference at both ends. Notice too that add_gift_card sets card._holder, an internal attribute of another class. Both classes live in the same module and are designed together, which makes that acceptable here; across modules you would add a proper method instead.

A name is not an identity

add_account compares owner names, so two customers called Ada would be confused. Real systems give every customer a unique ID. The wallet keeps names to stay small, but that is the kind of weakness a diagram review is good at spotting.

ada = Customer("Ada", "ada@example.com")
ada.add_account(SavingsAccount("Linus", 100))
# ValueError: account belongs to another customer

docs.title: Step 7: Model interactions with sequence diagrams
docs.text:
A class diagram shows structure: what exists and how it connects. It says nothing about what happens when you call a method. For that, UML has the sequence diagram: the objects across the top, time running downwards, and one arrow per message.

Here is what happens when you run checkout(checking, 300):

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as __main__
    participant C as checkout()
    participant A as checking: CheckingAccount
    participant L as history: TransactionLog
    M->>C: checkout(checking, 300)
    C->>A: pay(300)
    A->>A: withdraw(300)
    alt within the overdraft limit
        A->>L: append(("withdraw", 300))
        A-->>C: -300
        C-->>M: -300
    else over the limit
        A-->>C: raises ValueError
        C-->>M: raises ValueError
    end
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as __main__
    participant C as checkout()
    participant A as checking: CheckingAccount
    participant L as history: TransactionLog
    M->>C: checkout(checking, 300)
    C->>A: pay(300)
    A->>A: withdraw(300)
    alt within the overdraft limit
        A->>L: append(("withdraw", 300))
        A-->>C: -300
        C-->>M: -300
    else over the limit
        A-->>C: raises ValueError
        C-->>M: raises ValueError
    end

The parts:

  • Participants, across the top: each one is an object, written name: Class, or a function. The vertical line below each is its lifeline.
  • ->>, a solid arrow, is a call. -->>, a dashed arrow, is the return value coming back.
  • An arrow to itself, A->>A, is an object calling its own method: pay calls withdraw.
  • alt ... else ... end shows alternatives, like an if. The condition goes in the label.

A loop has its own box. This is ada.month_end(), which runs every account's rule:

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as __main__
    participant C as ada: Customer
    participant A as account: Account
    M->>C: month_end()
    loop for each account in ada.accounts
        C->>A: month_end()
        Note right of A: runs the subclass's own month_end
        A-->>C: new balance
    end
    C-->>M: None

The participant is drawn as account: Account, the abstract type, because the customer does not know or care which subclass each account is. The note says where polymorphism takes over. Use the same technique to draw any loop over objects that share an interface.

A sequence diagram is for one scenario. Do not try to show every path through the code in one drawing; draw the important scenarios, one each.

docs.title: Step 8: Use Mermaid in practice
docs.text:
Mermaid diagrams are plain text, which is their biggest advantage: they live in your repository, show up in diffs, and get reviewed in pull requests like code.

  • GitHub draws them in any Markdown file: a README, a DESIGN.md, an issue or a pull request. Put the diagram in a fenced code block marked mermaid.
  • This site draws them the same way.
  • mermaid.live is an online editor that redraws as you type. Use it to sketch, then paste the text into your repository.
DESIGN.md
# Design

```mermaid
classDiagram
    Account <|-- SavingsAccount
    Customer "1" --> "0..*" Account : holds
```

The companion repository now has a DESIGN.md with every diagram on this page, drawn by GitHub.

AI in the loop

Assistants are good at turning code into Mermaid. Try it the other way round: draw your own class diagram from the description first, then ask an assistant to generate one from wallet.py, and compare. Where they differ, one of the two is wrong: your understanding, or the code. Also ask it to check your multiplicities against the written rules, one sentence at a time.

docs.title: The code so far
docs.text:
This is version 4 of the wallet, tagged v4-uml. The changes from version 3 are the new Customer class, the holder of a gift card, and the demo at the bottom.

wallet.py · version 4 wallet.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small digital wallet, built up across the OOP tutorials.

Version 4: Introduction to UML Modeling.
"""
import json
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


def _check_amount(amount):
    """Raise if amount is not a positive whole number."""
    if isinstance(amount, bool) or not isinstance(amount, int):
        raise TypeError("amount must be an integer")
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")


class TransactionLog(list):
    """A list that only accepts (kind, amount) transaction entries."""

    KINDS = ("deposit", "withdraw", "payment", "interest", "fee")

    def __init__(self, entries=()):
        super().__init__()
        self.extend(entries)

    def append(self, entry):
        """Add one entry, after checking it."""
        self._check(entry)
        super().append(entry)

    def extend(self, entries):
        """Add several entries; check them all before adding any."""
        entries = list(entries)
        for entry in entries:
            self._check(entry)
        super().extend(entries)

    def total(self, kind):
        """Return the sum of all amounts of one kind."""
        return sum(amount for k, amount in self if k == kind)

    def _check(self, entry):
        if not isinstance(entry, tuple) or len(entry) != 2:
            raise TypeError("entry must be a (kind, amount) tuple")
        kind, amount = entry
        if kind not in self.KINDS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown kind: {kind!r}")
        _check_amount(amount)


class HistoryMixin:
    """Give a class a transaction history."""

    def _record(self, kind, amount):
        """Add one entry to this object's history."""
        if "_history" not in vars(self):
            self._history = TransactionLog()
        self._history.append((kind, amount))

    @property
    def history(self):
        """A copy of the transaction history."""
        return TransactionLog(vars(self).get("_history", ()))


class JSONMixin:
    """Give a class a dictionary and JSON form of its simple attributes."""

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the type and simple attributes as a dictionary."""
        data = {"type": type(self).__name__}
        for name, value in vars(self).items():
            if isinstance(value, (str, int, float, bool)):
                data[name.lstrip("_")] = value
        return data

    def to_json(self):
        """Return to_dict() as a JSON string."""
        return json.dumps(self.to_dict())


class Payer(ABC):
    """Interface: anything that can pay an amount."""

    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount, or raise ValueError; return what is left."""


class Account(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """Abstract base for wallet accounts holding money, in whole lek."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        """Create an account for owner with an opening balance."""
        self.owner = owner
        if isinstance(balance, bool) or not isinstance(balance, int):
            raise TypeError("balance must be an integer")
        if balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("balance must not be negative")
        self._balance = balance
        if balance:
            self._record("deposit", balance)

    @property
    def owner(self):
        """The account holder's name."""
        return self._owner

    @owner.setter
    def owner(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("owner must be a string")
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("owner must not be empty")
        self._owner = value.strip()

    @property
    def balance(self):
        """The current balance. Read-only: use deposit and withdraw."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        """Add amount to the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        self._balance += amount
        self._record("deposit", amount)
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount from the balance and return the new balance."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from this account; return the new balance."""
        return self.withdraw(amount)

    @abstractmethod
    def month_end(self):
        """Apply end-of-month rules and return the new balance."""

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance})")


class SavingsAccount(Account):
    """An account that earns interest every month."""

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=1):
        """Create a savings account; rate is monthly interest in percent."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(rate, bool) or not isinstance(rate, int):
            raise TypeError("rate must be an integer")
        if not 0 <= rate <= 10:
            raise ValueError("rate must be between 0 and 10")
        self._rate = rate

    @property
    def rate(self):
        """Monthly interest rate, in whole percent."""
        return self._rate

    def add_interest(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the amount added."""
        interest = self._balance * self._rate // 100
        if interest > 0:
            self._balance += interest
            self._record("interest", interest)
        return interest

    def month_end(self):
        """Add this month's interest and return the new balance."""
        self.add_interest()
        return self._balance

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, rate={self.rate})")


class CheckingAccount(Account):
    """An everyday account that may go below zero, up to a limit."""

    fee = 100

    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft=0):
        """Create a checking account with an overdraft limit."""
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        if isinstance(overdraft, bool) or not isinstance(overdraft, int):
            raise TypeError("overdraft must be an integer")
        if overdraft < 0:
            raise ValueError("overdraft must not be negative")
        self._overdraft = overdraft

    @property
    def overdraft(self):
        """How far below zero the balance may go."""
        return self._overdraft

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        """Take amount out, letting the balance go down to -overdraft."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if self._balance - amount < -self._overdraft:
            raise ValueError("overdraft limit exceeded")
        self._balance -= amount
        self._record("withdraw", amount)
        return self._balance

    def month_end(self):
        """Charge the monthly fee if overdrawn; return the new balance."""
        if self._balance < 0:
            self._balance -= self.fee
            self._record("fee", self.fee)
        return self._balance

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{super().__str__()} (overdraft {self.overdraft})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"{type(self).__name__}(owner={self.owner!r}, "
                f"balance={self.balance}, overdraft={self.overdraft})")


class GiftCard(HistoryMixin, JSONMixin, Payer):
    """A prepaid card with a fixed value. It is not an account."""

    currency = "ALL"

    def __init__(self, code, value):
        """Create a gift card with a code and a starting value."""
        if not isinstance(code, str) or not code.strip():
            raise ValueError("code must be a non-empty string")
        _check_amount(value)
        self._code = code.strip()
        self._value = value
        self._holder = None

    @property
    def holder(self):
        """The customer holding this card, or None."""
        return self._holder

    @property
    def value(self):
        """What is left on the card."""
        return self._value

    def pay(self, amount):
        """Pay amount from the card; return the value left."""
        _check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self._value:
            raise ValueError("not enough value on the card")
        self._value -= amount
        self._record("payment", amount)
        return self._value

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Gift card {self._code}: {self.value} {self.currency}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"GiftCard(code={self._code!r}, value={self.value})"


class Customer(JSONMixin):
    """A wallet customer, who can hold accounts and gift cards."""

    def __init__(self, name, email):
        """Create a customer with a name and an email address."""
        if not isinstance(name, str) or not name.strip():
            raise ValueError("name must be a non-empty string")
        if not isinstance(email, str) or "@" not in email:
            raise ValueError("email must contain @")
        self._name = name.strip()
        self._email = email.strip()
        self._accounts = []
        self._gift_cards = []

    @property
    def name(self):
        """The customer's name."""
        return self._name

    @property
    def email(self):
        """The customer's email address."""
        return self._email

    @property
    def accounts(self):
        """The customer's accounts, as a tuple."""
        return tuple(self._accounts)

    @property
    def gift_cards(self):
        """The customer's gift cards, as a tuple."""
        return tuple(self._gift_cards)

    def add_account(self, account):
        """Add an account this customer owns, and return it."""
        if not isinstance(account, Account):
            raise TypeError("account must be an Account")
        if account.owner != self._name:
            raise ValueError("account belongs to another customer")
        if account in self._accounts:
            raise ValueError("account already added")
        self._accounts.append(account)
        return account

    def add_gift_card(self, card):
        """Give this customer a gift card nobody else holds; return it."""
        if not isinstance(card, GiftCard):
            raise TypeError("card must be a GiftCard")
        if card.holder is not None:
            raise ValueError("gift card already has a holder")
        card._holder = self
        self._gift_cards.append(card)
        return card

    def total_balance(self):
        """Return the sum of all account balances."""
        return sum(account.balance for account in self._accounts)

    def month_end(self):
        """Run the end-of-month rules on every account."""
        for account in self._accounts:
            account.month_end()

    def __str__(self):
        return (f"{self.name} <{self.email}>: "
                f"accounts: {len(self._accounts)}, "
                f"gift cards: {len(self._gift_cards)}")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Customer(name={self.name!r}, email={self.email!r})"


def checkout(payer, amount):
    """Charge amount to anything that can pay; return what it returns."""
    return payer.pay(amount)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ada = Customer("Ada", "ada@example.com")
    savings = ada.add_account(SavingsAccount("Ada", 1000, rate=2))
    checking = ada.add_account(CheckingAccount("Ada", overdraft=500))
    card = ada.add_gift_card(GiftCard("HB-2026", 300))

    checkout(checking, 300)
    checkout(card, 120)
    ada.month_end()

    print(ada)
    for item in ada.accounts + ada.gift_cards:
        print(item)
    print(f"Total in accounts: {ada.total_balance()} {Account.currency}")

./wallet.py

Ada <ada@example.com>: accounts: 2, gift cards: 1
Ada: 1020 ALL
Ada: -400 ALL (overdraft 500)
Gift card HB-2026: 180 ALL
Total in accounts: 620 ALL

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
The diagram does not draw; the page shows the Mermaid text

The code block must be marked exactly mermaid on its first line, and the first line inside must name the diagram type: classDiagram or sequenceDiagram. On mermaid.live, the error message points to the line that failed.

Parse error on a relationship line

Multiplicities need double quotes, "0..*", and the arrow must be one of the forms in the table, with no spaces inside it: <|--, <|.., -->, o--, *--, ..>.

A member shows up in the wrong compartment

Mermaid decides by the brackets: a line with (...) is a method, anything else is an attribute.

I don't know whether a relationship is aggregation or composition

Ask whether the part can exist without the whole. If you are still unsure, draw a plain association and add a multiplicity. That is never wrong, only less specific.

docs.title: How to work through a project
docs.text:
1. Read

    Work through the tutorial, typing every example yourself.

  2. Build

    Do the tasks on the intranet, in your own repository.

  3. Check

    Run pycodestyle, compare your output, then let the Checker run.

  4. Explain

    Go through the tutorial's checklist out loud, ideally to a peer.

AI in the loop

In this module, use assistants to explain, not to write. Ask what an error means, ask for a hint, or ask it to trace your loop. Clippy on the intranet is built for exactly this. If you can only get a task to work by pasting generated code, you are not ready for the next project yet.

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text:
60 min Python Needs: Hello, World

So far your programs run every line once, top to bottom. Control flow changes that: if decides which lines run, and loops decide how many times. With those two ideas you can write almost any algorithm.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Every program you will ever write is built from three things: steps in order, decisions, and repetition. This tutorial covers the last two.

The other skill here is precision. A loop that runs one time too many or one too few is the most common bug in programming, and the Checker compares your output character by character. Learning to reason about where a loop starts and stops, before you run it, saves hours.

docs.title: Step 1: Compare and combine
docs.text:
A condition is an expression that is either True or False.

Operator Meaning Example Result == equal to 3 == 3.0 True != not equal to "a" != "b" True < <= less than, or equal 5 <= 5 True > >= greater than, or equal 2 > 7 False and both are true x > 0 and x < 10 or at least one is true day == "Sat" or day == "Sun" not the opposite not finished in is contained in "py" in "python" True

Two things catch everyone at the start:

  • = stores, == compares. if x = 5: is a syntax error.
  • Python can chain comparisons. 0 <= x < 10 means exactly what it says, and is clearer than x >= 0 and x < 10.

Every value also counts as true or false on its own. 0, 0.0, the empty string "", None and empty collections count as false; everything else counts as true. So if name: means "if name is not empty". Careful: "0" is a non-empty string, so it counts as true.

docs.title: Step 2: Decide with if, elif and else
Step 3: Repeat with while
docs.text:
A while loop repeats its block for as long as its condition is true.

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Go!")

3
2
1
Go!

To understand a loop, trace it: write down the variables on every pass.

Pass count at start count > 0? Prints 1 3 yes 3 2 2 yes 2 3 1 yes 1 — 0 no, loop ends Go! (after the loop)

Something inside the loop must eventually make the condition false. Delete count -= 1 and the loop never ends. If that happens, press Ctrl+C to stop the program.

docs.title: Step 4: Repeat with for and range
docs.text:
A for loop runs its block once for each item in a sequence. To loop over numbers, use range.

for i in range(5):
    print(i)       # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

range takes up to three numbers, and the same rule as slicing applies: the start is included, the stop is not.

Call Gives Count range(5) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 5 range(2, 6) 2, 3, 4, 5 4 range(2, 11, 3) 2, 5, 8 3 range(10, 0, -3) 10, 7, 4, 1 4 range(2, 11, 3) on a number line On a number line from 0 to 12, range of 2, 11, 3 starts at 2, adds 3 each time to reach 5 and 8, and stops before 11. The next value, 11, would equal the stop, so it is not included. 0123456789101112 +3 +3 +3 start stop: not included

Two questions to ask about any loop, before you run it:

  • What is the first value, and what is the last? For range(a, b), the first is a and the last is b - 1.
  • How many times does it run? For range(a, b), exactly b - a times.

If you want the numbers 1 to 10 inclusive, the stop is 11: range(1, 11). Getting this wrong by one is called an off-by-one error, and checking the first value, the last value and the count catches nearly all of them.

docs.title: Leave early with break and continue
docs.text:
• break ends the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this pass and moves to the next one.
for n in range(1, 10):
    if n % 4 == 0:
        continue        # skip multiples of 4
    if n > 7:
        break           # stop once we pass 7
    print(n)

This prints 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, one per line. Trace it on paper first to check you agree.

docs.title: Step 5: Produce formatted output
docs.text:
Most projects ask for output in an exact format. Combine loops with what you learned about print and f-strings.

Aligned columns. A format spec gives every number the same width:

n = 7
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(f"{n} x {i} = {n * i:2}")

7 x 1 =  7
7 x 2 = 14
7 x 3 = 21
7 x 4 = 28
7 x 5 = 35

A separator between items, not after the last one. A common requirement, and a common mistake. Decide on each pass whether you are at the end:

for i in range(1, 6):
    if i < 5:
        print(i, end=", ")
    else:
        print(i)

1, 2, 3, 4, 5

A loop inside a loop builds a grid. The inner loop prints one row; the empty print() after it ends the line.

for row in range(1, 4):
    for col in range(1, 5):
        print(f"{row * col:3}", end="")
    print()

  1  2  3  4
  2  4  6  8
  3  6  9 12

The outer loop runs 3 times and the inner loop runs 4 times for each, so the inner print runs 3 × 4 = 12 times.

docs.title: Step 6: Make your output deterministic, and prove it
docs.text:
A program is deterministic when the same input always produces exactly the same output. That is what the Checker relies on: it runs your script and compares the output with the expected output, byte for byte. An extra space at the end of a line, or a missing final newline, is a failure.

You can do the same comparison yourself. Save the expected output to a file, then:

./table.py > got.txt
diff got.txt expected.txt

No output from diff means the two are identical. Anything else shows you exactly which lines differ. To see invisible characters such as trailing spaces, run cat -A got.txt: every line end is shown as $, so a space before it is easy to spot.

AI in the loop

When a loop does not do what you expect, do not ask an assistant to fix it. Ask it to trace it: "Trace this loop pass by pass in a table, showing each variable at the start of every pass." Then compare its table with your own. Where they differ is where your understanding is off, and that is the thing to fix.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
IndentationError: expected an indented block

The line after if, for or while must be indented by four spaces. Check VS Code is set to spaces, not tabs, in the status bar.

The loop never ends

Nothing inside it changes the condition. Press Ctrl+C, then add the line that moves the loop towards its end, such as count -= 1.

My output is almost right but the Checker fails it

Run ./script.py | cat -A and look for spaces before the $, a missing last line, or a separator after the last item.

The loop runs one time too many, or too few

Write down the first value, the last value and the count of your range, and compare them with what the task asks for. The stop is never included.

docs.text: Code What it does if cond: / elif cond: / else: Run the first block whose condition is true while cond: Repeat while cond is true for x in range(a, b, step): Repeat for a, a + step, ... up to, not including, b break / continue Leave the loop / skip to the next pass print(x, end="") Print without a newline f"{x:3}", f"{x:02}" Width 3, or width 2 padded with zeros diff got.txt expected.txt Compare two outputs; silence means identical cat -A file Show invisible characters, with $ at each line end

Functions & Modularity

docs.title: Core Data Structures
docs.text:
90 min Python Needs: Functions & Modularity

Real programs work with collections: a list of users, a grid of values, a set of tags, a table of prices. Python has four built-in collections, and each is good at one thing. This tutorial covers all four, how to use them without crashing on unexpected input, and the one behaviour that surprises everyone: two names for the same list.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Choosing the right collection makes code shorter, faster and easier to read. Checking whether a word is in a set of ten thousand words is instant; in a list, Python checks them one by one.

The other half of this page is about edge cases: empty lists, missing keys, repeated values, indices that do not exist. Your code will meet all of them, because real data is messy and the Checker tests with exactly these inputs on purpose.

docs.title: The four collections
docs.text: Example Ordered Changeable Duplicates Use it for list [3, 1, 3] yes yes yes A sequence you add to, change and loop over tuple (3, 4) yes no yes A fixed group of values, such as a point or several return values set {1, 3} no yes no Unique items, membership tests, comparing groups dict {"a": 1} yes yes keys: no Looking values up by a key

docs.title: Step 1: Lists
docs.text:
A list is an ordered, changeable sequence. Indexing and slicing work exactly as they do on strings.

langs = ["python", "c", "javascript"]
langs[0]               # 'python'
langs[-1]              # 'javascript'
len(langs)             # 3

langs.append("sql")    # add to the end
langs.insert(1, "bash")
langs.pop()            # remove and return the last item: 'sql'
langs.remove("c")      # remove the first "c"
"go" in langs          # False

Unlike strings, lists are mutable: append, insert, pop and remove change the list itself and return nothing useful (except pop). Compare two ways to sort:

nums = [3, 1, 2]
s = sorted(nums)       # a NEW sorted list; nums is unchanged
nums.sort()            # sorts nums itself; returns None

new_list = old_list.sort() is a common bug: new_list is None.

docs.title: Loop with or without the index
docs.text:
for lang in langs:                 # when you only need the items
    print(lang)

for i in range(len(langs)):        # when you need the position too
    print(i, langs[i])

docs.title: Step 2: Two names, one list
docs.text:
This is the behaviour behind most list bugs.

Assignment shares a list; copy makes a new one After b equals a, both names point to the same list object, so appending through b also changes what a shows. After c equals a dot copy, c points to a separate new list, so changing c leaves a alone. b = a two names, one list a b [1, 2, 3, 4] b.append(4) → a is [1, 2, 3, 4] too c = a.copy() two names, two lists a c [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] c.append(5) → a is unchanged

A variable does not hold a list. It points to one. b = a does not copy anything; it gives the same list a second name.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]  a changed too: it is the same list

c = a.copy()    # a.copy(), a[:] and list(a) all make a new list
c.append(5)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]  unchanged
print(c)        # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

The same thing happens when you pass a list to a function. The parameter is another name for the caller's list, so a function that changes it changes the caller's data:

def add_bonus(scores):           # changes the list it was given
    for i in range(len(scores)):
        scores[i] += 5


def with_bonus(scores):          # builds and returns a new list
    return [s + 5 for s in scores]


marks = [70, 85]
new = with_bonus(marks)          # marks is still [70, 85]; new is [75, 90]
add_bonus(marks)                 # marks is now [75, 90]

Both are valid. What matters is that the function's name and docstring make clear which one it does. When a task says without modifying the original, build and return a new collection.

docs.title: Build a new list with a comprehension
docs.text:
The with_bonus function used a list comprehension: a short way to build a new list from an existing one.

[n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]]                 # [2, 4, 6]
[n for n in [4, 7, 10, 13] if n % 2 == 0]  # [4, 10]  only the even ones

Read it as "this expression, for each item, if this condition". It never changes the original list.

docs.title: Step 3: Access elements safely
docs.text:
items[i] raises an IndexError when i is out of range. When a function should cope with bad input instead of crashing, check first:

def item_at(items, index):
    """Return the item at index, or None if there is none."""
    if index < 0 or index >= len(items):
        return None
    return items[index]


item_at(["a", "b"], 1)     # 'b'
item_at(["a", "b"], 5)     # None
item_at([], 0)             # None: the empty list is handled too

Note the decision to reject negative indices. Python would accept items[-1], but if the task defines index as a position counted from 0, a negative number is invalid input. Read what the task means by valid, then check exactly that.

The same idea, without changing the original:

def replaced(items, index, value):
    """Return a copy of items with one element replaced."""
    copy = items[:]
    if 0 <= index < len(items):
        copy[index] = value
    return copy

docs.title: Step 4: Matrices
docs.text:
A matrix is a list of lists: each inner list is a row.

A matrix as a list of rows grid has two rows and three columns. grid at 0 is the row 1, 2, 3; grid at 1 is the row 4, 5, 6. grid at 1, 2 picks row 1, then column 2 inside it, which is 6. The outer loop goes over rows and the inner loop over the numbers in each row. col 0col 1col 2 grid[0] grid[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 grid[1][2] → 6 row 1 first, then column 2 each row is a list len(grid) = 2, len(grid[0]) = 3 outer loop: rows · inner loop: numbers in the row 
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6]]

grid[1][2]     # 6: row 1, then column 2
len(grid)      # 2 rows
len(grid[0])   # 3 columns

To print it, loop over rows, and over the numbers in each row. The cleanest way to put exactly one space between numbers, and none at the end, is join, which glues strings together with a separator:

for row in grid:
    print(" ".join(str(n) for n in row))

1 2 3
4 5 6

join only accepts strings, so each number is converted with str first, or with an f-string such as f"{n:2}" to align columns. A comprehension inside a comprehension builds a new matrix and leaves the original alone:

times_ten = [[n * 10 for n in row] for row in grid]
# [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]]; grid is unchanged

Edge case: an empty matrix, [[]], has one row with no numbers. The loop above prints one empty line, which is usually exactly what the task expects.

docs.title: Step 5: Tuples
docs.text:
A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed. Use one for a fixed group of values that belong together.

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point          # unpacking: x is 3, y is 4
point[0] = 1          # TypeError: tuples cannot be changed
x, y = y, x           # swap two variables in one line

Tuples are the clean way to return several values from a function. return a, b returns a tuple, and the caller unpacks it:

def min_max(numbers):
    """Return the smallest and largest number, or (None, None) if empty."""
    if not numbers:
        return None, None
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)


low, high = min_max([4, 9, 1])    # low is 1, high is 9
min_max([])                       # (None, None)

Notice the empty case returns the same shape: two values. The caller can always write low, high = min_max(...) without checking first. Returning a single None there would crash the unpacking.

docs.title: Step 6: Sets
docs.text:
A set holds unique values, in no particular order. Its strength is comparing groups.

Intersection and symmetric difference of two sets Alice knows python, git and sql. Bob knows git, javascript and python. The intersection, alice and bob, is the overlap: git and python. The symmetric difference, alice caret bob, is everything in exactly one of the two sets: sql and javascript. alice bob sql git python javascript alice & bob alice bob sql git python javascript alice ^ bob 
alice = {"python", "git", "sql"}
bob = {"git", "javascript", "python"}

alice & bob     # intersection:         {'git', 'python'}   in both
alice | bob     # union:                all four            in either
alice - bob     # difference:           {'sql'}             only in alice
alice ^ bob     # symmetric difference: {'javascript', 'sql'}  in exactly one

Sets also remove duplicates: set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) is {1, 2, 3}, and len(set(items)) counts the distinct values in a list.

Sets have no order

Printing a set can show its items in any order, and the order may change between runs. When output must be exact, sort it first: sorted(alice & bob) always gives ['git', 'python'].

docs.title: Step 7: Dictionaries
docs.text:
A dictionary maps keys to values. You look a value up by its key, not by a position.

stock = {"apples": 5, "pears": 2}

stock["apples"]          # 5
stock["kiwis"]           # KeyError: 'kiwis'
stock.get("kiwis")       # None: no error
stock.get("kiwis", 0)    # 0: a default of your choice
"pears" in stock         # True: `in` checks keys

stock["kiwis"] = 7       # add a new key
stock["apples"] += 1     # update an existing one
del stock["pears"]       # remove a key (KeyError if it is missing)

Loop over keys, or over keys and values together. For exact output, sort the keys:

for name in sorted(stock):
    print(f"{name}: {stock[name]}")

for name, qty in stock.items():
    ...

apples: 6
kiwis: 7

A dictionary is the natural way to count repeated values. Use get with a default of 0, so the first time a word appears is not a special case:

words = ["git", "python", "git", "sql", "git"]
counts = {}
for word in words:
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
# {'git': 3, 'python': 1, 'sql': 1}

docs.title: Step 8: Think about edge cases first
docs.text:
Before you write a function, list the awkward inputs and decide what it should do with each. Most failed checks are one of these.

Input Question to ask Usual answer Empty list [] What is the max of nothing? Return None, or the documented default Index out of range, or negative Crash, or return something? Check bounds; follow the task Missing key d[key] or d.get(key)? get with a default when missing is normal Repeated values Count them, or once each? dict to count, set to deduplicate None passed instead of a list Is that valid input? Check if items is None if the task allows it Original must not change Am I mutating it? Build and return a new collection

Then test the function with each of them, not only with the friendly example from the task.

AI in the loop

Assistants are good at finding edge cases you missed. Write your function first, then ask: "List inputs that could break this function or make it return something unexpected. Don't fix the code." Test each one yourself. Asking for the cases rather than the fix keeps the reasoning on your side.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
My original list changed and I did not touch it

Somewhere you have two names for one list: an assignment such as b = a, or a function that modifies its parameter. Copy with a[:] or a.copy(), or build a new list.

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...

You stored the result of a method that changes a list in place, such as nums = nums.sort(). Use nums.sort() on its own line, or nums = sorted(nums).

KeyError with a dictionary

The key is not there. Check with key in d, or read it with d.get(key, default).

My set output is in a different order from the expected output

Sets have no order. Sort before printing.

TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found

join needs strings. Convert each item: " ".join(str(n) for n in row).

docs.text:
• When to use a list, a tuple, a set and a dictionary
  • How to loop over a list and a matrix and print exact, formatted output
  • How to read or change a list element without risking an IndexError
  • Why b = a does not copy a list, and three ways that do
  • How to return a new collection instead of changing the input
  • How to return several values with a tuple, and unpack them
  • How to compute an intersection and a symmetric difference with sets
  • How to add, update, read and delete dictionary entries, safely
  • How you handle empty inputs, missing keys and repeated values

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Code What it does lst.append(x), lst.pop() Add to the end / remove the last sorted(lst) vs lst.sort() New sorted list / sort in place, returns None lst.copy(), lst[:] A new list with the same items [f(x) for x in lst if cond] Build a new list " ".join(str(x) for x in row) Items joined by single spaces return a, b / a, b = f() Return several values / unpack them s1 & s2, s1 ^ s2 Intersection / symmetric difference d.get(k, default) Read a key without a KeyError d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1 Count occurrences for k in sorted(d): Loop over keys in a fixed order

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Your functions now handle awkward input by checking for it. Next, learn what to do when something fails anyway.

Exception Handling

docs.title: Environment & First Programs
docs.text:
45 min Python Needs: WSL, VS Code

Before you write real programs, you need to know the two ways Python runs code, how to turn a file into a program you can run like any other command, and how to keep each project's packages separate. This tutorial covers all three.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Most beginner confusion in Python is not about the language. It is about the environment: code that prints in one place and not another, a package that is installed but "not found", a script that works on your laptop and fails on the Checker. Each of those has a simple cause, and you will meet all of them in this tutorial on purpose.

docs.title: Two ways to run Python
docs.text:
Interactive mode compared with a script In interactive mode you type one line at a time after the three-arrow prompt, and Python shows the value of every expression automatically: typing 2 plus 3 shows 5. In a script, Python runs the whole file from top to bottom and shows nothing unless you call print: the line 2 plus 3 produces no output, and print of 2 plus 3 prints 5. INTERACTIVE MODE python3 >>> 2 + 3 5 >>> x = 10 >>> x * 2 20 value shown for you statement: no output SCRIPT ./calc.py 2 + 3 print(2 + 3) $ ./calc.py 5 computed, then thrown away printed

Interactive mode is for trying things. You type one line, Python runs it and shows you the result straight away. A script is a file Python runs from top to bottom. It is what you submit for projects, and it shows only what you explicitly print.

docs.title: Step 1: Use the interpreter
docs.text:
Open the Ubuntu terminal and start the interpreter:

python3

Python 3.12.3 (main, ...) [GCC 13.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

The >>> is Python's prompt, the same idea as the shell's $. Leave with exit() or Ctrl+D.

docs.title: Expressions and statements
docs.text:
Python code is made of two kinds of thing.

  • An expression produces a value: 2 + 3, "hi".upper(), len("abc"), x * 2.
  • A statement does something: x = 10 stores a value, import math loads a module, if and for control what runs.

In interactive mode, when you type an expression on its own, Python shows its value. When you type a statement, it shows nothing, because there is no value to show. Predict each line, then try it:

You type Python shows Why 7 * 6 42 Expression: value shown answer = 7 * 6 nothing Assignment is a statement answer 42 Expression: value shown "python".upper() 'PYTHON' Expression, shown as Python writes it, with quotes print("python".upper()) PYTHON print writes the text itself, no quotes import math nothing Statement math.sqrt(16) 4.0 Expression

Look closely at the fourth and fifth rows. The interpreter shows a value the way you would type it in code ('PYTHON', with quotes). print shows it the way a person would read it (PYTHON). In a script only the second kind of output exists.

Ask Python, not Google

The interpreter has its own manual. help(str) describes every string method, help(print) describes print, and dir("text") lists everything you can call on a string. Press Q to leave a help page.

docs.title: Step 2: Write a portable, executable script
docs.text:
Make a folder for this module and a first script:

mkdir -p ~/holberton/python-basics
cd ~/holberton/python-basics
code calc.py
calc.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
2 + 3
print(2 + 3)

Make it executable and run it:

chmod u+x calc.py
./calc.py

You see 5 once. The bare 2 + 3 was calculated and thrown away, because a script never shows values on its own.

docs.title: Why #!/usr/bin/env python3
docs.text:
The first line is the shebang you met in Shell Basics. You could write #!/usr/bin/python3, but that only works on machines where Python lives at exactly that path. /usr/bin/env python3 asks the system to find python3 wherever it is installed, including inside the virtual environment you build in Step 4. That is what makes the script portable.

An executable script needs three things: the shebang on the first line, execute permission from chmod u+x, and Unix line endings (see When something goes wrong).

docs.title: Step 3: Global installs and isolated environments
docs.text:
pip installs Python packages. The question is where.

Global installation compared with virtual environments With a global installation, every project shares one set of packages in the system Python, so project A needing version 1 of a library and project B needing version 2 conflict. With virtual environments, each project has its own dot venv folder with its own packages, so the two versions live side by side and the system Python stays clean. GLOBAL: ONE SHARED SET System Python requests 1.x or 2.x? project A needs 1.x project B needs 2.x conflict: only one version fits ISOLATED: ONE VENV PER PROJECT System Python stays clean project A .venv requests 1.x project B .venv requests 2.x each project gets exactly what it needs

A global installation puts a package into the Python that the whole system shares. Every project sees it, which sounds convenient until two projects need different versions of the same package, or an install breaks a tool Ubuntu itself relies on.

A virtual environment, or venv, is a folder inside your project with its own copy of pip and its own packages. Activate it and Python uses that folder; deactivate it and you are back to the system. Nothing leaks between projects.

Recent Ubuntu versions enforce this. Try a global install:

pip install pycodestyle

error: externally-managed-environment
× This environment is externally managed

That error is Ubuntu protecting its own Python. It is pointing you at the right answer: a virtual environment.

docs.title: Step 4: Isolate a project with venv
docs.text:
Create a venv in your project folder and activate it:

cd ~/holberton/python-basics
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). Check which Python you are using:

which python3

/home/you/holberton/python-basics/.venv/bin/python3

That path is inside your project. Now install a development tool: pycodestyle, which checks your code against Python's official style guide. You use it in every project from the next tutorial on.

pip install pycodestyle
pycodestyle --version
pycodestyle calc.py

No error this time. Record what the project needs, so anyone can rebuild the same environment:

pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt

Now see the isolation for yourself:

deactivate
pycodestyle --version      # command not found: it only exists in the venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pycodestyle --version      # back again

The tool exists inside the environment and nowhere else. That is the whole idea.

A few habits to keep:

  • One venv per project, named .venv, inside the project folder.
  • Never commit it. Add .venv/ to your .gitignore. Commit requirements.txt instead; anyone can rebuild the venv with pip install -r requirements.txt.
  • Activate it every time you open a new terminal for the project. If (.venv) is missing from the prompt, you are using the system Python.

Point VS Code at the venv

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run Python: Select Interpreter and pick the one in ./.venv. VS Code then activates it in every new terminal and uses its packages for error checking.

AI in the loop

When you hit the externally-managed-environment error, an assistant may suggest --break-system-packages. Ask it what that flag breaks before you consider it. The honest answer is in the name: use a venv instead. This is a good habit in general: when a fix contains the words force or break, find out why.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
/usr/bin/env: 'python3\r': No such file or directory

The file has Windows line endings (CRLF). Linux reads the invisible \r as part of the program name. In VS Code, click CRLF in the status bar and change it to LF, then save. To stop it happening again, add "files.eol": "\n" to your VS Code settings.

Permission denied when running ./script.py

It is not executable yet. Run chmod u+x script.py.

The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available

Ubuntu's venv support is a separate package. Run sudo apt install -y python3-venv, then create the venv again.

python: command not found

Ubuntu calls it python3. Use python3, or inside an active venv, python also works.

I installed a package but Python says ModuleNotFoundError

You installed it in one environment and ran Python from another. Check the prompt shows (.venv) and that which python3 points inside your project, then install again.

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text:
60 min Python Needs: Core Data Structures

Programs fail. A user types letters where you expected a number, a list is empty, a key is missing. An exception is how Python reports a failure while the program is running. This tutorial shows you how to read one, catch the ones you expect, raise your own, and write functions that fail in a way their callers can rely on.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
There are two bad ways to deal with errors: ignore them, so the program crashes on the first odd input, or swallow all of them, so it carries on with wrong data and nobody knows why. Good code sits between the two. It handles the failures it expects, in a precise and visible way, and lets real bugs surface.

In the previous tutorial you prevented errors by checking first. This one adds the other tool: try it, and handle the failure. You need both.

docs.title: Step 1: Read a traceback
docs.text:
When an exception is not handled, Python stops and prints a traceback. Most people read it from the top. Read it from the bottom.

avg.py
def average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)


print(average([4, 8]))
print(average([]))

6.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/holberton/python-basics/avg.py", line 6, in <module>
    print(average([]))
          ~~~~~~~^^^^
  File "/home/you/holberton/python-basics/avg.py", line 2, in average
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
  1. The last line says what went wrong: the exception type, ZeroDivisionError, and a message.
  2. The frame above it says where: line 2, inside average. The ^ marks point at the exact operation.
  3. The frames above that say how you got there: line 6 called average with an empty list.

The fix is rarely on the last line of code shown. Here the division is fine; the question is what average should do with an empty list.

docs.title: Step 2: Know the common exceptions
docs.text:
Each exception type names a different kind of mistake. Recognising them on sight tells you where to look.

Exception Raised when Example TypeError A value is the wrong type for the operation "3" + 4 ValueError The type is right but the value is not int("forty") IndexError A list index is out of range [1, 2][5] KeyError A dictionary key is missing {"a": 1}["b"] ZeroDivisionError Dividing by zero 10 / 0 NameError A name is not defined, often a typo prnt("hi") AttributeError The object has no such method or attribute "text".push("x") FileNotFoundError A file to open does not exist open("missing.txt")

docs.title: Step 3: Catch a specific exception
docs.text:
Put the code that might fail in a try block, and say what to do if it fails in an except block naming the exception:

def ratio(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("b must not be zero")
    except TypeError:
        print("a and b must be numbers")
    return None


ratio(6, 3)       # 2.0
ratio(6, 0)       # prints "b must not be zero", returns None
ratio("6", 3)     # prints "a and b must be numbers", returns None

Python runs the try block. If an exception is raised, it jumps straight to the first except that matches the type, and the rest of the try block is skipped. If none matches, the exception carries on up to the caller as if there were no try at all.

To use the error message, name the exception with as:

try:
    value = settings["timeout"]
except KeyError as e:
    print(f"Missing key: {e}")       # Missing key: 'timeout'

You can catch several types in one clause with a tuple: except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:.

docs.title: Why catch specific exceptions
docs.text:
It is tempting to write except Exception: and catch everything. Look at what it hides:

prices = {"apple": 0.5}
try:
    total = prices["aple"] * quantity
except Exception:
    total = 0

total is 0 and nothing complains, yet there are two bugs: a typo in the key and a variable, quantity, that might not exist. A broad except turns bugs into silent wrong answers, which are far harder to find than a crash.

Catch only the exceptions you expect, and know what you will do about each. A bare except: with no type is worse still: it even catches Ctrl+C, so you cannot stop the program.

Keep the try block small, too. Wrap only the line that can fail in the way you expect, not the whole function.

docs.title: Step 4: else and finally
docs.text:
A try statement can have two more parts.

How try, except, else and finally run Python runs the try block. If no exception is raised, the else block runs. If a matching exception is raised, its except block runs. If an exception is raised that no except clause matches, neither runs. In all three cases the finally block runs next. Then the program continues after the try statement, except in the unmatched case, where the exception goes on to the caller. try else except ValueError (nothing matches) finally always runs no error ValueError other error carry on after try error goes to the caller
  • else runs only if the try block raised no exception. Put the code that depends on the try succeeding here, instead of inside the try, so that an error in it is not mistaken for the one you are catching.
  • finally runs no matter what: after success, after a handled exception, after an unhandled one, even after a return. Use it for clean-up that must always happen, such as closing a file or a connection, or reporting that a step finished.
def parse_age(text):
    try:
        age = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"Not a number: {text!r}")
        return None
    else:
        print(f"Parsed {age}")
        return age
    finally:
        print("Done checking")


parse_age("42")
parse_age("forty")

Parsed 42
Done checking
Not a number: 'forty'
Done checking

Notice that Done checking prints even though both branches have already reached a return. finally runs on the way out of the function, before the value is handed back.

docs.title: Step 5: Raise exceptions yourself
docs.text:
Your own functions can raise exceptions too. Do it when the caller passed something your function cannot sensibly handle. Silently returning a made-up value would hide their mistake.

def set_age(age):
    """Return age if it is valid; raise otherwise."""
    if not isinstance(age, int):
        raise TypeError("age must be an integer")
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("age must not be negative")
    return age

Pick the type that describes the problem, TypeError for the wrong kind of value and ValueError for a wrong value of the right kind, and write a message that says what was expected. The caller can then catch exactly that:

for value in [30, -1, "30"]:
    try:
        print(set_age(value))
    except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")

30
ValueError: age must not be negative
TypeError: age must be an integer

Inside an except block, a bare raise re-raises the exception you caught. Use it to note that something failed, for example by printing a message, while still letting the caller decide what to do about it.

docs.title: Step 6: Fail safely and predictably
docs.text:
A function fails safely when bad input never crashes the program unexpectedly and never produces a wrong answer that looks right. It fails predictably when the caller knows in advance what happens on failure, because the docstring says so.

There are two honest designs. Choose one per function and document it.

Return NoneRaise an exception

Catch the expected exceptions, report them on standard error, and return None. Good when failure is normal and the caller just needs to know there is no answer.

import sys


def safe_average(numbers):
    """Return the average of numbers, or None if it cannot be computed."""
    try:
        return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Cannot average an empty list", file=sys.stderr)
    except TypeError:
        print("All items must be numbers", file=sys.stderr)
    return None

Check the input and raise a specific exception with a helpful message. Good when bad input is the caller's mistake and they should fix it, not carry on.

def average(numbers):
    """Return the average of numbers.

    Raises ValueError if numbers is empty.
    """
    if not numbers:
        raise ValueError("numbers must not be empty")
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

print(..., file=sys.stderr) sends a message to standard error instead of standard output. Both appear in your terminal, but they are separate streams: anyone redirecting your program's output to a file, or a Checker comparing it, sees only the real output, not your error messages.

What a safe function must never do: return a value that looks valid when it is not, such as 0 for the average of nothing, or catch everything and carry on as if nothing happened.

AI in the loop

Paste a full traceback into an assistant and ask it to walk you through it from the bottom: which line failed, with what values, and how the program got there. Then ask "what inputs would make this function raise, and which of those should it handle?" Decide the answer to the second question yourself. That decision is the design of your function.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
My except block never runs

The exception raised is a different type from the one you catch. Read the last line of the traceback and catch that exact type.

The program keeps going with a wrong result, and I cannot see why

Look for a broad except Exception: or bare except:. Narrow it to the exception you expect, and the real bug will show itself.

My error message appears in the output and the Checker fails

Print error messages to standard error: print("message", file=sys.stderr), with import sys at the top.

finally printed something I did not expect

finally always runs, including after a return in try, except or else. Move code that should run only on success into else.
