docs.title: Database Design & Normalization
docs.text:
90 min Data & APIs Needs: SQL: Joins & Relationships

In the last tutorial the library already had a good schema. This time you start where real projects often start: one big table copied from a spreadsheet. You find the problems it causes, fix them one rule at a time with normalization, and move the data into the clean schema without losing a row.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A badly designed table works on day one. The trouble comes later: one customer with two email addresses, a product that cannot be added until someone orders it, history that disappears with a single delete. Those bugs live in the design, so no amount of careful code fixes them. Learning to see them before they happen is one of the most valuable skills in back-end work, and it is exactly what you will need to design the tables of your own projects.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Download the spreadsheet data and load it into a new database, design.db:

cd ~/library
curl -O https://evisp.github.io/augmented_software_engineering/assets/sql/loans_sheet.sql
sqlite3 design.db < loans_sheet.sql
sqlite3 design.db

Or download loans_sheet.sql from the browser. It creates two tables: loans_sheet, used in the steps, and orders_sheet, for the practice set. As in the last tutorial, the outputs use .headers on, .mode box and PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.

docs.title: Step 1: A spreadsheet in a database
docs.text:
The library used to track loans in a spreadsheet, one line per loan, with everything about the loan on that line. Imported as it was, it looks like this:

SELECT * FROM loans_sheet LIMIT 6;

┌────────────┬─────────────┬─────────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────┬───────────────────┐
│ loaned_on  │ returned_on │   member_name   │    member_email    │      book_title      │      author      │ author_country │       tags        │
├────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ 2026-09-02 │ 2026-09-16  │ Arta Hoxha      │ arta@example.com   │ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ George Orwell    │ United Kingdom │ classic, dystopia │
│ 2026-09-05 │ 2026-09-30  │ Besnik Krasniqi │ besnik@example.com │ Dune                 │ Frank Herbert    │ United States  │ classic, sci-fi   │
│ 2026-09-18 │ 2026-10-01  │ Arta Hoxha      │ arta@example.com   │ Kronikë në gur       │ Ismail Kadare    │ Albania        │ albanian          │
│ 2026-09-20 │ 2026-10-04  │ Drita Leka      │ drita@example.com  │ The Hobbit           │ J. R. R. Tolkien │ United Kingdom │ classic, fantasy  │
│ 2026-09-25 │             │ Erion Shehu     │ erion@example.com  │ Pride and Prejudice  │ Jane Austen      │ United Kingdom │ classic           │
│ 2026-10-01 │ 2026-10-12  │ Besnik Krasniqi │ besnik@example.com │ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ George Orwell    │ UK             │ classic, dystopia │
└────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────┴───────────────────┘

It is easy to read, and for a while it works. But look at how often the same facts repeat: Arta's email on every one of her loans, Orwell's country on every loan of every Orwell book. And one row already disagrees with the others: UK instead of United Kingdom.

docs.title: Step 2: Three anomalies
docs.text:
Repeated facts cause three kinds of bugs, called anomalies. Each demo below runs inside a transaction and ends with ROLLBACK, so the sheet stays as it was.

Update anomaly: a change must be made in many rows. Arta has a new email. Whoever updates the sheet changes it on her latest loan only, and now the database holds two emails for one person:

BEGIN;
UPDATE loans_sheet SET member_email = 'arta.hoxha@example.com'
WHERE loaned_on = '2026-10-22';
SELECT DISTINCT member_name, member_email FROM loans_sheet
WHERE member_name = 'Arta Hoxha';
ROLLBACK;

┌─────────────┬────────────────────────┐
│ member_name │      member_email      │
├─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
│ Arta Hoxha  │ arta@example.com       │
│ Arta Hoxha  │ arta.hoxha@example.com │
└─────────────┴────────────────────────┘

The UK row is the same bug, already in the data:

SELECT DISTINCT author, author_country FROM loans_sheet
WHERE author = 'George Orwell';

┌───────────────┬────────────────┐
│    author     │ author_country │
├───────────────┼────────────────┤
│ George Orwell │ United Kingdom │
│ George Orwell │ UK             │
└───────────────┴────────────────┘

Insert anomaly: a fact cannot be stored without another fact. Lea joins the library but has not borrowed anything yet. The only way to record her is a "loan" with no book, which every count of loans then gets wrong:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO loans_sheet (member_name, member_email)
VALUES ('Lea Marku', 'lea@example.com');
SELECT COUNT(*) AS loans FROM loans_sheet;
ROLLBACK;

┌───────┐
│ loans │
├───────┤
│ 13    │
└───────┘

The same goes for a new book on the shelf: until someone borrows it, there is nowhere to write its title and author.

Delete anomaly: removing one fact removes others. Pride and Prejudice has been borrowed once. Delete that loan, and the library forgets the book, and Jane Austen, entirely:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM loans_sheet WHERE book_title = 'Pride and Prejudice';
SELECT COUNT(*) AS austen_rows FROM loans_sheet WHERE author = 'Jane Austen';
ROLLBACK;

┌─────────────┐
│ austen_rows │
├─────────────┤
│ 0           │
└─────────────┘

All three have the same cause: one table holds facts about several different things, members, books, authors and loans. Normalization is the process of splitting it so that each fact is stored exactly once.

docs.title: Step 3: Keys and dependencies
docs.text:
To split a table well, you need two ideas.

A candidate key is a set of columns whose values identify each row, with nothing extra. In the sheet, one loan is identified by who borrowed which book when: member_email, book_title and loaned_on together. A key made of several columns is a composite key. Check that no two rows share it:

SELECT member_email, book_title, loaned_on, COUNT(*) AS rows
FROM loans_sheet
GROUP BY member_email, book_title, loaned_on
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

It returns no rows, so no duplicates. A query can only show that the current data has no duplicates, though; a key is a rule for all data, now and later. Could the same member borrow the same book twice? Yes, on different days, so loaned_on has to be part of the key.

A functional dependency says that one column decides another. If you know a member's email, you know their name: member_email → member_name. Draw every dependency in the sheet, and the problems light up:

What depends on what in the loans sheet member_email decides member_name, which depends on only part of the key. book_title decides author, and author decides author_country: part of the key, then a chain. book_title also decides tags, but tags holds a list in one cell. Only returned_on needs the whole key: member_email, book_title and loaned_on. member_email member_name book_title author author_country book_title tags: a list email + title + loaned_on returned_on Part of the key → 2NFa member fact: own table Part of the key, then a chain→ 2NF and 3NF: books, authors Several values in one cell→ 1NF: one row per tag Needs the whole keya loan fact: stays in loans

Only returned_on truly belongs to the loan. Everything else is a fact about a member, a book or an author that happens to be copied onto the loan. The three normal forms turn that picture into rules.

docs.title: Step 4: First normal form
docs.text:
1NF: every cell holds one value, and every row is unique. The tags column breaks it: 'classic, dystopia' is a list. To SQL, a list in a cell is just a string, so you cannot work with the tags inside it. Group by tag, and you get combinations instead:

SELECT tags, COUNT(*) AS loans FROM loans_sheet GROUP BY tags;

┌───────────────────┬───────┐
│       tags        │ loans │
├───────────────────┼───────┤
│ albanian          │ 3     │
│ classic           │ 1     │
│ classic, albanian │ 1     │
│ classic, dystopia │ 3     │
│ classic, fantasy  │ 2     │
│ classic, sci-fi   │ 2     │
└───────────────────┴───────┘

LIKE can find a tag inside the string, but it is fragile: searching for '%fi%' would match sci-fi and also any future fiction.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS loans FROM loans_sheet WHERE tags LIKE '%classic%';

┌───────┐
│ loans │
├───────┤
│ 9     │
└───────┘

The fix is one row per value:

From a list in a cell to one row per tag Before: Dune has the tags classic, sci-fi in one cell, and The Hobbit has classic, fantasy. After: four rows, Dune classic, Dune sci-fi, The Hobbit classic and The Hobbit fantasy. NOT 1NF · a list in a cell1NF · one value per cell book_titletags Duneclassic, sci-fi The Hobbitclassic, fantasy book_titletag Duneclassic Dunesci-fi The Hobbitclassic The Hobbitfantasy

In the final schema those rows live in the junction table book_tags, with a tags table holding each tag's name once. Then "loans per tag" is an ordinary join and GROUP BY.

docs.title: Step 5: Second normal form
docs.text:
2NF: 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole key, not on part of it. The sheet's key is member_email + book_title + loaned_on. But member_name depends on member_email alone, and author on book_title alone. Those are partial dependencies, and they are exactly the repeated facts behind the anomalies.

The fix: move each group of facts to a table whose key is the part they depend on.

Table Key Columns members email name books title author, author_country loans email + title + loaned_on returned_on

Now Arta's name is stored once, in members, and a book can exist before anyone borrows it.

docs.title: Step 6: Third normal form
docs.text:
3NF: 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column. Look at books from Step 5: title decides author, and author decides author_country. The country is a fact about the author, reached through a chain. That is a transitive dependency, and it is why UK and United Kingdom could disagree.

The fix is the same move: the author's facts go to their own table.

Table Key Columns authors name country books title author

A common way to remember the three forms: every column depends on the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF).

docs.title: Natural keys or surrogate keys?
docs.text:
So far the keys are natural keys, values from the real world: emails, titles, names. They have two problems. They change: Arta just changed her email, and every loan pointing at the old one would need updating. And they are not always unique: two different books can have the same title.

So the final schema gives every table a surrogate key: an id number with no meaning outside the database, which never needs to change. The natural values stay as ordinary columns, with UNIQUE where they must not repeat, like members.email.

docs.title: Step 7: The normalized schema
docs.text:
Put it all together and you arrive at the schema of the last tutorial, without the library cards:

erDiagram
    authors ||--o{ books : writes
    books ||--o{ loans : "is lent in"
    members ||--o{ loans : borrows
    books ||--o{ book_tags : has
    tags ||--o{ book_tags : labels
    authors {
        integer id PK
        text name
        text country
    }
    books {
        integer id PK
        text title
        integer author_id FK
        integer year
    }
    members {
        integer id PK
        text name
        text email
        text joined_on
    }
    loans {
        integer id PK
        integer book_id FK
        integer member_id FK
        text loaned_on
        text returned_on
    }
    tags {
        integer id PK
        text name
    }
    book_tags {
        integer book_id PK, FK
        integer tag_id PK, FK
    }

Create the tables in design.db, next to the sheet:

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE authors (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name    TEXT NOT NULL,
    country TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE books (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    title     TEXT    NOT NULL,
    author_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES authors (id),
    year      INTEGER CHECK (year BETWEEN 1400 AND 2100)
);

CREATE TABLE members (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    email     TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    joined_on TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    book_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id),
    member_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES members (id),
    loaned_on   TEXT    NOT NULL,
    returned_on TEXT,
    CHECK (returned_on IS NULL OR returned_on >= loaned_on)
);

CREATE TABLE tags (
    id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE book_tags (
    book_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id),
    tag_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES tags (id),
    PRIMARY KEY (book_id, tag_id)
);

.tables

authors       books         loans_sheet   orders_sheet
book_tags     loans         members       tags

docs.title: Step 8: Move the data
docs.text:
Now copy the sheet's data into the new tables. The tool is INSERT ... SELECT: instead of VALUES, the rows come from a query.

Clean first. Every inconsistency in the sheet would be copied into the new tables. Look at the distinct authors:

SELECT DISTINCT author, author_country FROM loans_sheet ORDER BY author;

┌──────────────────┬────────────────┐
│      author      │ author_country │
├──────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Frank Herbert    │ United States  │
│ George Orwell    │ United Kingdom │
│ George Orwell    │ UK             │
│ Ismail Kadare    │ Albania        │
│ J. R. R. Tolkien │ United Kingdom │
│ Jane Austen      │ United Kingdom │
└──────────────────┴────────────────┘

Orwell appears twice. Fix the data before moving it:

UPDATE loans_sheet SET author_country = 'United Kingdom'
WHERE author_country = 'UK';
SELECT changes() AS fixed;

┌───────┐
│ fixed │
├───────┤
│ 1     │
└───────┘

Authors. SELECT DISTINCT gives each author once:

INSERT INTO authors (name, country)
SELECT DISTINCT author, author_country FROM loans_sheet ORDER BY author;
SELECT * FROM authors;

┌────┬──────────────────┬────────────────┐
│ id │       name       │    country     │
├────┼──────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ 1  │ Frank Herbert    │ United States  │
│ 2  │ George Orwell    │ United Kingdom │
│ 3  │ Ismail Kadare    │ Albania        │
│ 4  │ J. R. R. Tolkien │ United Kingdom │
│ 5  │ Jane Austen      │ United Kingdom │
└────┴──────────────────┴────────────────┘

Books. Each distinct title, with its author's new id, found by joining on the name:

INSERT INTO books (title, author_id)
SELECT DISTINCT s.book_title, a.id
FROM loans_sheet AS s
JOIN authors AS a ON a.name = s.author
ORDER BY s.book_title;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS books FROM books;

┌───────┐
│ books │
├───────┤
│ 8     │
└───────┘

The sheet never recorded the year a book was published, so year stays NULL. Migrations often reveal missing data like this.

Members. The sheet does not know when each member joined either, but joined_on is required. The best evidence we have is the first loan, so the migration uses that. Decisions like this one belong in writing, as you will see in Step 11.

INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on)
SELECT member_name, member_email, MIN(loaned_on)
FROM loans_sheet
GROUP BY member_email
ORDER BY MIN(loaned_on);
SELECT * FROM members;

┌────┬─────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────┐
│ id │      name       │       email        │ joined_on  │
├────┼─────────────────┼────────────────────┼────────────┤
│ 1  │ Arta Hoxha      │ arta@example.com   │ 2026-09-02 │
│ 2  │ Besnik Krasniqi │ besnik@example.com │ 2026-09-05 │
│ 3  │ Drita Leka      │ drita@example.com  │ 2026-09-20 │
│ 4  │ Erion Shehu     │ erion@example.com  │ 2026-09-25 │
└────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────┘

Loans. Each sheet row becomes one loan, with the ids looked up by title and email:

INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on, returned_on)
SELECT b.id, m.id, s.loaned_on, s.returned_on
FROM loans_sheet AS s
JOIN books AS b ON b.title = s.book_title
JOIN members AS m ON m.email = s.member_email
ORDER BY s.loaned_on;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS loans FROM loans;

┌───────┐
│ loans │
├───────┤
│ 12    │
└───────┘

Tags. Splitting a list inside a cell is awkward in SQL, which is the 1NF problem again. Here, insert the five tag names directly, then link each book to every tag whose name appears in its list:

INSERT INTO tags (name) VALUES
    ('albanian'), ('classic'), ('dystopia'), ('fantasy'), ('sci-fi');

INSERT INTO book_tags (book_id, tag_id)
SELECT DISTINCT b.id, t.id
FROM loans_sheet AS s
JOIN books AS b ON b.title = s.book_title
JOIN tags AS t ON s.tags LIKE '%' || t.name || '%';
SELECT COUNT(*) AS book_tags FROM book_tags;

┌───────────┐
│ book_tags │
├───────────┤
│ 13        │
└───────────┘

Check that nothing was lost. Rebuild the sheet from the new tables with joins, and subtract it from the original with EXCEPT, which returns the rows of the first query that are not in the second:

SELECT s.loaned_on, s.returned_on, s.member_name, s.member_email,
       s.book_title, s.author, s.author_country
FROM loans_sheet AS s
EXCEPT
SELECT l.loaned_on, l.returned_on, m.name, m.email,
       b.title, a.name, a.country
FROM loans AS l
JOIN members AS m ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id;

It returns no rows: every row of the sheet can be rebuilt from the normalized tables. And the counts agree:

SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans_sheet) AS sheet_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans) AS loans;

┌────────────┬───────┐
│ sheet_rows │ loans │
├────────────┼───────┤
│ 12         │ 12    │
└────────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Step 9: Let the database enforce the rules
docs.text:
Normalization removes duplicated facts. Constraints stop wrong facts from getting in at all. The schema above uses all of the common ones:

Constraint Rule In the schema PRIMARY KEY Unique, identifies the row every id; book_tags has a composite one NOT NULL A value is required books.title, loans.loaned_on, ... UNIQUE No two rows share the value members.email, tags.name REFERENCES Must point at an existing row every ..._id column CHECK (...) Must make the condition true a sensible year; returned after loaned DEFAULT Value used when none is given DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, in the CRUD tutorial

Each one turns a bug that could happen into an error that must be dealt with at once. Now that the data is in, try to break the rules:

UPDATE loans SET returned_on = '2026-01-01' WHERE id = 1;

Runtime error: CHECK constraint failed: returned_on IS NULL OR returned_on >= loaned_on (19)

UPDATE books SET year = 19650 WHERE title = 'Dune';

Runtime error: CHECK constraint failed: year BETWEEN 1400 AND 2100 (19)

INSERT INTO members (name, email) VALUES ('Nobody', 'nobody@example.com');

Runtime error: NOT NULL constraint failed: members.joined_on (19)

A good rule of thumb: if a rule about the data is always true, write it into the schema. Code can forget a rule; the database never does.

docs.title: Step 10: The anomalies, gone
docs.text:
Run the three anomalies from Step 2 against the new tables.

Update. Arta's new email is one change, in one row:

UPDATE members SET email = 'arta.hoxha@example.com' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT changes() AS changed;

┌─────────┐
│ changed │
├─────────┤
│ 1       │
└─────────┘

Insert. Lea can join without a loan, and a new book can arrive before anyone borrows it:

INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on)
VALUES ('Lea Marku', 'lea@example.com', '2026-09-01');
INSERT INTO authors (name, country) VALUES ('Chinua Achebe', 'Nigeria');
INSERT INTO books (title, author_id, year)
VALUES ('Things Fall Apart', last_insert_rowid(), 1958);
SELECT b.title, a.name FROM books AS b JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.title = 'Things Fall Apart';

┌───────────────────┬───────────────┐
│       title       │     name      │
├───────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ Things Fall Apart │ Chinua Achebe │
└───────────────────┴───────────────┘

last_insert_rowid() is the id of the row just inserted, here Achebe's.

Delete. Deleting the only loan of Pride and Prejudice no longer deletes the book:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM loans
WHERE book_id = (SELECT id FROM books WHERE title = 'Pride and Prejudice');
SELECT title FROM books WHERE title = 'Pride and Prejudice';
ROLLBACK;

┌─────────────────────┐
│        title        │
├─────────────────────┤
│ Pride and Prejudice │
└─────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 11: Design decisions
docs.text:
Normalization gives you rules; design still takes judgement. Here are the decisions you will meet most often.

Stored or computed? The books table in the CRUD tutorial had an available column. The normalized schema has none: a book is available when it has no open loan, and that can be computed:

SELECT b.title,
       NOT EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l
           WHERE l.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL
       ) AS available
FROM books AS b
ORDER BY b.title;

┌────────────────────────────────┬───────────┐
│             title              │ available │
├────────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
│ Animal Farm                    │ 1         │
│ Dune                           │ 0         │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ 1         │
│ Kronikë në gur                 │ 1         │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four           │ 1         │
│ Pride and Prejudice            │ 0         │
│ Prilli i thyer                 │ 0         │
│ The Hobbit                     │ 0         │
│ Things Fall Apart              │ 1         │
└────────────────────────────────┴───────────┘

A stored available is faster to read, but it is a second copy of a fact that loans already holds, and the two can disagree: a loan recorded, the flag not updated. A computed value can never be wrong. Start with computed values; store a copy only when you have measured a real need, and then keep it in sync deliberately.

When repeating data is right. A supplier's price for a book changes over time. An order must keep the price paid on that day, even though it looks like a copy of the book's price. That is not duplication: it is a different fact, "the price on this order". You will design exactly that in the practice set.

Write decisions down. A design decision record is a short note next to the schema, for the next person, who may be you in six months:

DECISIONS.md
## DDR-002: Availability is computed, not stored

Context: a book is available when it has no loan without a return date.
Decision: no `available` column; compute it from `loans` when needed.
Consequence: one source of truth. If the query becomes slow, add an
index on loans (book_id, returned_on) before considering a stored flag.

## DDR-003: Members' joined_on during migration

Context: the old sheet never recorded when members joined.
Decision: use each member's first loan date.
Consequence: some dates are later than the real ones.

Discuss with a peer

Pick one and argue both sides for five minutes:

  1. Should loans store the member's name too, "to save a join"?
  2. Should members.email be the primary key instead of id?
  3. A book can have two authors. What changes in the schema?

AI in the loop

Describe your data to an assistant and it will propose a schema in seconds. Treat the proposal as a draft to check, not a design. Ask it to list the functional dependencies it assumed, and check each one against your real data: can two members share an email? can a book have two authors? A schema is a set of claims about the world; only you know whether they are true.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
UNIQUE constraint failed during a migration

The source data has two different spellings of what should be one row, or the same row twice. Find them with SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, clean the source, and run the INSERT ... SELECT again.

NOT NULL constraint failed during a migration

The new schema requires a value the old data does not have. Decide on a value, document the decision, and supply it in the SELECT, as MIN(loaned_on) did for joined_on.

A migrated table has more rows than expected

A join in the INSERT ... SELECT matched more than once, often because a name or title is not unique. Run the SELECT alone and count its rows before inserting.

table authors already exists

You ran the CREATE TABLE statements twice. To start over, drop the new tables, children first: book_tags, tags, loans, members, books, authors. Then reload loans_sheet.sql.

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
The library also kept its book orders in a spreadsheet, orders_sheet, loaded together with the loans:

SELECT * FROM orders_sheet;

┌────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
│ ordered_on │      supplier      │  supplier_phone  │   book_title   │      author      │ quantity │ unit_price │
├────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────┼────────────┤
│ 2026-08-03 │ Tirana Book Supply │ +355 69 000 0001 │ Dune           │ Frank Herbert    │ 3        │ 1200       │
│ 2026-08-03 │ Tirana Book Supply │ +355 69 000 0001 │ The Hobbit     │ J. R. R. Tolkien │ 2        │ 1100       │
│ 2026-08-17 │ North Books        │ +355 69 000 0002 │ Kronikë në gur │ Ismail Kadare    │ 5        │ 900        │
│ 2026-09-01 │ Tirana Book Supply │ +355 69 000 0001 │ Animal Farm    │ George Orwell    │ 4        │ 700        │
│ 2026-09-01 │ Tirana Book Supply │ +355 69 000 0001 │ Dune           │ Frank Herbert    │ 2        │ 1250       │
│ 2026-09-15 │ North Books        │ +355 69 000 0002 │ Prilli i thyer │ Ismail Kadare    │ 3        │ 950        │
└────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────┴────────────┘

Run these in design.db, after the steps above: the answers use the normalized books table.

1. The key. Which columns identify one row of orders_sheet? Check that no two rows share them.

Answer

One line of an order: the date, the supplier and the book.

SELECT ordered_on, supplier, book_title, COUNT(*) AS rows
FROM orders_sheet
GROUP BY ordered_on, supplier, book_title
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

No rows, so no duplicates in the current data.

2. Dependencies. Write down the functional dependencies. Which ones break 2NF or 3NF?

Answer
  • supplier → supplier_phone: depends on part of the key, so 2NF is broken. Suppliers get their own table.
  • book_title → author: part of the key again. The book already exists in books.
  • ordered_on + supplier → the order itself: both lines of 3 August belong to one order. That is a fact about the order, separate from its lines.
  • ordered_on + supplier + book_title → quantity, unit_price: these need the whole key, so they stay on the order line.

3. The price. Should unit_price move to the books table?

Answer

No. Dune cost 1200 in August and 1250 in September:

SELECT ordered_on, book_title, unit_price FROM orders_sheet
WHERE book_title = 'Dune';

┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
│ ordered_on │ book_title │ unit_price │
├────────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
│ 2026-08-03 │ Dune       │ 1200       │
│ 2026-09-01 │ Dune       │ 1250       │
└────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

The price depends on the order line, not on the book alone. Moving it to books would rewrite the history of past orders.

4. The schema. Write the CREATE TABLE statements: suppliers, orders, and order lines that point at books.

Answer 
CREATE TABLE suppliers (
    id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    phone TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    supplier_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES suppliers (id),
    ordered_on  TEXT    NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_lines (
    order_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id),
    book_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id),
    quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    unit_price INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, book_id)
);

5. Migrate. Fill the three tables from orders_sheet with INSERT ... SELECT, and count the rows.

Answer 
INSERT INTO suppliers (name, phone)
SELECT DISTINCT supplier, supplier_phone FROM orders_sheet ORDER BY supplier;

INSERT INTO orders (supplier_id, ordered_on)
SELECT DISTINCT p.id, o.ordered_on
FROM orders_sheet AS o
JOIN suppliers AS p ON p.name = o.supplier
ORDER BY o.ordered_on;

INSERT INTO order_lines (order_id, book_id, quantity, unit_price)
SELECT r.id, b.id, o.quantity, o.unit_price
FROM orders_sheet AS o
JOIN suppliers AS p ON p.name = o.supplier
JOIN orders AS r ON r.supplier_id = p.id AND r.ordered_on = o.ordered_on
JOIN books AS b ON b.title = o.book_title;

SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM suppliers) AS suppliers,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_lines) AS lines;

┌───────────┬────────┬───────┐
│ suppliers │ orders │ lines │
├───────────┼────────┼───────┤
│ 2         │ 4      │ 6     │
└───────────┴────────┴───────┘

Six sheet rows became four orders with six lines: the two orders that had two lines each became one order each.

6. Use it. Show each order's date, supplier and total cost.

Answer 
SELECT r.ordered_on, p.name AS supplier,
       SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders AS r
JOIN suppliers AS p ON r.supplier_id = p.id
JOIN order_lines AS l ON l.order_id = r.id
GROUP BY r.id
ORDER BY r.ordered_on;

┌────────────┬────────────────────┬───────┐
│ ordered_on │      supplier      │ total │
├────────────┼────────────────────┼───────┤
│ 2026-08-03 │ Tirana Book Supply │ 5800  │
│ 2026-08-17 │ North Books        │ 4500  │
│ 2026-09-01 │ Tirana Book Supply │ 5300  │
│ 2026-09-15 │ North Books        │ 2850  │
└────────────┴────────────────────┴───────┘

7. Draw it. Write the ER diagram of the four tables in Mermaid.

Answer

Paste it into mermaid.live to see it drawn:

erDiagram
    suppliers ||--o{ orders : receives
    orders ||--|{ order_lines : contains
    books ||--o{ order_lines : "appears in"

||--|{ means one order has one or more lines: an order with no lines makes no sense.

docs.title: Explain it to someone
docs.text:
• What update, insert and delete anomalies are, with an example of each
  • What a candidate key, a composite key and a functional dependency are
  • The rules of 1NF, 2NF and 3NF, and the problem each one removes
  • The difference between natural and surrogate keys
  • How to turn a set of facts into tables, and draw them as an ER diagram
  • Which constraints a schema can enforce, and why to enforce rules in the database
  • How to migrate data with INSERT ... SELECT, and check that nothing was lost
  • When to compute a value instead of storing it, and when repeating data is correct
  • What a design decision record is for

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Idea In one line Update anomaly One fact in many rows: change one, the others disagree Insert anomaly Cannot store a fact until an unrelated fact exists Delete anomaly Removing one fact removes others with it 1NF One value per cell, unique rows 2NF No column depends on only part of a composite key 3NF No column depends on another non-key column Surrogate key A meaningless id that never changes INSERT INTO t (cols) SELECT ... Copy rows from a query into a table SELECT DISTINCT ... Each different row once query1 EXCEPT query2 Rows of the first that are not in the second CHECK (condition) A rule every row must satisfy

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You can now design a database, fill it and query it. Next, you connect it to Python properly: instead of writing SQL strings by hand, you map tables to classes and work with rows as objects, with an ORM.

Object-Relational Mapping

docs.title: File Handling
docs.text:
75 min Data & APIs Needs: Exception Handling

Every program you have written so far forgets everything the moment it stops. A file is the simplest way to keep data: write it once, read it back tomorrow. In this tutorial you open, write, read and close text files, and save structured data as JSON, all on a small library's book list.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Almost every program touches files: settings, logs, exports, data someone else produced. And JSON is how programs pass data to each other: the configuration of a tool, the answer from a web API, the body of a request. Once you can read and write it, a whole world of data opens up.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Python 3 in your WSL terminal and VS Code, as set up in Environment & First Programs. Create a practice folder and download the two files this tutorial uses:

mkdir -p ~/library && cd ~/library
curl -O https://evisp.github.io/augmented_software_engineering/assets/files/books.txt
curl -O https://evisp.github.io/augmented_software_engineering/assets/files/catalog.json
ls

You can also download them from the browser: books.txt and catalog.json.

books.txt lists ten books, one per line, with the title, author and year separated by semicolons:

books.txt
Kronikë në gur;Ismail Kadare;1971
Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur;Ismail Kadare;1963
The Little Prince;Antoine de Saint-Exupéry;1943
Nineteen Eighty-Four;George Orwell;1949
Things Fall Apart;Chinua Achebe;1958
Pride and Prejudice;Jane Austen;1813
Dune;Frank Herbert;1965
The Hobbit;J. R. R. Tolkien;1937
Don Quixote;Miguel de Cervantes;1605
One Hundred Years of Solitude;Gabriel García Márquez;1967

Create every script in this tutorial inside ~/library, and run it from there with python3 name.py. You will see why that matters in the first step. If you mess up a file, download it again.

docs.title: Step 1: Files and paths
docs.text:
A file is a named piece of data on disk. A text file, like books.txt, holds characters. On disk, each character is stored as one or more bytes, and the rule that maps characters to bytes is the encoding. The modern standard is UTF-8, which can store any character: ë, é, ç, Chinese, emoji.

To open a file, Python needs its path, the directions to it:

Absolute and relative paths A folder tree: the root folder contains home, which contains ada, which contains library, which holds books.txt and where.py. The absolute path /home/ada/library/books.txt starts at the root. The terminal is in the library folder, so the relative path books.txt starts there. / home ada library books.txt where.py ◀ the terminal is here ABSOLUTE PATH · starts at the root, / RELATIVE PATH · starts at the current folder /home/ada/library/books.txt books.txt Works from anywhere, but only on this computer. Short, but only correct from ~/library. Run from elsewhere: FileNotFoundError.
  • An absolute path starts at the root, /, and works from anywhere.
  • A relative path, like books.txt, is looked up from the current working directory: the folder your terminal is in when you run python3. Not the folder the script is in.

Python tells you the current working directory:

where.py
import os

print(os.getcwd())

python3 where.py

/home/ada/library

These examples run as a user called ada; your folder will show your own user name.

Try it

From ~/library, run cd .. and then python3 library/where.py. What does it print, and would open("books.txt") still work?

Answer

It prints /home/ada, the folder the terminal is in, even though the script is in library. A relative books.txt would now be looked up in /home/ada, and fail with FileNotFoundError. Run your scripts from the folder that holds the files.

docs.title: Step 2: Open and close a file
docs.text:
open() connects your program to a file and returns a file object. You read and write through that object, then close it:

first_open.py
file = open("books.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")
print(file)
print(file.read(25))
file.close()
print(file.closed)

<_io.TextIOWrapper name='books.txt' mode='r' encoding='utf-8'>
Kronikë në gur;Ismail Kad
True

open() takes three things:

  • the path, here "books.txt";
  • the mode, "r" for read. It is the default, so you can leave it out, as later examples do;
  • the encoding, here "utf-8".

file.read(25) read the first 25 characters, and after close(), file.closed is True.

Always pass encoding="utf-8". Without it, Python uses your system's default, which differs between computers. With the wrong encoding, books.txt cannot even be read, because of the ë in the very first title:

wrong_encoding.py
file = open("books.txt", encoding="ascii")
print(file.read())
file.close()

UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0xc3 in position 6: ordinal not in range(128)

Try it

Open catalog.json and print its first 40 characters.

Answer try_open.py
file = open("catalog.json", encoding="utf-8")
print(file.read(40))
file.close()

[
  {
    "title": "Kronikë në gur",

docs.title: Step 3: Choose a mode
docs.text:
The mode decides what open() does to the file, and it matters most when the file already exists:

What r, w and a do to a file that exists The file holds two lines, Dune and The Hobbit. Opened with r, the content stays and the cursor is at the start, ready to read. Opened with w, the file is emptied immediately. Opened with a, the content stays and the cursor is at the end, so new text is added after it. open(path, "r") open(path, "w") open(path, "a") BEFOREBEFOREBEFORE AFTER OPENINGAFTER OPENINGAFTER OPENING DuneThe Hobbit DuneThe Hobbit DuneThe Hobbit DuneThe Hobbit DuneThe Hobbit emptied at once unchanged · cursor at the start content gone · cursor at the start unchanged · cursor at the end Mode Meaning File exists File missing "r" read reads from the start FileNotFoundError "w" write empties it first, then writes creates it "a" append keeps it, writes at the end creates it "x" create FileExistsError creates it

The red bar in the diagram is the cursor: the position where the next read or write happens. Step 7 is about it.

"w" empties the file when it opens, not when it writes

Opening a file with "w" deletes its content immediately, even if you never write anything:

w_empties.py
file = open("scratch.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
file.write("first version\n")
file.close()

file = open("scratch.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
file.close()

file = open("scratch.txt", encoding="utf-8")
print(repr(file.read()))
file.close()

''

When you want to add to a file, use "a". When you must not overwrite an existing file, use "x", which refuses.

docs.title: Step 4: Write text
docs.text:
write() writes a string and returns how many characters it wrote. It does not start a new line: you add "\n", the newline character, yourself.

write_list.py
file = open("reading-list.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
file.write("Dune\n")
file.write("The Hobbit\n")
count = file.write("Kronikë në gur\n")
file.close()
print(count)

15

Kronikë në gur is 14 characters, plus the newline: 15. Look at the result from the terminal:

cat reading-list.txt

Dune
The Hobbit
Kronikë në gur

Now add a book with mode "a":

append_list.py
file = open("reading-list.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8")
file.write("Don Quixote\n")
file.close()

Run it twice, then look again:

Dune
The Hobbit
Kronikë në gur
Don Quixote
Don Quixote

Append never removes anything: each run adds one more line. That is what you want for a log, and a surprise if you expected a single copy.

Forget the "\n", and the lines run together:

no_newline.py
file = open("squashed.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
file.write("Dune")
file.write("The Hobbit")
file.close()

DuneThe Hobbit

print() can also write to a file, with file=. It adds the newline for you:

print_file.py
file = open("shortlist.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
print("Dune", file=file)
print("The Hobbit", file=file)
file.close()

Try it

Write a function add_title(path, title) that adds one title to the end of a list file, on its own line. Call it twice to start a wishlist.txt.

Answer add_title.py
def add_title(path, title):
    """Add one title to the end of a list file, on its own line."""
    file = open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8")
    file.write(title + "\n")
    file.close()


add_title("wishlist.txt", "Things Fall Apart")
add_title("wishlist.txt", "Pride and Prejudice")

cat wishlist.txt

Things Fall Apart
Pride and Prejudice

docs.title: Step 5: Read a file
docs.text:
Python gives you four ways to read text:

Call Returns file.read() the whole file, as one string file.readline() the next line, as a string, "\n" included file.readlines() all the lines, as a list of strings for line in file: one line at a time, in a loop

Every line you read ends with the newline character, "\n". repr() shows it:

read_line.py
file = open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8")
first = file.readline()
print(repr(first))
file.close()

'Kronikë në gur;Ismail Kadare;1971\n'

That is why you usually remove it with rstrip("\n") before using the line. Then split(";") cuts the line into its three parts. Every book from before 1900:

old_books.py
file = open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8")
for line in file:
    title, author, year = line.rstrip("\n").split(";")
    if int(year) < 1900:
        print(f"{title} ({year}), {author}")
file.close()

Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Austen
Don Quixote (1605), Miguel de Cervantes

readlines() and read() load the whole file at once, which is fine for small files:

read_all.py
file = open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8")
lines = file.readlines()
file.close()
print(len(lines))
print(repr(lines[-1]))

file = open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8")
text = file.read()
file.close()
print(text.count("Kadare"))

10
'One Hundred Years of Solitude;Gabriel García Márquez;1967\n'
2

The loop, for line in file:, reads one line at a time and never holds the whole file in memory. Prefer it: it works the same on a file of ten lines and on one of ten million.

Try it

Find the oldest book in books.txt and print its title and year.

Answer oldest.py
oldest_title = None
oldest_year = None

file = open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8")
for line in file:
    title, author, year = line.rstrip("\n").split(";")
    if oldest_year is None or int(year) < oldest_year:
        oldest_title, oldest_year = title, int(year)
file.close()

print(f"Oldest: {oldest_title} ({oldest_year})")

Oldest: Don Quixote (1605)

docs.title: Step 6: Close files with with
docs.text:
Closing a file is not a formality. Python buffers what you write: it collects it in memory and saves it to disk in batches, and the last batch is only saved when the file is closed. Until then, other programs, or even your own, may see nothing:

buffer_demo.py
writer = open("buffer-demo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
writer.write("not saved yet\n")

reader = open("buffer-demo.txt", encoding="utf-8")
print(repr(reader.read()))

writer.close()
print(repr(reader.read()))
reader.close()

''
'not saved yet\n'

The second open() read an empty file. Only after writer.close() was the text really on disk.

The danger is an error between open() and close(): the close() never runs. The with statement solves it. It closes the file when the block ends, whatever happens inside:

with_read.py
with open("reading-list.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read(), end="")

print(file.closed)

Dune
The Hobbit
Kronikë në gur
Don Quixote
Don Quixote
True

Even when an exception interrupts the block, the file is closed:

with_error.py
try:
    with open("reading-list.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        for line in file:
            year = int(line)
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

print(file.closed)

Error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'Dune\n'
True

From here on, every example uses with. One with can open several files. This one copies just the titles from books.txt into a new file:

titles_only.py
with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as source, \
        open("titles.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as target:
    for line in source:
        title = line.split(";")[0]
        target.write(title + "\n")

head -n 4 titles.txt

Kronikë në gur
Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur
The Little Prince
Nineteen Eighty-Four

Try it

Rewrite add_title from Step 4 with with.

Answer add_title_with.py
def add_title(path, title):
    """Add one title to the end of a list file, on its own line."""
    with open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        file.write(title + "\n")


add_title("wishlist.txt", "Dune")

Things Fall Apart
Pride and Prejudice
Dune

docs.title: Step 7: Move the cursor
docs.text:
An open file remembers a cursor: the position of the next read or write. Each read moves it forward. tell() reports where it is, and seek() moves it.

The cursor moves forward as you read The file starts with the characters D, u, n, e, a newline, then The Hobbit and another newline. The cursor starts at position 0. After readline the cursor is at position 5, at the start of the second line. seek(0) moves it back to the start. Dune The Hobbit \n\n 0516 tell() → 0 after readline(): tell() → 5 seek(0) cursor.py
with open("reading-list.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.tell())
    print(repr(file.readline()))
    print(file.tell())
    print(repr(file.read()))
    print(repr(file.read()))
    file.seek(0)
    print(repr(file.readline()))

0
'Dune\n'
5
'The Hobbit\nKronikë në gur\nDon Quixote\nDon Quixote\n'
''
'Dune\n'

Notice the last read() returned '': the cursor was already at the end, so there was nothing left. That is the classic "my second read is empty" bug. seek(0) goes back to the start.

Positions in text files

In a text file, tell() counts bytes, not characters, and ë takes two bytes in UTF-8. So with text files, only seek() to 0 or to a number that tell() gave you earlier.

Try it

In a single with block, count the lines of books.txt, then go back and read the first line again.

Answer twice.py
with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    count = len(file.readlines())
    file.seek(0)
    first = file.readline().rstrip("\n")

print(count, "books")
print("First:", first)

10 books
First: Kronikë në gur;Ismail Kadare;1971

docs.title: Step 8: Handle missing files
docs.text:
Opening a file can fail, and the error says why:

Exception Cause FileNotFoundError No file at that path, in mode "r" PermissionError The file's permissions do not allow it IsADirectoryError The path is a folder, not a file FileExistsError The file exists, in mode "x"

Catch the one you expect with try and except, as in Exception Handling. A missing list is often just an empty list:

missing.py
def read_titles(path):
    """Return the lines of a list file, or an empty list if it is missing."""
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
            return [line.rstrip("\n") for line in file]
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"No file called {path}, starting with an empty list")
        return []


print(read_titles("reading-list.txt"))
print(read_titles("favourites.txt"))

['Dune', 'The Hobbit', 'Kronikë në gur', 'Don Quixote', 'Don Quixote']
No file called favourites.txt, starting with an empty list
[]

And a file with no read permission:

echo "secret" > locked.txt
chmod 000 locked.txt
python3 -c 'open("locked.txt", encoding="utf-8")'

PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'locked.txt'

Try it

What happens with open("~/library/books.txt", encoding="utf-8")? The file is right there.

Answer tilde.py
file = open("~/library/books.txt", encoding="utf-8")

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '~/library/books.txt'

~ is a shortcut that the shell understands, not Python. Python looks for a folder literally called ~. Expand it first:

tilde_fix.py
import os

path = os.path.expanduser("~/library/books.txt")
print(path)
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.readline(), end="")

/home/ada/library/books.txt
Kronikë në gur;Ismail Kadare;1971

docs.title: Step 9: Save data as JSON
docs.text:
Lines of text suit a simple list. But a catalog has structure: each book has a title, a year that is a number, a yes-or-no available, and a list of tags. For that, use JSON, a text format for data. Here is the start of catalog.json:

catalog.json
[
  {
    "title": "Kronikë në gur",
    "author": "Ismail Kadare",
    "year": 1971,
    "available": true,
    "tags": ["albanian", "novel"]
  },
  {
    "title": "The Little Prince",
    "author": "Antoine de Saint-Exupéry",
    "year": 1943,
    "available": false,
    "tags": ["classic", "children"]
  },
  ...

JSON looks like Python, with a few differences:

Python JSON dict object {...}, keys always strings in double quotes list, tuple array [...] str string, in double quotes int, float number True, False true, false None null

Turning data into text like this is called serialisation; turning the text back into data is deserialisation. The json module does both, with four functions:

The four json functions Python data, such as a list of dictionaries, becomes a JSON string with json.dumps, and comes back with json.loads. json.dump writes Python data straight into an open file, and json.load reads it back from the file. Going towards text is serialisation; coming back is deserialisation. PYTHON DATAJSON TEXTFILE ON DISK {"year": 1965, "available": True} '{"year": 1965, "available": true}' catalog.json dumps loads serialise: json.dump(data, file) deserialise: data = json.load(file)

The s stands for string: dumps and loads work with strings, dump and load work with files.

json_text.py
import json

book = {
    "title": "Dune",
    "author": "Frank Herbert",
    "year": 1965,
    "available": True,
    "tags": ["sci-fi"],
    "borrower": None,
}

text = json.dumps(book)
print(text)
print(type(text).__name__)

back = json.loads(text)
print(back == book)

{"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert", "year": 1965, "available": true, "tags": ["sci-fi"], "borrower": null}
str
True

Notice the changes in the text: True became true, None became null, and everything is in double quotes. loads turned it back into an equal dictionary.

Reading a JSON file gives you ordinary Python lists and dictionaries:

load_catalog.py
import json

with open("catalog.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    catalog = json.load(file)

print(type(catalog).__name__, len(catalog))
print(catalog[0]["title"], catalog[0]["tags"])

for book in catalog:
    if book["available"]:
        print("-", book["title"])

list 6
Kronikë në gur ['albanian', 'novel']
- Kronikë në gur
- Nineteen Eighty-Four
- Pride and Prejudice
- The Hobbit

To save, change the data and dump it back. indent=2 makes the file readable for people, and ensure_ascii=False keeps letters such as ë as they are:

save_catalog.py
import json

with open("catalog.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    catalog = json.load(file)

catalog.append({
    "title": "Things Fall Apart",
    "author": "Chinua Achebe",
    "year": 1958,
    "available": True,
    "tags": ["classic", "novel"],
})

with open("catalog.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    json.dump(catalog, file, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

print(len(catalog), "books saved")

7 books saved

tail -n 9 catalog.json

    "author": "Chinua Achebe",
    "year": 1958,
    "available": true,
    "tags": [
      "classic",
      "novel"
    ]
  }
]

Without ensure_ascii=False, JSON escapes every non-English letter. Still valid, but hard to read:

ascii.py
import json

print(json.dumps("Kronikë në gur"))
print(json.dumps("Kronikë në gur", ensure_ascii=False))

"Kronik\u00eb n\u00eb gur"
"Kronikë në gur"

JSON cannot store everything Python can. Keys become strings, tuples come back as lists, sets are refused, and text that is not valid JSON cannot be loaded:

json_limits.py
import json

print(json.loads(json.dumps({1: "one"})))
print(json.loads(json.dumps(("Dune", 1965))))

try:
    json.dumps({"Dune", "The Hobbit"})
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)

try:
    json.loads("{'title': 'Dune'}")
except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
    print("JSONDecodeError:", error)

{'1': 'one'}
['Dune', 1965]
TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable
JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)

The last one is the most common JSON mistake: single quotes are not JSON.

Try it

Load catalog.json and list the titles of the books tagged "classic".

Answer count_tag.py
import json

with open("catalog.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    catalog = json.load(file)

classics = [book["title"] for book in catalog if "classic" in book["tags"]]
print(len(classics), classics)

4 ['The Little Prince', 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', 'Pride and Prejudice', 'Things Fall Apart']

docs.title: Step 10: Save objects as JSON
docs.text:
In Object-Oriented Design you modelled data with classes. A library would have a Book class. But json only knows dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and None. An object of your own class is refused:

not_serializable.py
import json


class Book:
    """A book in the library catalog."""

    def __init__(self, title, year):
        self.title = title
        self.year = year


dune = Book("Dune", 1965)
try:
    json.dumps(dune)
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)

TypeError: Object of type Book is not JSON serializable

The usual solution: give the class two methods that translate between an object and a dictionary. to_dict() turns the object into a dictionary that json can save, and the class method from_dict() builds an object back from a loaded dictionary. Then two small functions save and load a whole list of books:

book.py
"""A Book class that can be saved to and loaded from JSON."""
import json


class Book:
    """A book in the library catalog."""

    def __init__(self, title, author, year, available=True):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.year = year
        self.available = available

    def __repr__(self):
        state = "in" if self.available else "out"
        return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.year}, {state})"

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the book as a dictionary that json can save."""
        return {
            "title": self.title,
            "author": self.author,
            "year": self.year,
            "available": self.available,
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data):
        """Build a book from a dictionary loaded from JSON."""
        return cls(data["title"], data["author"], data["year"],
                   data["available"])


def save_books(path, books):
    """Save a list of books to a JSON file."""
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        json.dump([book.to_dict() for book in books], file,
                  indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)


def load_books(path):
    """Load a list of books from a JSON file."""
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
        return [Book.from_dict(data) for data in json.load(file)]

from_dict reads only the keys it needs, so it can even load the books in catalog.json, which have extra tags:

shelf.py
from book import load_books, save_books

shelf = load_books("catalog.json")
print(shelf[:3])

shelf[0].available = False
save_books("shelf.json", shelf)

again = load_books("shelf.json")
print(again[0])
print(again[0] is shelf[0], again[0].title == shelf[0].title)

[Book('Kronikë në gur', 1971, in), Book('The Little Prince', 1943, out), Book('Nineteen Eighty-Four', 1949, in)]
Book('Kronikë në gur', 1971, out)
False True

head -n 8 shelf.json

[
  {
    "title": "Kronikë në gur",
    "author": "Ismail Kadare",
    "year": 1971,
    "available": false
  },
  {

The loaded book is a new object with the same data: is is False, but the titles match. That is what deserialisation means: you get the data back, not the same object.

What about vars()?

For a simple object, vars(book), or book.__dict__, already gives a dictionary of its attributes:

vars_demo.py
from book import Book

dune = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965)
print(vars(dune))

{'title': 'Dune', 'author': 'Frank Herbert', 'year': 1965, 'available': True}

It is a handy shortcut. An explicit to_dict() is safer: you choose exactly what goes into the file, and renaming an attribute later does not silently change your file format.

Try it

Add a borrower attribute to Book, None by default, and save it in to_dict(). Make sure from_dict() can still load shelf.json, which was saved before borrower existed.

Answer book_borrower.py
"""Book with a borrower: still loads files saved before the change."""
import json


class Book:
    """A book in the library catalog."""

    def __init__(self, title, author, year, available=True, borrower=None):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.year = year
        self.available = available
        self.borrower = borrower

    def to_dict(self):
        """Return the book as a dictionary that json can save."""
        return {
            "title": self.title,
            "author": self.author,
            "year": self.year,
            "available": self.available,
            "borrower": self.borrower,
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data):
        """Build a book from a dictionary loaded from JSON."""
        return cls(data["title"], data["author"], data["year"],
                   data["available"], data.get("borrower"))


with open("shelf.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    shelf = [Book.from_dict(data) for data in json.load(file)]

print(shelf[0].title, shelf[0].borrower)
shelf[0].borrower = "Ada"
print(json.dumps(shelf[0].to_dict(), ensure_ascii=False))

Kronikë në gur None
{"title": "Kronikë në gur", "author": "Ismail Kadare", "year": 1971, "available": false, "borrower": "Ada"}

data.get("borrower") returns None when the key is missing, where data["borrower"] would raise KeyError. Old files keep loading.

AI in the loop

Assistants write file code in seconds, and one wrong letter in a mode destroys data: a "w" where you meant "a" empties the file without a word. Before you run file code you did not write, find every open() and say out loud which file it touches and in which mode. Try it on a copy of your data first.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
FileNotFoundError, but the file is right there

The path is relative and the terminal is in another folder. Run pwd and ls; cd to the folder with the file, or use an absolute path. Also check for ~ in the path (see Step 8) and for typos in the extension: book.txt is not books.txt.

UnicodeDecodeError

The file was opened without encoding="utf-8", or with the wrong encoding. Add encoding="utf-8" to every open().

My file is empty after the script ran

It was opened with "w", which empties the file as it opens. To add to a file, use "a".

Every line prints with an empty line after it

Each line ends with "\n", and print() adds another. Use line.rstrip("\n"), or print(line, end="").

The second read returns nothing

The cursor is at the end of the file. seek(0) goes back to the start, or read the file once into a variable and reuse it.

json.decoder.JSONDecodeError

The text is not valid JSON. The usual causes are single quotes, a comma after the last item, or an empty file. The message gives the line and column of the problem.

TypeError: Object of type ... is not JSON serializable

You passed something json does not know: a set, or an object of your own class. Convert it first: list(the_set), or the_object.to_dict().

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
Seven exercises, from easy to harder. All of them run in ~/library, on books.txt and on catalog.json as you left it after Step 9, with seven books. Try each one before you open the answer.

1. Count. Print how many books books.txt lists, and how many of them are by Ismail Kadare.

Answer p1_count.py
total = 0
kadare = 0

with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        title, author, year = line.rstrip("\n").split(";")
        total += 1
        if author == "Ismail Kadare":
            kadare += 1

print(f"{total} books, {kadare} by Ismail Kadare")

10 books, 2 by Ismail Kadare

2. Authors. Write every author in books.txt to authors.txt, each one once, in alphabetical order.

Answer p2_authors.py
authors = set()

with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        authors.add(line.split(";")[1])

with open("authors.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for author in sorted(authors):
        file.write(author + "\n")

print(len(authors), "authors written")

9 authors written

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
Chinua Achebe
Frank Herbert
Gabriel García Márquez
George Orwell
Ismail Kadare
J. R. R. Tolkien
Jane Austen
Miguel de Cervantes

3. Numbered list. Write numbered.txt, with lines such as 1. Kronikë në gur (1971).

Answer p3_numbered.py
with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as source, \
        open("numbered.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as target:
    for number, line in enumerate(source, start=1):
        title, author, year = line.rstrip("\n").split(";")
        target.write(f"{number}. {title} ({year})\n")

head -n 4 numbered.txt

1. Kronikë në gur (1971)
2. Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur (1963)
3. The Little Prince (1943)
4. Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949)

4. Text to JSON. Convert books.txt into books.json: a list of dictionaries with title, author and year, where year is a number, not a string.

Answer p4_to_json.py
import json

books = []
with open("books.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        title, author, year = line.rstrip("\n").split(";")
        books.append({"title": title, "author": author, "year": int(year)})

with open("books.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    json.dump(books, file, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

print(len(books), "books converted")

10 books converted

5. Report. From catalog.json, print how many books are available, and list the borrowed ones, oldest first.

Answer p5_report.py
import json

with open("catalog.json", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    catalog = json.load(file)

available = [book for book in catalog if book["available"]]
borrowed = [book for book in catalog if not book["available"]]

print(f"{len(available)} of {len(catalog)} books available")
print("Borrowed:")
for book in sorted(borrowed, key=lambda book: book["year"]):
    print(f"  {book['year']}  {book['title']}")

5 of 7 books available
Borrowed:
  1943  The Little Prince
  1965  Dune

6. Safe loading. Write load_or_empty(path), which returns the data in a JSON file, or [] if the file is missing or is not valid JSON, with a warning in that second case. Test it on an empty file.

Answer p6_safe_load.py
import json


def load_or_empty(path):
    """Return the data in a JSON file, or [] if it is missing or broken."""
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
            return json.load(file)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return []
    except json.JSONDecodeError as error:
        print(f"Warning: {path} is not valid JSON ({error})")
        return []


open("empty.json", "w", encoding="utf-8").close()

print(len(load_or_empty("catalog.json")))
print(load_or_empty("nothing-here.json"))
print(load_or_empty("empty.json"))

7
[]
Warning: empty.json is not valid JSON (Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0))
[]

7. Borrow a book. Write borrow(path, title), which loads the catalog, marks the book as not available, and saves the file. It should refuse a book that is already borrowed, or that does not exist.

Answer p7_borrow.py
import json


def borrow(path, title):
    """Mark a book in a catalog file as borrowed, and save the file."""
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:
        catalog = json.load(file)

    for book in catalog:
        if book["title"] == title:
            if not book["available"]:
                print(f"{title} is already borrowed")
                return False
            book["available"] = False
            with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                json.dump(catalog, file, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
            print(f"{title} borrowed")
            return True

    print(f"No book called {title}")
    return False


borrow("catalog.json", "The Hobbit")
borrow("catalog.json", "The Hobbit")
borrow("catalog.json", "Ulysses")

The Hobbit borrowed
The Hobbit is already borrowed
No book called Ulysses

Run the report from exercise 5 again, and The Hobbit is now borrowed:

4 of 7 books available
Borrowed:
  1937  The Hobbit
  1943  The Little Prince
  1965  Dune
