docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Code What it does open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") Open a file; mode "r", "w", "a" or "x" with open(...) as file: Open, and close automatically when the block ends file.write(text) Write text; add "\n" yourself print(text, file=file) Write text and a newline file.read() The whole file as one string file.readline() / file.readlines() One line / all lines as a list for line in file: Line by line line.rstrip("\n") Remove the newline at the end file.tell() / file.seek(0) Where the cursor is / back to the start os.getcwd() The current working directory json.dumps(data) / json.loads(text) Data to a JSON string / back json.dump(data, file, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) Save data to a JSON file json.load(file) Load data from a JSON file obj.to_dict() / Cls.from_dict(data) Your own class to JSON-ready data / back

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Files are perfect for a list or a settings file. But when you need to find, sort, count and change thousands of records, and keep them correct while several programs use them, you need a database. Next, SQL.

SQL: CRUD Operations

docs.title: Object-Relational Mapping
docs.text:
2 h Data & APIs Needs: Database Design & Normalization

So far you have written SQL by hand and got rows back as tuples. An object-relational mapper, or ORM, lets you work with the database through Python classes instead: a table becomes a class, a row becomes an object, and the ORM writes the SQL for you. In this tutorial you map the library database with SQLAlchemy, the most widely used ORM in Python, and read, create, change and delete data without writing a single SQL string.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Almost every Python web application talks to its database through an ORM. It removes a lot of repetitive code, keeps queries safe from injection, and lets you follow links between tables as easily as following attributes: book.author.name. It also hides the SQL, which is exactly why you learned SQL first: when an ORM is slow or does something surprising, the answer is always in the SQL it generates.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need the library database from SQL: Joins & Relationships. Reload it, so your results match this page:

cd ~/library
sqlite3 library.db < library.sql

SQLAlchemy is a package, so install it in a virtual environment, as in Environment & First Programs:

sudo apt install -y python3-venv     # only if the next line fails
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install sqlalchemy
python3 -c "import sqlalchemy; print(sqlalchemy.__version__)"

2.1.6

Any version from 2.0 up works with this page. Create every file in ~/library, next to library.db, and run it with the venv active.

docs.title: Step 1: What an ORM does
docs.text:
An ORM connects two worlds that organise data differently:

How an ORM maps classes to tables On the Python side, the class Book with attributes id, title, author_id and year, and one object, Dune. On the database side, the books table with the same columns, and one row for Dune. A class maps to a table, an attribute to a column, and an object to a row. SQLAlchemy sits between them and turns Python calls into SQL. PYTHONDATABASE class Book id: inttitle: strauthor_id: intyear: int | None dune = Book(...) dune.title = "Dune"dune.year = 1965dune.author → Author TABLE books id INTEGERtitle TEXTauthor_id INTEGERyear INTEGER one row 8 | Dune | 5 | 1965author_id 5 → authors SQLAlchemy writes the SQL class ↔ table, attribute ↔ columnobject ↔ row, relationship ↔ foreign key Python Database a class, Book a table, books an attribute, title a column, title an object, dune a row a relationship, dune.author a foreign key, author_id

You describe the mapping once, in models: classes that say which table and columns they stand for. From then on you ask for objects, and SQLAlchemy writes the SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

docs.title: Step 2: Map your first classes
docs.text:
Create models.py with two models, for authors and books:

models.py
"""SQLAlchemy models for the library database: a first version."""
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    """The base class of every model."""


class Author(Base):
    """A row of the authors table."""

    __tablename__ = "authors"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    country: Mapped[str | None]

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Author({self.name!r})"


class Book(Base):
    """A row of the books table."""

    __tablename__ = "books"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str]
    author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("authors.id"))
    year: Mapped[int | None]

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.year})"
  • Every model inherits from one Base class, made from DeclarativeBase. Base keeps the list of all your tables.
  • __tablename__ names the table the class stands for.
  • Each Mapped[...] line is a column, and its type comes from the annotation: Mapped[int] is an integer column that cannot be NULL, Mapped[int | None] one that can.
  • mapped_column(...) adds details: primary_key=True, or ForeignKey("authors.id") for a foreign key.

The tables already exist in library.db, so these classes just describe them.

docs.title: Step 3: Engine, session and a first query
docs.text:
Two objects connect your models to the database:

  • the engine knows where the database is, from a URL: sqlite:///library.db is the file library.db in the current folder. Three slashes; four would mean an absolute path;
  • a session is one conversation with the database. You open it, ask for objects or change them, and close it.
first_query.py
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Book

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///library.db")

with Session(engine) as session:
    books = session.scalars(select(Book).order_by(Book.year).limit(4)).all()

print(books)
first = books[0]
print(type(first).__name__, first.id, first.title, first.author_id)

[Book('Pride and Prejudice', 1813), Book('The Hobbit', 1937), Book('Animal Farm', 1945), Book('Nineteen Eighty-Four', 1949)]
Book 7 Pride and Prejudice 4

select(Book) builds a query for Book objects; session.scalars(...) runs it and gives you the objects, and .all() collects them in a list. What comes back are real Book objects, with attributes, not tuples.

docs.title: Step 4: See the SQL
docs.text:
A query object prints as the SQL it stands for:

show_sql.py
from sqlalchemy import select

from models import Book

query = select(Book).where(Book.year < 1950).order_by(Book.year)
print(query)

SELECT books.id, books.title, books.author_id, books.year
FROM books
WHERE books.year < :year_1 ORDER BY books.year

That is the same SELECT you would write by hand. :year_1 is a placeholder: the value 1950 is sent separately, exactly like the ? in sqlite3. An ORM always uses placeholders, so its queries are safe from SQL injection.

Whenever an ORM query surprises you, print it.

docs.title: Step 5: Query with select
docs.text:
The usual operations, side by side with the SQL they produce:

SQLAlchemy SQL session.get(Book, 8) ... WHERE id = 8 (by primary key) select(Book).where(Book.year < 1950) WHERE year < 1950 .where(cond1, cond2) WHERE cond1 AND cond2 .order_by(Book.year.desc()) ORDER BY year DESC .limit(3).offset(3) LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3 session.scalars(query).all() every row, as objects session.scalars(query).first() the first row, or None session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Book)) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books reading.py
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, func, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Book

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///library.db")

with Session(engine) as session:
    print(session.get(Book, 8))
    print(session.get(Book, 99))

    old = session.scalars(
        select(Book).where(Book.year < 1950).order_by(Book.year)
    ).all()
    print(old)

    kadare = session.scalars(
        select(Book).where(Book.author_id == 1, Book.year > 1965)
    ).all()
    print(kadare)

    newest = session.scalars(select(Book).order_by(Book.year.desc())).first()
    print(newest)

    count = session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Book))
    print(count, "books")

Book('Dune', 1965)
None
[Book('Pride and Prejudice', 1813), Book('The Hobbit', 1937), Book('Animal Farm', 1945), Book('Nineteen Eighty-Four', 1949)]
[Book('Kronikë në gur', 1971), Book('Prilli i thyer', 1978)]
Book('Prilli i thyer', 1978)
10 books

session.get returns None when there is no such row, so check it before you use the result. Conditions are written with ordinary Python operators on the class attributes: Book.year < 1950 does not compare anything yet; it builds a piece of SQL.

Try it

Print the titles of the books published in the 1940s, oldest first.

Answer

Book.year.between(1940, 1949) is the ORM's BETWEEN:

query = (select(Book.title)
         .where(Book.year.between(1940, 1949))
         .order_by(Book.year))
print(session.scalars(query).all())

['Animal Farm', 'Nineteen Eighty-Four']

docs.title: Step 6: Relationships
docs.text:
Columns are only half of the mapping. The other half is the links between tables. Replace models.py with the full version, which maps all seven tables:

models.py
"""SQLAlchemy models for the library database, library.db."""
from sqlalchemy import Column, ForeignKey, Table, create_engine, event
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    """The base class of every model."""


book_tags = Table(
    "book_tags",
    Base.metadata,
    Column("book_id", ForeignKey("books.id"), primary_key=True),
    Column("tag_id", ForeignKey("tags.id"), primary_key=True),
)


class Author(Base):
    """A row of the authors table."""

    __tablename__ = "authors"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    country: Mapped[str | None]

    books: Mapped[list["Book"]] = relationship(back_populates="author")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Author({self.name!r})"


class Book(Base):
    """A row of the books table."""

    __tablename__ = "books"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str]
    author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("authors.id"))
    year: Mapped[int | None]

    author: Mapped["Author"] = relationship(back_populates="books")
    tags: Mapped[list["Tag"]] = relationship(
        secondary=book_tags, back_populates="books"
    )
    loans: Mapped[list["Loan"]] = relationship(back_populates="book")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.year})"


class Member(Base):
    """A row of the members table."""

    __tablename__ = "members"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True)
    joined_on: Mapped[str]

    card: Mapped["LibraryCard | None"] = relationship(back_populates="member")
    loans: Mapped[list["Loan"]] = relationship(back_populates="member")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Member({self.name!r})"


class LibraryCard(Base):
    """A row of the library_cards table: at most one per member."""

    __tablename__ = "library_cards"

    member_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        ForeignKey("members.id"), primary_key=True
    )
    card_number: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True)
    expires_on: Mapped[str]

    member: Mapped["Member"] = relationship(back_populates="card")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"LibraryCard({self.card_number!r})"


class Loan(Base):
    """A row of the loans table: one member borrowing one book."""

    __tablename__ = "loans"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    book_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("books.id"))
    member_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("members.id"))
    loaned_on: Mapped[str]
    returned_on: Mapped[str | None]

    book: Mapped["Book"] = relationship(back_populates="loans")
    member: Mapped["Member"] = relationship(back_populates="loans")

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Loan({self.book.title!r}, {self.loaned_on})"


class Tag(Base):
    """A row of the tags table."""

    __tablename__ = "tags"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True)

    books: Mapped[list["Book"]] = relationship(
        secondary=book_tags, back_populates="tags"
    )

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Tag({self.name!r})"


def make_engine(path="library.db"):
    """Return an engine for a SQLite file, with foreign keys turned on."""
    engine = create_engine(f"sqlite:///{path}")

    @event.listens_for(engine, "connect")
    def turn_on_foreign_keys(dbapi_connection, connection_record):
        dbapi_connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")

    return engine

New things in this version:

  • relationship() adds an attribute that follows a foreign key. Book.author gives the Author object, and Author.books the list of that author's books. back_populates connects the two sides, so changing one updates the other.
  • One-to-one. Member.card is annotated "LibraryCard | None", a single object or nothing, instead of a list.
  • Many-to-many. book_tags is a plain Table, not a class: it only holds two foreign keys. relationship(secondary=book_tags) tells SQLAlchemy to go through it, so book.tags is a list of Tag objects.
  • make_engine() turns on foreign keys for every connection, the same PRAGMA as in the SQL tutorials, using an event that runs each time SQLAlchemy connects.

Now follow the links like attributes:

relations.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Book, Member, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    dune = session.get(Book, 8)
    print(dune.author, dune.author.country)
    print([tag.name for tag in dune.tags])

    kadare = session.scalars(
        select(Author).where(Author.name == "Ismail Kadare")
    ).one()
    print(kadare.books)

    arta = session.get(Member, 1)
    print(arta.card)
    for loan in arta.loans:
        print(" ", loan.loaned_on, loan.book.title, loan.returned_on)

    lea = session.get(Member, 5)
    print(lea.card, lea.loans)

Author('Frank Herbert') United States
['classic', 'sci-fi']
[Book('Kronikë në gur', 1971), Book('Prilli i thyer', 1978), Book('Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur', 1963)]
LibraryCard('LIB-0001')
  2026-09-02 Nineteen Eighty-Four 2026-09-16
  2026-09-18 Kronikë në gur 2026-10-01
  2026-10-03 Prilli i thyer None
  2026-10-22 The Hobbit None
None []

No joins written anywhere: each attribute access runs the query it needs. Lea has no card and no loans, so she gets None and [].

docs.title: Step 7: Create
docs.text:
To add a row, create an object, add it to the session, and commit:

create.py
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Book, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    le_guin = session.get(Author, 8)
    earthsea = Book(title="A Wizard of Earthsea", year=1968, author=le_guin)
    session.add(earthsea)
    print("before commit:", earthsea.id)
    session.commit()
    print("after commit:", earthsea.id)

    mjeda = Author(name="Ndre Mjeda", country="Albania",
                   books=[Book(title="Juvenilia", year=1917)])
    session.add(mjeda)
    session.commit()
    print(mjeda.id, mjeda.books, mjeda.books[0].id)

before commit: None
after commit: 11
9 [Book('Juvenilia', 1917)] 12
  • Before the commit, the new book has no id: the database assigns it during the INSERT, and SQLAlchemy fills it in.
  • author=le_guin sets the relationship, and SQLAlchemy works out author_id from it. You think in objects, not ids.
  • Adding Mjeda also added his book: objects reachable through a relationship are saved with it. This is called a cascade.

docs.title: Step 8: Update
docs.text:
To change a row, change the object's attributes and commit. The session notices what changed, and lists those objects in session.dirty:

update.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Book, Loan, Tag, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    loan = session.get(Loan, 12)
    loan.returned_on = "2026-10-31"
    print(session.dirty)

    achebe_book = session.get(Book, 10)
    classic = session.scalars(select(Tag).where(Tag.name == "classic")).one()
    achebe_book.tags.append(classic)

    session.commit()
    print(loan, loan.returned_on)
    print(achebe_book.tags)

IdentitySet([Loan('The Hobbit', 2026-10-22)])
Loan('The Hobbit', 2026-10-22) 2026-10-31
[Tag('classic')]

achebe_book.tags.append(classic) added a row to the junction table book_tags, without you ever naming it. The commit sends every pending change in one transaction: all of them are saved, or none.

docs.title: Step 9: Delete
docs.text:
session.delete(obj), then commit. An unused tag goes without trouble. Deleting an author who still has books is refused, and the session is rolled back to undo the attempt:

delete.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Tag, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    poetry = session.scalars(select(Tag).where(Tag.name == "poetry")).one()
    session.delete(poetry)
    session.commit()
    print(session.scalars(select(Tag.name)).all())

    kadare = session.get(Author, 1)
    session.delete(kadare)
    try:
        session.commit()
    except IntegrityError as error:
        session.rollback()
        print("Refused:", error.orig)
    print(session.get(Author, 1))

['classic', 'albanian', 'dystopia', 'sci-fi', 'fantasy']
Refused: NOT NULL constraint failed: books.author_id
Author('Ismail Kadare')

The message is not the foreign key error you might expect. Before deleting Kadare, SQLAlchemy tried to unlink his books by setting their author_id to NULL, which is its default. The NOT NULL rule on author_id refused, and nothing was changed.

That default is deliberate: an ORM never deletes rows you did not ask it to delete. Making it delete an author's books with the author is possible, with cascade="all, delete-orphan" on the relationship, but think twice: it is the delete anomaly from the design tutorial, on purpose.

docs.title: Step 10: Joins and aggregates
docs.text:
For reports, ask for columns instead of whole objects. join uses a relationship to know how two tables connect, outerjoin is a LEFT JOIN, and func gives you SQL functions such as count:

aggregates.py
from sqlalchemy import func, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Book, Loan, Member, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

per_author = (
    select(Author.name, func.count(Book.id).label("books"))
    .outerjoin(Author.books)
    .group_by(Author.id)
    .order_by(func.count(Book.id).desc(), Author.name)
)

out_now = (
    select(Member.name, Book.title)
    .join(Loan.member)
    .join(Loan.book)
    .where(Loan.returned_on.is_(None))
    .order_by(Loan.loaned_on)
)

with Session(engine) as session:
    for name, books in session.execute(per_author):
        print(f"{books}  {name}")
    print()
    for name, title in session.execute(out_now):
        print(f"{name}: {title}")

3  Ismail Kadare
2  George Orwell
1  Chinua Achebe
1  Dritëro Agolli
1  Frank Herbert
1  J. R. R. Tolkien
1  Jane Austen
1  Ndre Mjeda
1  Ursula K. Le Guin

Erion Shehu: Pride and Prejudice
Arta Hoxha: Prilli i thyer
Drita Leka: Dune

session.execute(query) returns rows, and each row unpacks like a tuple. outerjoin kept every author, and Le Guin now counts one book, the one you added in Step 7.

Try it

Print the SQL of the per_author query.

Answer

Add print(per_author) at the end of the script:

SELECT authors.name, count(books.id) AS books 
FROM authors LEFT OUTER JOIN books ON authors.id = books.author_id GROUP BY authors.id ORDER BY count(books.id) DESC, authors.name

The LEFT OUTER JOIN, the count, the GROUP BY and the ORDER BY all came from the Python calls.

docs.title: Step 11: The N+1 problem
docs.text:
Following relationships is convenient, and it hides a trap. This script counts the SQL statements the session sends:

n_plus_one.py
from sqlalchemy import event, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, selectinload

from models import Book, make_engine

engine = make_engine()
queries = []


@event.listens_for(engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def count_query(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, many):
    queries.append(statement)


with Session(engine) as session:
    for book in session.scalars(select(Book)):
        book.author.name
print("lazy loading:", len(queries), "queries")

queries.clear()
with Session(engine) as session:
    query = select(Book).options(selectinload(Book.author))
    for book in session.scalars(query):
        book.author.name
print("selectinload:", len(queries), "queries")

lazy loading: 10 queries
selectinload: 2 queries

The first loop ran 1 query for the books, then one more per author the first time each book.author was used: 1 + N queries. The session remembers objects it has already loaded, so it was 10, not 13. With 10 books that is fine. With 10,000 rows on a web page it is the most common reason ORM code is slow.

selectinload(Book.author) tells the session to load all the authors in one extra query. Whenever a loop follows a relationship, load it up front like this.

docs.title: Step 12: Create tables from models
docs.text:
The models describe the schema, so SQLAlchemy can also create it. On a new, empty file:

create_all.py
from sqlalchemy import inspect
from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateTable

from models import Base, Book, make_engine

engine = make_engine("fresh.db")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

print(inspect(engine).get_table_names())
print(CreateTable(Book.__table__).compile(engine))

['authors', 'book_tags', 'books', 'library_cards', 'loans', 'members', 'tags']

CREATE TABLE books (
    id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    title VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    author_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    year INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (id),
    FOREIGN KEY(author_id) REFERENCES authors (id)
)

create_all creates every table that does not exist yet, and leaves existing ones alone. That is how a new project starts: write the models, and let SQLAlchemy create the tables. CreateTable shows the SQL it used.

When a project's models change later, create_all will not alter existing tables. Real projects use a migration tool for that, such as Alembic, which records each schema change as a small script.

docs.title: Step 13: Raw SQL when you need it
docs.text:
An ORM does not forbid SQL. For a query that is easier to write by hand, text() runs it, with named placeholders:

raw_sql.py
from sqlalchemy import text
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    rows = session.execute(
        text("SELECT name, joined_on FROM members WHERE joined_on < :day"),
        {"day": "2026-03-01"},
    ).all()

for name, joined_on in rows:
    print(joined_on, name)

2026-01-15 Arta Hoxha
2026-02-03 Besnik Krasniqi

Use the ORM for everyday work, and SQL for reports and special cases. Knowing both is the point.

AI in the loop

Assistants write SQLAlchemy code readily, but often in the 1.x style, with session.query(Book).filter(...), which still runs and is now legacy. Tell the assistant you use SQLAlchemy 2.x with select(). And for any ORM code that runs in a loop, print the query or count the statements, as in Step 11: the assistant cannot see your data, and N+1 is invisible until it is slow.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sqlalchemy'

The venv is not active, or SQLAlchemy was installed outside it. Run source .venv/bin/activate, then pip install sqlalchemy.

sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: no such table: books

The engine opened a different file, usually because the script ran from another folder and sqlite:///library.db is relative. Run it from ~/library, or use an absolute path: sqlite:////home/you/library/library.db.

DetachedInstanceError: ... is not bound to a Session

You used a relationship, such as book.author, after the with Session(...) block ended. The session is closed, so it cannot run the query. Do the work inside the block, or load the relationship up front with selectinload.

IntegrityError on commit

The change breaks a rule of the schema: a NOT NULL, UNIQUE or foreign key constraint. Read the message after IntegrityError, call session.rollback(), and fix the data.

ArgumentError or InvalidRequestError when the models load

Usually a typo in back_populates: both sides must name each other exactly. Check that Author.books says back_populates="author" and Book.author says back_populates="books".

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
Six exercises on library.db, with the full models.py, continuing from the steps above. Each answer is a small script; run it from ~/library with the venv active.

1. A join. List the titles of the books by authors from the United Kingdom, alphabetically.

Answer p1_uk.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Book, make_engine

engine = make_engine()

with Session(engine) as session:
    titles = session.scalars(
        select(Book.title)
        .join(Book.author)
        .where(Author.country == "United Kingdom")
        .order_by(Book.title)
    ).all()

print(titles)

['Animal Farm', 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', 'Pride and Prejudice', 'The Hobbit']

2. Many-to-many. Write titles_with_tag(session, name), which returns the sorted titles of the books with that tag, or [] if there is no such tag.

Answer p2_by_tag.py
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Tag, make_engine


def titles_with_tag(session, name):
    """Return the titles of the books with one tag, or [] if no such tag."""
    tag = session.scalars(select(Tag).where(Tag.name == name)).first()
    if tag is None:
        return []
    return sorted(book.title for book in tag.books)


with Session(make_engine()) as session:
    print(titles_with_tag(session, "dystopia"))
    print(titles_with_tag(session, "western"))

['Animal Farm', 'Nineteen Eighty-Four']
[]

3. One-to-one. Give Lea a library card, LIB-0005, expiring on 2027-09-01.

Answer

Assigning to the relationship is enough; the card's member_id is filled in for you:

p3_card.py
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import LibraryCard, Member, make_engine

with Session(make_engine()) as session:
    lea = session.get(Member, 5)
    lea.card = LibraryCard(card_number="LIB-0005", expires_on="2027-09-01")
    session.commit()
    print(lea.card, lea.card.member)

LibraryCard('LIB-0005') Member('Lea Marku')

4. Borrow a book. Write borrow(session, member_id, book_id), which creates a loan dated today and returns it, or returns None if the book is already out.

Answer p4_borrow.py
from datetime import date

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Book, Loan, Member, make_engine


def borrow(session, member_id, book_id):
    """Lend a book to a member and return the loan, or None if it is out."""
    open_loan = session.scalars(
        select(Loan).where(Loan.book_id == book_id,
                           Loan.returned_on.is_(None))
    ).first()
    if open_loan is not None:
        return None
    loan = Loan(member=session.get(Member, member_id),
                book=session.get(Book, book_id),
                loaned_on=date.today().isoformat())
    session.add(loan)
    session.commit()
    return loan


with Session(make_engine()) as session:
    print(borrow(session, 5, 8))
    print(borrow(session, 5, 10))

None
Loan('Things Fall Apart', 2026-10-31)

Dune is out, so the first call refused. The date is the day the page was written; yours will be today.

5. Count with zeros. Count the loans of every member, including any member with none, most first.

Answer p5_counts.py
from sqlalchemy import func, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Loan, Member, make_engine

query = (
    select(Member.name, func.count(Loan.id))
    .outerjoin(Member.loans)
    .group_by(Member.id)
    .order_by(func.count(Loan.id).desc(), Member.name)
)

with Session(make_engine()) as session:
    for name, loans in session.execute(query):
        print(f"{loans}  {name}")

4  Arta Hoxha
3  Besnik Krasniqi
3  Drita Leka
2  Erion Shehu
1  Lea Marku

Lea has one loan now, from exercise 4.

6. A computed answer. Write is_available(book), which is True when the book has no loan without a return date.

Answer p6_available.py
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Book, make_engine


def is_available(book):
    """True if the book has no loan without a return date."""
    return all(loan.returned_on is not None for loan in book.loans)


with Session(make_engine()) as session:
    for book_id in (5, 8, 9):
        book = session.get(Book, book_id)
        print(book.title, is_available(book))

Nineteen Eighty-Four True
Dune False
The Hobbit True

The Hobbit was returned in Step 8, so it is available again.

docs.title: Explain it to someone
docs.text:
• What an ORM is, and what maps to what: class, attribute, object, relationship
  • How to write a model with Mapped, mapped_column, a primary key and a foreign key
  • What the engine and the session are, and how to open a session
  • How to query with select, where, order_by, limit, get, first and count
  • How to see the SQL behind a query, and why ORM queries are safe from injection
  • How relationship and back_populates map one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many links
  • How to create, update and delete with add, attribute changes, delete and commit
  • What happens on commit, and when to call rollback
  • What the N+1 problem is, and how selectinload fixes it
  • How to create tables from models, and when to use raw SQL instead

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Code What it does class Book(Base): __tablename__ = "books" Map a class to a table id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) A primary key column year: Mapped[int | None] A column that may be NULL mapped_column(ForeignKey("authors.id")) A foreign key relationship(back_populates="...") Follow a link between tables relationship(secondary=table) Many-to-many through a junction table create_engine("sqlite:///library.db") Where the database is with Session(engine) as session: One conversation with the database session.scalars(select(Book).where(...)).all() Query objects session.get(Book, 8) One object by primary key, or None session.add(obj), session.delete(obj) Mark an object to insert or delete session.commit(), session.rollback() Save every change, or undo them .options(selectinload(Book.author)) Load a relationship up front Base.metadata.create_all(engine) Create the tables from the models session.execute(text("..."), {...}) Run raw SQL with named placeholders

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The library's data now lives behind Python objects. Next you open it to other programs, a web page, a phone app, another service, through a REST API that speaks HTTP and JSON.

RESTful API

docs.title: RESTful API
docs.text:
2 h Data & APIs Needs: Object-Relational Mapping

The library's data lives in a database, and Python code can reach it through the ORM. Other programs cannot: not a web page, not a phone app, not another team's service. An API opens the data to them, over HTTP, in JSON. In this tutorial you learn how HTTP requests and responses work, what makes an API RESTful, and you build one for the library with Flask, test it with curl, use it from Python, and write automated tests for it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Almost every modern application is a set of programs talking over HTTP: the front end asks the back end for data, the back end asks payment and email services, and so on. REST is the most common way to design those conversations. Knowing it lets you build back ends, and also use the thousands of public APIs out there, which all follow the same ideas. Your portfolio projects are built exactly this way.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need models.py, the full version from Object-Relational Mapping, and a fresh library.db, both in ~/library. Install Flask and requests in the same venv:

cd ~/library
source .venv/bin/activate
sqlite3 library.db < library.sql
pip install flask requests

curl, which sends HTTP requests from the terminal, is already in Ubuntu. You will use two terminals: one runs the API, the other sends requests to it.

docs.title: Step 1: HTTP in one picture
docs.text:
Every exchange on the web is one request from a client and one response from a server:

An HTTP request and its response The request has a method, POST, a path, /books, headers such as Content-Type: application/json, and a JSON body with the new book. The response has a status code, 201 Created, headers such as Content-Type and Location: /books/11, and a JSON body with the created book. REQUEST · client → serverRESPONSE · server → client POST /books HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: application/json {"title": "A Wizard of Earthsea", "author_id": 8, "year": 1968} HTTP/1.1 201 CREATED Content-Type: application/json Location: /books/11 {"id": 11, "title": "A Wizard of Earthsea", "year": 1968, "author": {...}} method,path headers body
  • The method says what to do: GET to read, POST to create, and so on.
  • The path says what to do it to: /books, /books/8.
  • Headers carry details about the message, such as Content-Type: application/json: "the body is JSON".
  • The body carries data. A GET has none; a POST sends the new book.
  • The response starts with a status code: 201 Created, 404 Not Found. Then its own headers and body.

docs.title: Step 2: What makes an API RESTful
docs.text:
REST is a style for designing HTTP APIs, built on a few ideas:

  • Resources, named with nouns. Everything the API exposes is a resource with a URL: /books is the collection of books, /books/8 one book. No verbs in URLs: not /getBook?id=8.
  • Methods are the verbs. The same URL does different things with different methods.
  • Representations. The client never touches the database; it gets a representation of the resource, here JSON.
  • Stateless. Every request carries everything the server needs. The server does not remember the previous request.
  • Status codes tell the outcome, so a client can react without reading the body.

The methods line up with CRUD and with SQL:

Method Path Meaning SQL Success GET /books List the books SELECT 200 OK GET /books/8 Read one book SELECT ... WHERE id = 8 200 OK POST /books Create a book INSERT 201 Created PATCH /books/8 Change some fields UPDATE 200 OK PUT /books/8 Replace the whole book UPDATE 200 OK DELETE /books/8 Delete the book DELETE 204 No Content

GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: sending the same request twice leaves the data as sending it once. POST is not: send it twice, get two books.

Here is the API you will build, layer by layer:

The layers of the library API A client, such as curl, requests or a browser, sends an HTTP request to Flask. Flask calls the route function for the method and path. The function uses an ORM session, and the session runs SQL on library.db. The answer travels back as JSON. Clientcurl, requests Flaskmethod + path Routea function Sessionthe ORM SQLitelibrary.db HTTPcallobjectsSQL the answer travels back as JSON

docs.title: Step 3: A first endpoint
docs.text:
Create api.py. Start with the setup, a function that turns a Book into a dictionary, and one route: a function that Flask calls for a given method and path.

api.py
"""A REST API for the library, built with Flask and the ORM models."""
from flask import Flask, abort, jsonify, request
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from models import Author, Book, Member, make_engine

app = Flask(__name__)
app.json.ensure_ascii = False
app.json.sort_keys = False
engine = make_engine()

def book_json(book):
    """Return a book as a dictionary ready for JSON."""
    return {
        "id": book.id,
        "title": book.title,
        "year": book.year,
        "author": {"id": book.author.id, "name": book.author.name},
    }

@app.get("/books")
def list_books():
    """List the books, optionally only those of one author."""
    query = select(Book).order_by(Book.id)
    author_id = request.args.get("author_id", type=int)
    if author_id is not None:
        query = query.where(Book.author_id == author_id)
    with Session(engine) as session:
        return jsonify([book_json(book) for book in session.scalars(query)])
  • @app.get("/books") registers the function for GET /books.
  • Each request opens its own session, uses it, and closes it: the API is stateless, and so is each call.
  • jsonify turns Python lists and dictionaries into a JSON response, with the header Content-Type: application/json.
  • book_json decides what the outside world sees. The API does not just dump the table: it nests the author's name, and it could hide columns that are nobody else's business.

Start the API in the first terminal:

flask --app api run

 * Serving Flask app 'api'
 * Debug mode: off
WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment. Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000
Press CTRL+C to quit

Leave it running. In the second terminal, send a request. python3 -m json.tool pretty-prints the JSON, and head keeps the start of it:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/books | python3 -m json.tool --no-ensure-ascii | head -n 20

[
    {
        "id": 1,
        "title": "Kronikë në gur",
        "year": 1971,
        "author": {
            "id": 1,
            "name": "Ismail Kadare"
        }
    },
    {
        "id": 2,
        "title": "Prilli i thyer",
        "year": 1978,
        "author": {
            "id": 1,
            "name": "Ismail Kadare"
        }
    },
    {

In the first terminal, Flask logs each request with its status code. Stop the server with Ctrl+C, and restart it after every change to api.py.

docs.title: Step 4: One resource, and 404
docs.text:
A path parameter picks one resource: <int:book_id> matches a number in the path and passes it to the function.

@app.get("/books/<int:book_id>")
def get_book(book_id):
    """Return one book, with its tags, or 404."""
    with Session(engine) as session:
        book = session.get(Book, book_id)
        if book is None:
            abort(404, description=f"No book with id {book_id}")
        data = book_json(book)
        data["tags"] = [tag.name for tag in book.tags]
        return jsonify(data)

curl -i shows the status line and headers too:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/8

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":8,"title":"Dune","year":1965,"author":{"id":5,"name":"Frank Herbert"},"tags":["classic","sci-fi"]}

A book that does not exist must not crash the API or answer 200 with nothing. abort(404, ...) stops the function and answers 404 Not Found. By default Flask would send an HTML error page, which a program cannot use, so one more function at the end of api.py answers every error in JSON:

@app.errorhandler(400)
@app.errorhandler(404)
@app.errorhandler(405)
@app.errorhandler(409)
def error_json(error):
    """Answer every error with JSON instead of an HTML page."""
    return jsonify({"error": error.description}), error.code

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/999

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"No book with id 999"}

docs.title: Step 5: Query parameters
docs.text:
Filters, sorting and paging do not get their own URLs: they are query parameters, after the ?. list_books already reads author_id:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5000/books?author_id=1"

[{"id":1,"title":"Kronikë në gur","year":1971,"author":{"id":1,"name":"Ismail Kadare"}},{"id":2,"title":"Prilli i thyer","year":1978,"author":{"id":1,"name":"Ismail Kadare"}},{"id":3,"title":"Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur","year":1963,"author":{"id":1,"name":"Ismail Kadare"}}]

request.args.get("author_id", type=int) returns None when the parameter is missing or is not a number, so a bad value is ignored instead of crashing the query. Quote the URL in the shell: an unquoted & would mean something else to Bash.

docs.title: Step 6: Create with POST
docs.text:
To create a book, the client sends it as JSON in the request body:

@app.post("/books")
def create_book():
    """Create a book from the JSON body; answer 201 with the new book."""
    data = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}
    title = data.get("title")
    if not isinstance(title, str) or not title.strip():
        abort(400, description="'title' is required")
    with Session(engine) as session:
        author = session.get(Author, data.get("author_id"))
        if author is None:
            abort(400, description="'author_id' must be an existing author")
        book = Book(title=title.strip(), year=data.get("year"), author=author)
        session.add(book)
        session.commit()
        response = jsonify(book_json(book))
        response.status_code = 201
        response.headers["Location"] = f"/books/{book.id}"
        return response
  • request.get_json(silent=True) reads the body; silent=True returns None instead of failing when the body is not JSON.
  • Validate before you touch the database. Never trust what a client sends: a missing title or an unknown author is the client's mistake, so the answer is 400 Bad Request with a message saying what is wrong.
  • A successful create answers 201 Created, with the new resource in the body and its URL in the Location header.

With curl, -X sets the method, -H adds a header and -d sends the body:

curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/books -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title": "A Wizard of Earthsea", "author_id": 8, "year": 1968}'

HTTP/1.1 201 CREATED
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /books/11

{"id":11,"title":"A Wizard of Earthsea","year":1968,"author":{"id":8,"name":"Ursula K. Le Guin"}}

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/11

{"id":11,"title":"A Wizard of Earthsea","year":1968,"author":{"id":8,"name":"Ursula K. Le Guin"},"tags":[]}

And the client's mistakes:

curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/books -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"author_id": 8}'

HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"'title' is required"}

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/books -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title": "Ghost", "author_id": 99}'

{"error":"'author_id' must be an existing author"}

docs.title: Step 7: Update and delete
docs.text:
PATCH changes only the fields the client sends:

@app.patch("/books/<int:book_id>")
def update_book(book_id):
    """Change the title or year of a book."""
    data = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}
    with Session(engine) as session:
        book = session.get(Book, book_id)
        if book is None:
            abort(404, description=f"No book with id {book_id}")
        if "title" in data:
            book.title = data["title"]
        if "year" in data:
            book.year = data["year"]
        session.commit()
        return jsonify(book_json(book))

curl -s -X PATCH http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/11 -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"year": 1969}'

{"id":11,"title":"A Wizard of Earthsea","year":1969,"author":{"id":8,"name":"Ursula K. Le Guin"}}

PUT would replace the whole resource, so the client would have to send every field. PATCH is what most APIs use for edits.

DELETE answers 204 No Content on success: done, nothing to send back. A book with loans must not disappear, so that answers 409 Conflict: the request is valid, but clashes with the current state of the data.

@app.delete("/books/<int:book_id>")
def delete_book(book_id):
    """Delete a book that has never been lent; answer 204."""
    with Session(engine) as session:
        book = session.get(Book, book_id)
        if book is None:
            abort(404, description=f"No book with id {book_id}")
        if book.loans:
            abort(409, description="This book has loans and cannot be deleted")
        session.delete(book)
        session.commit()
        return "", 204

curl -i -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/11

HTTP/1.1 204 NO CONTENT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Deleting it again finds nothing:

curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/11

{"error":"No book with id 11"}

And Dune has loans:

curl -i -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/8

HTTP/1.1 409 CONFLICT
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"This book has loans and cannot be deleted"}

Flask itself answers a method that has no route on that path with 405 Method Not Allowed:

curl -i -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/8

HTTP/1.1 405 METHOD NOT ALLOWED
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"The method is not allowed for the requested URL."}

docs.title: Step 8: Nested resources
docs.text:
Some resources belong to others: a member's loans. The URL says so: /members/1/loans.

@app.get("/members/<int:member_id>/loans")
def member_loans(member_id):
    """List one member's loans, newest first."""
    with Session(engine) as session:
        member = session.get(Member, member_id)
        if member is None:
            abort(404, description=f"No member with id {member_id}")
        loans = sorted(member.loans, key=lambda loan: loan.loaned_on,
                       reverse=True)
        return jsonify([
            {"book": loan.book.title,
             "loaned_on": loan.loaned_on,
             "returned_on": loan.returned_on}
            for loan in loans
        ])

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/members/1/loans

[{"book":"The Hobbit","loaned_on":"2026-10-22","returned_on":null},{"book":"Prilli i thyer","loaned_on":"2026-10-03","returned_on":null},{"book":"Kronikë në gur","loaned_on":"2026-09-18","returned_on":"2026-10-01"},{"book":"Nineteen Eighty-Four","loaned_on":"2026-09-02","returned_on":"2026-09-16"}]

None became null: the book has not been returned.

Try it

What do /members/5/loans and /members/42/loans return, and with which status codes?

Answer

Lea, member 5, exists but has no loans: 200 with an empty list. Member 42 does not exist: 404. An empty collection is not an error.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/members/5/loans

[]

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/members/42/loans

{"error":"No member with id 42"}

docs.title: Step 9: Status codes
docs.text:
The status code is the first thing a client checks. The first digit gives the family:

Code Name Use it when 200 OK A read or an update worked 201 Created A POST created a resource; add a Location header 204 No Content It worked, and there is nothing to send back 400 Bad Request The client sent invalid data 401 Unauthorized The client must log in first 403 Forbidden Logged in, but not allowed 404 Not Found No resource at that URL 405 Method Not Allowed The URL exists, the method does not 409 Conflict Valid, but clashes with the current data 500 Internal Server Error A bug in the server

2xx means it worked, 4xx that the client must change something, 5xx that the server failed. A 500 is always your bug: an unhandled exception in a route. Users should only ever see the codes you chose.

docs.title: Step 10: Use the API from Python
docs.text:
Programs call APIs with an HTTP library. requests is the most used in Python. With the server running:

client.py
"""Use the library API from Python, with the requests package."""
import requests

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:5000"

response = requests.get(f"{BASE}/books", params={"author_id": 3})
print(response.status_code, response.headers["Content-Type"])
for book in response.json():
    print(book["id"], book["title"])

response = requests.post(f"{BASE}/books",
                         json={"title": "Homage to Catalonia",
                               "author_id": 3, "year": 1938})
print(response.status_code, response.headers["Location"])

response = requests.get(f"{BASE}/books/999")
print(response.status_code, response.json())

try:
    response.raise_for_status()
except requests.HTTPError as error:
    print("HTTPError:", error)

python3 client.py

200 application/json
5 Nineteen Eighty-Four
6 Animal Farm
201 /books/11
404 {'error': 'No book with id 999'}
HTTPError: 404 Client Error: NOT FOUND for url: http://127.0.0.1:5000/books/999
  • params= builds the query string, and json= sends a JSON body with the right Content-Type.
  • response.json() turns the body back into Python data.
  • raise_for_status() raises an exception for any 4xx or 5xx, which is handy when an error should stop the program.

The same code works against any REST API on the internet, given its URL and its documentation.

docs.title: Step 11: Test the API
docs.text:
Clicking around with curl does not scale. Flask has a test client that sends requests to the app without a server, so tests can check every endpoint in a second. These tests use a copy of the database, so they never change the real one:

test_api.py
"""Tests for the library API, run against a fresh copy of the data."""
import shutil
import unittest

shutil.copy("library.db", "test-library.db")

import api  # noqa: E402
from models import make_engine  # noqa: E402

api.engine = make_engine("test-library.db")


class BooksApiTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """Check the /books endpoints."""

    def setUp(self):
        self.client = api.app.test_client()

    def test_list_books(self):
        response = self.client.get("/books")
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertGreaterEqual(len(response.get_json()), 10)

    def test_missing_book_is_404(self):
        response = self.client.get("/books/999")
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)
        self.assertIn("error", response.get_json())

    def test_create_needs_title(self):
        response = self.client.post("/books", json={"author_id": 1})
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 400)

    def test_create_and_read_back(self):
        response = self.client.post(
            "/books", json={"title": "Test Book", "author_id": 1})
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 201)
        location = response.headers["Location"]
        self.assertEqual(self.client.get(location).get_json()["title"],
                         "Test Book")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Stop the server first, then run the tests:

python3 test_api.py

test_create_and_read_back (__main__.BooksApiTest.test_create_and_read_back) ... ok
test_create_needs_title (__main__.BooksApiTest.test_create_needs_title) ... ok
test_list_books (__main__.BooksApiTest.test_list_books) ... ok
test_missing_book_is_404 (__main__.BooksApiTest.test_missing_book_is_404) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 4 tests in 0.05s

OK

Run the tests after every change. When one fails, you know at once what you broke.

docs.title: The whole API
When something goes wrong
docs.text:
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1 port 5000

The server is not running. Start it in the other terminal with flask --app api run, from ~/library, with the venv active.

Address already in use

Another server is still on port 5000, often one you forgot in another terminal. Stop it, or start this one on another port: flask --app api run --port 5001.

My change to api.py does nothing

The server is still running the old code. Restart it, or start it with --debug, which reloads the code when you save the file.

A POST answers 400 although the JSON looks right

Check the Content-Type: application/json header and the quotes: in the shell, wrap the JSON in single quotes, and use double quotes inside it, as JSON requires.

500 Internal Server Error

An exception in a route. The traceback is in the server's terminal, not in the response. Read it there, fix the bug, and handle the case with the right 4xx if it was caused by bad input.

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
Five exercises. Add each route to api.py, before the error handler, restart the server, and reload library.sql first for exactly these results. Exercise 3 also needs Loan imported from models, and date from datetime.

1. Authors. Add GET /authors: every author with their number of books, sorted by name.

Answer 
@app.get("/authors")
def list_authors():
    """List every author, with how many books each has."""
    with Session(engine) as session:
        authors = session.scalars(select(Author).order_by(Author.name))
        return jsonify([
            {"id": a.id, "name": a.name, "books": len(a.books)}
            for a in authors
        ])

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/authors

[{"id":7,"name":"Chinua Achebe","books":1},{"id":2,"name":"Dritëro Agolli","books":1},{"id":5,"name":"Frank Herbert","books":1},{"id":3,"name":"George Orwell","books":2},{"id":1,"name":"Ismail Kadare","books":3},{"id":6,"name":"J. R. R. Tolkien","books":1},{"id":4,"name":"Jane Austen","books":1},{"id":8,"name":"Ursula K. Le Guin","books":0}]

2. Nested books. Add GET /authors/<id>/books, with 404 for an unknown author.

Answer 
@app.get("/authors/<int:author_id>/books")
def author_books(author_id):
    """List one author's books, or 404 if there is no such author."""
    with Session(engine) as session:
        author = session.get(Author, author_id)
        if author is None:
            abort(404, description=f"No author with id {author_id}")
        return jsonify([book_json(book) for book in author.books])

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/authors/3/books

[{"id":5,"title":"Nineteen Eighty-Four","year":1949,"author":{"id":3,"name":"George Orwell"}},{"id":6,"title":"Animal Farm","year":1945,"author":{"id":3,"name":"George Orwell"}}]

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/authors/42/books

{"error":"No author with id 42"}

3. Borrow. Add POST /members/<id>/loans, with a body such as {"book_id": 10}. Answer 201 with the new loan, 404 for an unknown member or book, and 409 if the book is already out.

Answer 
@app.post("/members/<int:member_id>/loans")
def borrow_book(member_id):
    """Lend the book in the JSON body to a member: 201, or 409 if it is out."""
    data = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}
    with Session(engine) as session:
        member = session.get(Member, member_id)
        book = session.get(Book, data.get("book_id"))
        if member is None or book is None:
            abort(404, description="No such member or book")
        if any(loan.returned_on is None for loan in book.loans):
            abort(409, description=f"'{book.title}' is already out")
        loan = Loan(member=member, book=book,
                    loaned_on=date.today().isoformat())
        session.add(loan)
        session.commit()
        return jsonify({"id": loan.id, "book": book.title,
                        "loaned_on": loan.loaned_on}), 201

curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/members/5/loans -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"book_id": 10}'

HTTP/1.1 201 CREATED
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":13,"book":"Things Fall Apart","loaned_on":"2026-10-31"}

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/members/5/loans -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"book_id": 8}'

{"error":"'Dune' is already out"}

4. Paging. Let GET /books take ?limit= and ?offset=, with a default of 20 and a maximum of 50 books per page.

Answer

Replace list_books. min and max keep the numbers in range, so a client cannot ask for a million rows at once:

@app.get("/books")
def list_books():
    """List the books, one page at a time: ?limit= (1 to 50) and ?offset=."""
    limit = min(max(request.args.get("limit", 20, type=int), 1), 50)
    offset = max(request.args.get("offset", 0, type=int), 0)
    query = select(Book).order_by(Book.id).limit(limit).offset(offset)
    author_id = request.args.get("author_id", type=int)
    if author_id is not None:
        query = query.where(Book.author_id == author_id)
    with Session(engine) as session:
        return jsonify([book_json(book) for book in session.scalars(query)])

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5000/books?limit=2&offset=4"

[{"id":5,"title":"Nineteen Eighty-Four","year":1949,"author":{"id":3,"name":"George Orwell"}},{"id":6,"title":"Animal Farm","year":1945,"author":{"id":3,"name":"George Orwell"}}]

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5000/books?limit=1000&offset=9"

[{"id":10,"title":"Things Fall Apart","year":1958,"author":{"id":7,"name":"Chinua Achebe"}}]

5. A test. Write tests that DELETE /books/8 answers 409 and leaves the book in place, and that deleting a book with no loans answers 204, then 404 when you read it.

Answer test_conflict.py
"""A test for deleting a book that has loans."""
import shutil
import unittest

shutil.copy("library.db", "test-library.db")

import api  # noqa: E402
from models import make_engine  # noqa: E402

api.engine = make_engine("test-library.db")


class DeleteTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """Check DELETE /books/<id>."""

    def test_book_with_loans_is_409(self):
        client = api.app.test_client()
        response = client.delete("/books/8")
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 409)
        self.assertEqual(client.get("/books/8").status_code, 200)

    def test_unused_book_is_204_then_404(self):
        client = api.app.test_client()
        self.assertEqual(client.delete("/books/4").status_code, 204)
        self.assertEqual(client.get("/books/4").status_code, 404)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

python3 test_conflict.py

test_book_with_loans_is_409 (__main__.DeleteTest.test_book_with_loans_is_409) ... ok
test_unused_book_is_204_then_404 (__main__.DeleteTest.test_unused_book_is_204_then_404) ... ok
