docs.title: SQL: CRUD Operations
docs.text:
90 min Data & APIs Needs: File Handling

Files are good for a list or a settings file. When you need to find, sort, count and change many records, you need a database. In this tutorial you meet the relational model and learn the language every relational database speaks, SQL: you create a table, then read, filter, sort, add, change, delete and summarise the library's books.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Nearly every application keeps its data in a relational database: user accounts, orders, bookings, messages. SQL has been the way to talk to those databases for fifty years, and the SQL you learn here works, almost unchanged, in SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server.

It is also the skill that answers questions. "How many books does each author have?" needs a loop and a dictionary in Python. In SQL it is three short lines.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
We use SQLite: a whole database in one file, with no server to install. Install its command-line tool in your WSL terminal:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y sqlite3
sqlite3 --version

Then download the practice data and load it into a new database file, books.db:

mkdir -p ~/library && cd ~/library
curl -O https://evisp.github.io/augmented_software_engineering/assets/sql/books.sql
sqlite3 books.db < books.sql

You can also download books.sql from the browser. It creates a table of 20 books. Loading it again resets the table, so if you break something, run the last command again.

docs.title: Step 1: Tables, rows and columns
docs.text:
A relational database stores data in tables. A table looks like a spreadsheet, but it is stricter, and that strictness is what makes it reliable.

The parts of the books table The books table has named columns: id, title, author, year, genre and pages. Each row is one book. The id column is the primary key, a unique number for every row. The year column holds one kind of fact. A cell with no value, such as the genre and pages of Vargjet e lira, holds NULL. primary key: unique for every row column: one kind of fact, one type, a name idtitleauthoryeargenrepages 1Kronikë në gurIsmail Kadare1971novel320 18Fluent PythonL. Ramalho2015programmingNULL 19Vargjet e liraMigjeni1936NULLNULL row: one book NULL: no value books · 20 rows · the available column is not shown
  • A table holds one kind of thing: the books table holds books, one per row.
  • A column has a name and a type, and every value in it is the same kind of fact: year is always a whole number, title always text.
  • A row is one record: one book, with a value for each column.
  • The primary key, here id, has a different value in every row, so each row can be found and changed on its own.
  • NULL means "no value": unknown or missing. It is not zero and not an empty string, and it needs special care, as you will see.

The order of rows in a table means nothing. A database returns rows in whatever order is fastest, unless you ask for an order.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the database
docs.text:
Open books.db in the SQLite shell:

sqlite3 books.db

The prompt changes to sqlite>. Everything you type there is either SQL, which ends with a semicolon ;, or a shell command, which starts with a dot. Make the results readable first:

sqlite> .headers on
sqlite> .mode box

Every output on this page uses those two settings. To have them every time, put both lines in a file called ~/.sqliterc. Now look around. .tables lists the tables:

.tables

books

.schema shows how a table was created:

.schema books

CREATE TABLE books (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    title     TEXT    NOT NULL,
    author    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    year      INTEGER,
    genre     TEXT,
    pages     INTEGER,
    available INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);

Leave the shell with .quit or Ctrl+D. You can also run a file of SQL without opening the shell: sqlite3 books.db < some-file.sql, which is exactly how you loaded the practice data.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a table
docs.text:
That schema is a CREATE TABLE statement. Read it line by line:

  • INTEGER PRIMARY KEY makes id the primary key. Leave it out when you add a row, and SQLite fills in the next number.
  • TEXT and INTEGER are the types. SQLite also has REAL for decimals and BLOB for raw bytes. There is no true/false type: available uses 1 for yes and 0 for no.
  • NOT NULL means the column must always have a value. genre and pages have no such rule, so they may be NULL.
  • DEFAULT 1 fills in a value when a new row does not give one.

books.sql also starts with DROP TABLE IF EXISTS books;, which deletes the whole table, data and all. That is what makes reloading the file a reset.

Dates have no special type in SQLite either. Store them as text in the form YYYY-MM-DD: in that form they sort and compare correctly.

Try it

The library also needs its members. Create a table members with an id primary key, a name that is required, an email that is required and must be different for every member, and a joined_on date that defaults to today. Check it with .tables.

Answer

UNIQUE refuses a value that is already in the column, and CURRENT_DATE is today's date:

CREATE TABLE members (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    email     TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    joined_on TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

.tables

books    members

docs.title: Step 4: Read data with SELECT
docs.text:
SELECT reads rows. * means "every column", and LIMIT keeps only the first few rows:

SELECT * FROM books LIMIT 5;

┌────┬───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────┬────────┬───────┬───────────┐
│ id │               title               │     author     │ year │ genre  │ pages │ available │
├────┼───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────┼────────┼───────┼───────────┤
│ 1  │ Kronikë në gur                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1971 │ novel  │ 320   │ 1         │
│ 2  │ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1963 │ novel  │ 288   │ 0         │
│ 3  │ Prilli i thyer                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1978 │ novel  │ 216   │ 1         │
│ 4  │ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ Dritëro Agolli │ 1973 │ satire │ 224   │ 1         │
│ 5  │ I humburi                         │ Fatos Kongoli  │ 1992 │ novel  │ 192   │ 1         │
└────┴───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────┴──────┴────────┴───────┴───────────┘

Ask only for the columns you need. The result is easier to read, and it says exactly what you meant:

SELECT title, author, year FROM books LIMIT 5;

┌───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────┐
│               title               │     author     │ year │
├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1971 │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1963 │
│ Prilli i thyer                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ 1978 │
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ Dritëro Agolli │ 1973 │
│ I humburi                         │ Fatos Kongoli  │ 1992 │
└───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────┴──────┘

SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, but writing them in capitals makes queries easier to read. Text values go in single quotes: 'Ismail Kadare'.

Try it

Show the title, genre and number of pages of the first three books.

Answer 
SELECT title, genre, pages FROM books LIMIT 3;

┌────────────────────────────────┬───────┬───────┐
│             title              │ genre │ pages │
├────────────────────────────────┼───────┼───────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                 │ novel │ 320   │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ novel │ 288   │
│ Prilli i thyer                 │ novel │ 216   │
└────────────────────────────────┴───────┴───────┘

docs.title: Step 5: Filter rows with WHERE
docs.text:
WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true. All of Kadare's books:

SELECT id, title, year FROM books WHERE author = 'Ismail Kadare';

┌────┬────────────────────────────────┬──────┐
│ id │             title              │ year │
├────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────┤
│ 1  │ Kronikë në gur                 │ 1971 │
│ 2  │ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ 1963 │
│ 3  │ Prilli i thyer                 │ 1978 │
└────┴────────────────────────────────┴──────┘

The conditions you will use most:

Condition Example = <> < <= > >= year < 1900 AND, OR, NOT genre = 'novel' AND pages > 300 IN (...) genre IN ('satire', 'dystopia') BETWEEN a AND b year BETWEEN 1940 AND 1949, both ends included LIKE title LIKE 'The %': % is any text, _ one character IS NULL, IS NOT NULL genre IS NULL

Books from before 1900:

SELECT title, author, year FROM books WHERE year < 1900;

┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────┐
│        title        │       author        │ year │
├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────┤
│ Pride and Prejudice │ Jane Austen         │ 1813 │
│ Emma                │ Jane Austen         │ 1815 │
│ Don Quixote         │ Miguel de Cervantes │ 1605 │
└─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────┘

Novels longer than 300 pages:

SELECT title, pages FROM books
WHERE genre = 'novel' AND pages > 300;

┌───────────────────────────────┬───────┐
│             title             │ pages │
├───────────────────────────────┼───────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                │ 320   │
│ Don Quixote                   │ 1072  │
│ One Hundred Years of Solitude │ 417   │
└───────────────────────────────┴───────┘

Satires and dystopias:

SELECT title, genre FROM books
WHERE genre IN ('satire', 'dystopia');

┌───────────────────────────────────┬──────────┐
│               title               │  genre   │
├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────┤
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ satire   │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four              │ dystopia │
│ Animal Farm                       │ satire   │
└───────────────────────────────────┴──────────┘

The 1940s:

SELECT title, year FROM books
WHERE year BETWEEN 1940 AND 1949;

┌──────────────────────┬──────┐
│        title         │ year │
├──────────────────────┼──────┤
│ The Little Prince    │ 1943 │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ 1949 │
│ Animal Farm          │ 1945 │
└──────────────────────┴──────┘

Titles that start with "The ":

SELECT title FROM books WHERE title LIKE 'The %';

┌──────────────────────────┐
│          title           │
├──────────────────────────┤
│ The Little Prince        │
│ The Hobbit               │
│ The Pragmatic Programmer │
└──────────────────────────┘

And the books whose genre was never filled in. In box mode, NULL shows as an empty cell:

SELECT id, title, genre, pages FROM books WHERE genre IS NULL;

┌────┬────────────────┬───────┬───────┐
│ id │     title      │ genre │ pages │
├────┼────────────────┼───────┼───────┤
│ 19 │ Vargjet e lira │       │       │
│ 20 │ Sapiens        │       │ 443   │
└────┴────────────────┴───────┴───────┘

NULL is not equal to anything, not even NULL

WHERE genre = NULL looks right, and finds nothing:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS matches FROM books WHERE genre = NULL;

┌─────────┐
│ matches │
├─────────┤
│ 0       │
└─────────┘

Comparing anything with NULL gives "unknown", which WHERE treats as false. Always test for missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

Try it

Which books are out on loan right now, that is, not available?

Answer 
SELECT title, author FROM books WHERE available = 0;

┌────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│             title              │          author          │
├────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ Ismail Kadare            │
│ The Little Prince              │ Antoine de Saint-Exupéry │
│ Animal Farm                    │ George Orwell            │
│ Dune                           │ Frank Herbert            │
│ The Pragmatic Programmer       │ Andrew Hunt              │
└────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 6: Sort and limit
docs.text:
ORDER BY sorts the result, and DESC puts the largest first. Together with LIMIT, it answers "top N" questions. The three longest books:

SELECT title, pages FROM books ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 3;

┌─────────────┬───────┐
│    title    │ pages │
├─────────────┼───────┤
│ Don Quixote │ 1072  │
│ Dune        │ 612   │
│ Emma        │ 474   │
└─────────────┴───────┘

Sort by several columns, and the second one breaks ties in the first. Every novel, by author and then by year:

SELECT author, year, title FROM books
WHERE genre = 'novel'
ORDER BY author, year;

┌────────────────────────┬──────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│         author         │ year │             title              │
├────────────────────────┼──────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│ Chinua Achebe          │ 1958 │ Things Fall Apart              │
│ Fatos Kongoli          │ 1992 │ I humburi                      │
│ Gabriel García Márquez │ 1967 │ One Hundred Years of Solitude  │
│ Ismail Kadare          │ 1963 │ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │
│ Ismail Kadare          │ 1971 │ Kronikë në gur                 │
│ Ismail Kadare          │ 1978 │ Prilli i thyer                 │
│ Miguel de Cervantes    │ 1605 │ Don Quixote                    │
└────────────────────────┴──────┴────────────────────────────────┘

OFFSET skips rows, which is how a website shows page 2 of a list:

SELECT id, title FROM books ORDER BY id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

┌────┬──────────────────────┐
│ id │        title         │
├────┼──────────────────────┤
│ 6  │ The Little Prince    │
│ 7  │ Nineteen Eighty-Four │
│ 8  │ Animal Farm          │
│ 9  │ Things Fall Apart    │
│ 10 │ Pride and Prejudice  │
└────┴──────────────────────┘

Without ORDER BY, "the first five rows" means whichever five the database happens to return. Whenever the order matters, say so.

Try it

Show the three most recently published books, newest first.

Answer 
SELECT title, year FROM books ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 3;

┌───────────────┬──────┐
│     title     │ year │
├───────────────┼──────┤
│ Fluent Python │ 2015 │
│ Sapiens       │ 2011 │
│ Clean Code    │ 2008 │
└───────────────┴──────┘

docs.title: Step 7: Add rows with INSERT
docs.text:
INSERT INTO adds rows. Name the columns, then give the values in the same order. Leave out id, and SQLite assigns the next number; leave out available, and it gets its default, 1:

INSERT INTO books (title, author, year, genre, pages)
VALUES ('The Left Hand of Darkness', 'Ursula K. Le Guin', 1969, 'sci-fi', 304);

VALUES can take several rows at once, separated by commas, and NULL leaves a column empty:

INSERT INTO books (title, author, year, genre, pages) VALUES
    ('Python Crash Course', 'Eric Matthes', 2019, 'programming', 544),
    ('Atomic Habits', 'James Clear', 2018, NULL, 320);

Always check what you wrote:

SELECT * FROM books WHERE id > 20;

┌────┬───────────────────────────┬───────────────────┬──────┬─────────────┬───────┬───────────┐
│ id │           title           │      author       │ year │    genre    │ pages │ available │
├────┼───────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼──────┼─────────────┼───────┼───────────┤
│ 21 │ The Left Hand of Darkness │ Ursula K. Le Guin │ 1969 │ sci-fi      │ 304   │ 1         │
│ 22 │ Python Crash Course       │ Eric Matthes      │ 2019 │ programming │ 544   │ 1         │
│ 23 │ Atomic Habits             │ James Clear       │ 2018 │             │ 320   │ 1         │
└────┴───────────────────────────┴───────────────────┴──────┴─────────────┴───────┴───────────┘

Try it

Add three members to your members table from Step 3: two with a joined_on date, and one without, to see the default.

Answer 
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on) VALUES
    ('Arta Hoxha', 'arta@example.com', '2026-01-15'),
    ('Besnik Krasniqi', 'besnik@example.com', '2026-02-03');
INSERT INTO members (name, email) VALUES ('Drita Leka', 'drita@example.com');
SELECT * FROM members;

┌────┬─────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────┐
│ id │      name       │       email        │ joined_on  │
├────┼─────────────────┼────────────────────┼────────────┤
│ 1  │ Arta Hoxha      │ arta@example.com   │ 2026-01-15 │
│ 2  │ Besnik Krasniqi │ besnik@example.com │ 2026-02-03 │
│ 3  │ Drita Leka      │ drita@example.com  │ 2026-10-31 │
└────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────┘

The third member got today's date, the day this page was written.

docs.title: Step 8: Change and remove rows
docs.text:
UPDATE changes values in the rows that match WHERE. Atomic Habits has no genre yet; give it one:

UPDATE books SET genre = 'self-help' WHERE id = 23;

One UPDATE can change several columns at once. The Left Hand of Darkness went out on loan, and its page count was wrong:

UPDATE books SET available = 0, pages = 290 WHERE id = 21;

SELECT id, title, genre, pages, available FROM books WHERE id > 20;

┌────┬───────────────────────────┬─────────────┬───────┬───────────┐
│ id │           title           │    genre    │ pages │ available │
├────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────┼───────────┤
│ 21 │ The Left Hand of Darkness │ sci-fi      │ 290   │ 0         │
│ 22 │ Python Crash Course       │ programming │ 544   │ 1         │
│ 23 │ Atomic Habits             │ self-help   │ 320   │ 1         │
└────┴───────────────────────────┴─────────────┴───────┴───────────┘

DELETE FROM removes the rows that match WHERE. Python Crash Course was added by mistake. Check the row first, then delete it:

SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE id = 22;

┌────┬─────────────────────┐
│ id │        title        │
├────┼─────────────────────┤
│ 22 │ Python Crash Course │
└────┴─────────────────────┘

DELETE FROM books WHERE id = 22;

SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE id > 20;

┌────┬───────────────────────────┐
│ id │           title           │
├────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ 21 │ The Left Hand of Darkness │
│ 23 │ Atomic Habits             │
└────┴───────────────────────────┘

Notice that each statement used the primary key to pick exactly one row. A condition such as WHERE author = 'Jane Austen' would change every one of her books.

UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE change every row

DELETE FROM books; empties the table, and UPDATE books SET available = 0; marks every book as out. There is no undo. Two habits protect you:

  1. Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, as above. If it shows exactly the rows you mean, the same WHERE is safe.
  2. Use a transaction for anything risky. BEGIN starts one; nothing is final until COMMIT, and ROLLBACK undoes it all. changes() reports how many rows the last statement touched:
BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET available = 0;
SELECT changes() AS changed;
SELECT SUM(available) AS available FROM books;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT SUM(available) AS available FROM books;

┌─────────┐
│ changed │
├─────────┤
│ 22      │
└─────────┘
┌───────────┐
│ available │
├───────────┤
│ 0         │
└───────────┘
┌───────────┐
│ available │
├───────────┤
│ 16        │
└───────────┘

The update touched all 22 rows and nothing was available, until ROLLBACK put everything back.

These four statements, INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, are CRUD: create, read, update, delete. Almost everything an application does with its data is one of them.

Try it

In members, change Drita's email, delete Besnik, and show the table. Then try to add a member with an email that is already used.

Answer 
UPDATE members SET email = 'drita.leka@example.com' WHERE id = 3;
DELETE FROM members WHERE id = 2;
SELECT * FROM members;

┌────┬────────────┬────────────────────────┬────────────┐
│ id │    name    │         email          │ joined_on  │
├────┼────────────┼────────────────────────┼────────────┤
│ 1  │ Arta Hoxha │ arta@example.com       │ 2026-01-15 │
│ 3  │ Drita Leka │ drita.leka@example.com │ 2026-10-31 │
└────┴────────────┴────────────────────────┴────────────┘

INSERT INTO members (name, email) VALUES ('Arta H.', 'arta@example.com');

Runtime error: UNIQUE constraint failed: members.email (19)

The UNIQUE rule from Step 3 protects the data even from your own mistakes.

docs.title: Step 9: Summarise with aggregate functions
docs.text:
An aggregate function turns many rows into one value:

Function Returns COUNT(*) the number of rows COUNT(column) the number of rows where that column is not NULL SUM(column) the total AVG(column) the average MIN(column), MAX(column) the smallest and largest value 
SELECT COUNT(*) AS books, COUNT(genre) AS with_genre,
       COUNT(pages) AS with_pages, SUM(pages) AS total_pages
FROM books;

┌───────┬────────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ books │ with_genre │ with_pages │ total_pages │
├───────┼────────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
│ 22    │ 20         │ 20         │ 7171        │
└───────┴────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

COUNT(*) counts every row, while COUNT(genre) skips the rows whose genre is NULL. AS gives a result column a readable name.

Combine aggregates with WHERE to summarise only some rows. The shortest, longest and average novel:

SELECT MIN(pages) AS shortest, MAX(pages) AS longest,
       ROUND(AVG(pages), 1) AS average
FROM books WHERE genre = 'novel';

┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ shortest │ longest │ average │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 192      │ 1072    │ 387.7   │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

ROUND(..., 1) keeps one decimal place. Aggregates also skip NULLs: AVG(pages) averages only the books whose page count is known.

Try it

How many books are on the shelf, that is, available?

Answer 
SELECT COUNT(*) AS on_the_shelf FROM books WHERE available = 1;

┌──────────────┐
│ on_the_shelf │
├──────────────┤
│ 16           │
└──────────────┘

SUM(available) gives the same answer, because available books hold 1.

docs.title: Step 10: Group rows with GROUP BY
docs.text:
GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share a value, and runs the aggregate once per group. The result has one row per group.

GROUP BY author turns rows into one row per author Seven books in mixed order: three by Ismail Kadare, two by George Orwell and two by Jane Austen. GROUP BY author collects them into three groups, and COUNT counts each group: Ismail Kadare 3, George Orwell 2, Jane Austen 2. BOOKS, IN ANY ORDER Ismail Kadare1971 George Orwell1949 Jane Austen1813 Ismail Kadare1963 George Orwell1945 Ismail Kadare1978 Jane Austen1815 GROUP BY author COUNT(*) ONE ROW PER GROUP Ismail Kadare3 George Orwell2 Jane Austen2

How many books in each genre? The NULL genres form a group of their own, shown as an empty cell:

SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS books
FROM books
GROUP BY genre
ORDER BY books DESC, genre;

┌─────────────┬───────┐
│    genre    │ books │
├─────────────┼───────┤
│ novel       │ 7     │
│ programming │ 3     │
│             │ 2     │
│ romance     │ 2     │
│ satire      │ 2     │
│ sci-fi      │ 2     │
│ children    │ 1     │
│ dystopia    │ 1     │
│ fantasy     │ 1     │
│ self-help   │ 1     │
└─────────────┴───────┘

To keep only some groups, use HAVING. WHERE filters rows before they are grouped; HAVING filters the groups after. The authors with more than one book:

SELECT author, COUNT(*) AS books
FROM books
GROUP BY author
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY books DESC, author;

┌───────────────┬───────┐
│    author     │ books │
├───────────────┼───────┤
│ Ismail Kadare │ 3     │
│ George Orwell │ 2     │
│ Jane Austen   │ 2     │
└───────────────┴───────┘

Both can appear in one query. Genres whose books average more than 300 pages, leaving out the books with no genre:

SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS books, ROUND(AVG(pages)) AS avg_pages
FROM books
WHERE genre IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY genre
HAVING AVG(pages) > 300
ORDER BY avg_pages DESC;

┌─────────────┬───────┬───────────┐
│    genre    │ books │ avg_pages │
├─────────────┼───────┼───────────┤
│ romance     │ 2     │ 453.0     │
│ sci-fi      │ 2     │ 451.0     │
│ programming │ 3     │ 408.0     │
│ novel       │ 7     │ 388.0     │
│ dystopia    │ 1     │ 328.0     │
│ self-help   │ 1     │ 320.0     │
│ fantasy     │ 1     │ 310.0     │
└─────────────┴───────┴───────────┘

WHERE cannot test an aggregate, because when WHERE runs, the groups do not exist yet. SQLite says so:

SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY author;

Parse error: misuse of aggregate: COUNT()
  SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY author;
                             error here ---^

Try it

Count the available and the unavailable books, in one query.

Answer

Group by the available column itself:

SELECT available, COUNT(*) AS books FROM books GROUP BY available;

┌───────────┬───────┐
│ available │ books │
├───────────┼───────┤
│ 0         │ 6     │
│ 1         │ 16    │
└───────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Step 11: Interpret results correctly
docs.text:
A query that runs is not necessarily a query that answers your question. Most wrong results come from one fact: SQL does not run a query in the order you write it.

The order you write a query and the order it runs You write SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. The database runs FROM first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY and LIMIT. SELECT moves from first to fifth. YOU WRITE THE DATABASE RUNS SELECT FROM WHERE GROUP BY HAVING ORDER BY LIMIT 1 FROM 2 WHERE 3 GROUP BY 4 HAVING 5 SELECT 6 ORDER BY 7 LIMIT

Read it in that order, and the rules stop being arbitrary:

  • WHERE cannot use aggregates or column aliases: it runs before any groups or names exist. That is what HAVING is for.
  • ORDER BY can use aliases, such as ORDER BY books: it runs after SELECT has named them.
  • LIMIT applies last, to the sorted result. "Top three" only means something after an ORDER BY.

A few more traps when reading results:

  • An aggregate over no rows is NULL, not zero. The page count of an author the library does not have prints as an empty cell:

    SELECT SUM(pages) AS total FROM books WHERE author = 'Nobody';

    ┌───────┐
│ total │
├───────┤
│       │
└───────┘

  • Whole numbers divide as whole numbers. Make one side a decimal to get a decimal answer:

    SELECT 7 / 2 AS whole, 7 / 2.0 AS decimal;

    ┌───────┬─────────┐
│ whole │ decimal │
├───────┼─────────┤
│ 3     │ 3.5     │
└───────┴─────────┘

  • Every column in a grouped SELECT must be grouped or aggregated. SQLite lets this query run, and shows one title from each genre, whichever it met first:

    SELECT genre, title FROM books GROUP BY genre;

    ┌─────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
│    genre    │               title               │
├─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
│             │ Vargjet e lira                    │
│ children    │ The Little Prince                 │
│ dystopia    │ Nineteen Eighty-Four              │
│ fantasy     │ The Hobbit                        │
│ novel       │ Kronikë në gur                    │
│ programming │ Clean Code                        │
│ romance     │ Pride and Prejudice               │
│ satire      │ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │
│ sci-fi      │ Dune                              │
│ self-help   │ Atomic Habits                     │
└─────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

    That is not "the" novel; it is an arbitrary one. Most other databases refuse the query outright. Treat a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated as a bug.

docs.title: Step 12: SQL from Python
docs.text:
Programs use databases through code, not the shell. Python's built-in sqlite3 module runs SQL on a SQLite file. Save this next to books.db and run it:

kadare.py
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

with closing(sqlite3.connect("books.db")) as connection:
    cursor = connection.execute(
        "SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE author = ? ORDER BY year",
        ("Ismail Kadare",),
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()

print(rows[0])
for title, year in rows:
    print(year, title)

('Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur', 1963)
1963 Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur
1971 Kronikë në gur
1978 Prilli i thyer
  • sqlite3.connect() opens the database file.
  • connection.execute() runs one SQL statement and returns a cursor; fetchall() gives the rows as a list of tuples.
  • closing(...), from contextlib, closes the connection at the end of the block, like with open(...) closes a file.

Changing data needs one more thing: a commit, which makes the change permanent. Using the connection itself in a with statement does it: it commits if the block succeeds, and rolls back if an exception is raised inside.

add_book.py
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing


def add_book(path, title, author, year):
    """Insert one book and return its new id."""
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as connection, connection:
        cursor = connection.execute(
            "INSERT INTO books (title, author, year) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            (title, author, year),
        )
        return cursor.lastrowid


new_id = add_book("books.db", "Kështjella", "Ismail Kadare", 1970)
print("Added book", new_id)

Added book 24

On its own, with connection: commits but does not close the connection. That surprises almost everyone, hence closing as well. lastrowid is the id SQLite gave the new row.

docs.title: Placeholders, never f-strings
docs.text:
Every query above has ? where a value goes, and passes the values separately, as a tuple. Never build SQL by pasting values into the string. See what happens when the "author" comes from a user who types x' OR '1'='1:

injection.py
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

name = "x' OR '1'='1"

with closing(sqlite3.connect("books.db")) as connection:
    query = f"SELECT title FROM books WHERE author = '{name}'"
    print(query)
    print(len(connection.execute(query).fetchall()), "rows")

    safe = connection.execute(
        "SELECT title FROM books WHERE author = ?", (name,)
    ).fetchall()
    print(len(safe), "rows")

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author = 'x' OR '1'='1'
23 rows
0 rows

The text closed the quote and added a condition that is always true, so the f-string query returned every row. With a placeholder, the same text is treated as a name, and matches nothing. This attack is called SQL injection, and it is still one of the most common ways real applications are broken into.

AI in the loop

Assistants write SQL fluently, and a confident query can still answer the wrong question. Before you run one, predict the result: how many rows, roughly what values. If the real result surprises you, find out why before you use it. And never run an UPDATE or DELETE from an assistant until you have run its WHERE as a SELECT and seen exactly which rows it touches.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
The shell shows ...> and nothing happens

The statement has no semicolon yet, so the shell is waiting for the rest. Type ; and press Enter.

Parse error: no such table: books

You opened a different database, often a new, empty one created by a typo in the file name. Check with .databases, and load books.sql into the file you meant.

Parse error: no such column: Kadare

Text needs single quotes: WHERE author = 'Ismail Kadare'. Without them, SQL reads the word as a column name. Double quotes are for the names of tables and columns, not for values.

Parse error: misuse of aggregate

An aggregate such as COUNT or SUM is in WHERE. Move the condition to HAVING, after GROUP BY.

Runtime error: UNIQUE constraint failed or NOT NULL constraint failed

The row breaks a rule of the table: a value that must be unique is already there, or a required column is missing. Read the column name in the message, and fix the data, not the rule.

My query returns nothing, and I know the rows exist

Check for = NULL (use IS NULL), for capital letters in text ('kadare' is not 'Kadare'), and for extra spaces inside the quotes.

sqlite3.ProgrammingError: Cannot operate on a closed database.

The code used the connection after the closing(...) block ended. Do all the work, including fetchall(), inside the block.

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
Seven exercises, from easy to harder, on books.db as you left it after the steps above. Try each one before you open the answer. If your data looks different, reload books.sql and you will get slightly different numbers; the queries stay the same.

1. One author. List George Orwell's books, oldest first.

Answer 
SELECT title, year FROM books
WHERE author = 'George Orwell'
ORDER BY year;

┌──────────────────────┬──────┐
│        title         │ year │
├──────────────────────┼──────┤
│ Animal Farm          │ 1945 │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ 1949 │
└──────────────────────┴──────┘

2. Two conditions. Find the programming books longer than 400 pages.

Answer 
SELECT title, pages FROM books
WHERE genre = 'programming' AND pages > 400;

┌────────────┬───────┐
│   title    │ pages │
├────────────┼───────┤
│ Clean Code │ 464   │
└────────────┴───────┘

3. Count per genre. How many books does each genre have? Leave out the books with no genre, and show the biggest genre first.

Answer 
SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS books
FROM books
WHERE genre IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY genre
ORDER BY books DESC, genre;

┌─────────────┬───────┐
│    genre    │ books │
├─────────────┼───────┤
│ novel       │ 7     │
│ programming │ 3     │
│ romance     │ 2     │
│ satire      │ 2     │
│ sci-fi      │ 2     │
│ children    │ 1     │
│ dystopia    │ 1     │
│ fantasy     │ 1     │
│ self-help   │ 1     │
└─────────────┴───────┘

4. Filter groups. Which authors have more than 500 pages in the library, in total? Largest first.

Answer 
SELECT author, SUM(pages) AS total_pages
FROM books
GROUP BY author
HAVING SUM(pages) > 500
ORDER BY total_pages DESC;

┌─────────────────────┬─────────────┐
│       author        │ total_pages │
├─────────────────────┼─────────────┤
│ Miguel de Cervantes │ 1072        │
│ Jane Austen         │ 906         │
│ Ismail Kadare       │ 824         │
│ Frank Herbert       │ 612         │
└─────────────────────┴─────────────┘

5. Missing data. Add Juvenilia by Ndre Mjeda without a year, then list every book with no year.

Answer 
INSERT INTO books (title, author) VALUES ('Juvenilia', 'Ndre Mjeda');
SELECT id, title, author FROM books WHERE year IS NULL;

┌────┬───────────┬────────────┐
│ id │   title   │   author   │
├────┼───────────┼────────────┤
│ 25 │ Juvenilia │ Ndre Mjeda │
└────┴───────────┴────────────┘

6. Update a group. All the programming books have come back. Mark them as available, and check how many rows changed.

Answer 
UPDATE books SET available = 1 WHERE genre = 'programming';
SELECT changes() AS changed;
SELECT title, available FROM books WHERE genre = 'programming';

┌─────────┐
│ changed │
├─────────┤
│ 3       │
└─────────┘
┌──────────────────────────┬───────────┐
│          title           │ available │
├──────────────────────────┼───────────┤
│ Clean Code               │ 1         │
│ The Pragmatic Programmer │ 1         │
│ Fluent Python            │ 1         │
└──────────────────────────┴───────────┘

7. Delete safely. Remove every book shorter than 150 pages. Look at the rows first, then delete inside a transaction, and check the count before you COMMIT.

Answer 
SELECT id, title, pages FROM books WHERE pages < 150;

┌────┬───────────────────┬───────┐
│ id │       title       │ pages │
├────┼───────────────────┼───────┤
│ 6  │ The Little Prince │ 96    │
│ 8  │ Animal Farm       │ 112   │
└────┴───────────────────┴───────┘

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM books WHERE pages < 150;
SELECT changes() AS deleted;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS books_left FROM books;
COMMIT;

┌─────────┐
│ deleted │
├─────────┤
│ 2       │
└─────────┘
┌────────────┐
│ books_left │
├────────────┤
│ 22         │
└────────────┘

If the number had been wrong, ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT would have undone the delete.

8. From Python. Write a function titles_by(path, author) that returns a list of one author's titles, oldest first, using a placeholder.

Answer titles_by.py
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing


def titles_by(path, author):
    """Return the titles of one author's books, oldest first."""
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as connection:
        rows = connection.execute(
            "SELECT title FROM books WHERE author = ? ORDER BY year",
            (author,),
        ).fetchall()
    return [title for (title,) in rows]


print(titles_by("books.db", "Jane Austen"))
print(titles_by("books.db", "Nobody"))

['Pride and Prejudice', 'Emma']
[]

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The books table repeats the author's name on every one of their books, and it has no idea who borrowed what. Next you split the library into several tables that point at each other, and join them back together to answer questions.

SQL: Joins & Relationships

docs.title: SQL: Joins & Relationships
docs.text:
90 min Data & APIs Needs: SQL: CRUD Operations

One table took you a long way, but a real library has more than books: authors, members, library cards, loans, tags. Each lives in its own table, and the tables point at each other through keys. In this tutorial you learn how tables relate, and how to join them back together to answer questions that span several of them.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Almost every useful question crosses tables. "Who has a book out right now?" needs loans, members and books. "Which authors has nobody borrowed?" needs authors, books and loans. Real databases have dozens of tables; joins are how you get answers out of them, and how you notice what is missing, like a member who never borrowed anything.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need sqlite3, as installed in SQL: CRUD Operations. Download the library database script and load it into a new file, library.db:

cd ~/library
curl -O https://evisp.github.io/augmented_software_engineering/assets/sql/library.sql
sqlite3 library.db < library.sql
sqlite3 library.db

Or download library.sql from the browser. Loading it again resets every table. The outputs on this page use .headers on and .mode box, as before.

docs.title: Step 1: From one table to several
docs.text:
In books.db, every book repeated its author's name, and there was nowhere to put a member or a loan. The library database splits the data into seven tables, one for each kind of thing:

.tables

authors        books          loans          tags         
book_tags      library_cards  members

Instead of repeating the author's name, each book stores the author's id. The name is written once, in authors:

SELECT * FROM books LIMIT 4;

┌────┬───────────────────────────────────┬───────────┬──────┐
│ id │               title               │ author_id │ year │
├────┼───────────────────────────────────┼───────────┼──────┤
│ 1  │ Kronikë në gur                    │ 1         │ 1971 │
│ 2  │ Prilli i thyer                    │ 1         │ 1978 │
│ 3  │ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ 1         │ 1963 │
│ 4  │ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ 2         │ 1973 │
└────┴───────────────────────────────────┴───────────┴──────┘

SELECT * FROM authors LIMIT 4;

┌────┬────────────────┬────────────────┐
│ id │      name      │    country     │
├────┼────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ 1  │ Ismail Kadare  │ Albania        │
│ 2  │ Dritëro Agolli │ Albania        │
│ 3  │ George Orwell  │ United Kingdom │
│ 4  │ Jane Austen    │ United Kingdom │
└────┴────────────────┴────────────────┘

Book 1 has author_id 1, and author 1 is Ismail Kadare. That number is the link. An entity-relationship diagram, or ER diagram, draws all the tables and their links at once:

erDiagram
    authors ||--o{ books : writes
    books ||--o{ loans : "is lent in"
    members ||--o{ loans : borrows
    members ||--o| library_cards : holds
    books ||--o{ book_tags : has
    tags ||--o{ book_tags : labels
    authors {
        integer id PK
        text name
        text country
    }
    books {
        integer id PK
        text title
        integer author_id FK
        integer year
    }
    members {
        integer id PK
        text name
        text email
        text joined_on
    }
    library_cards {
        integer member_id PK, FK
        text card_number
        text expires_on
    }
    loans {
        integer id PK
        integer book_id FK
        integer member_id FK
        text loaned_on
        text returned_on
    }
    tags {
        integer id PK
        text name
    }
    book_tags {
        integer book_id PK, FK
        integer tag_id PK, FK
    }

Read the line ends as "how many": || is exactly one, o| is zero or one, and o{ is zero or more. So the line between authors and books says: one author writes zero or more books, and each book has exactly one author.

docs.title: Step 2: Turn on foreign keys
docs.text:
A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table: books.author_id points at authors.id. The schema declares it with REFERENCES authors (id), so the database can check that every link leads somewhere.

There is a catch. For historical reasons, SQLite does not check foreign keys unless you ask, on every connection:

PRAGMA foreign_keys;

┌──────────────┐
│ foreign_keys │
├──────────────┤
│ 0            │
└──────────────┘

With checks off, a loan of book 99, which does not exist, goes in without a word:

INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on) VALUES (99, 1, '2026-10-30');
SELECT changes() AS inserted;

┌──────────┐
│ inserted │
├──────────┤
│ 1        │
└──────────┘

That broken row points at nothing. Remove it, and turn the checks on:

DELETE FROM loans WHERE book_id = 99;

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA foreign_keys;

┌──────────────┐
│ foreign_keys │
├──────────────┤
│ 1            │
└──────────────┘

Add PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; to your ~/.sqliterc, next to .headers on and .mode box, so every session starts with it. Every query from here on runs with foreign keys on.

docs.title: Step 3: Primary and foreign keys at work
docs.text:
With checks on, the database refuses a link to nothing:

INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on) VALUES (99, 1, '2026-10-30');

Runtime error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed (19)

It also refuses to delete a row that others still point at. Kadare has three books, so he cannot simply disappear:

DELETE FROM authors WHERE id = 1;

Runtime error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed (19)

That is the point of foreign keys: the database itself keeps the links correct, so no program, and no tired person at a terminal, can leave a loan that points at a deleted book.

To sum up the two kinds of key:

Primary key Foreign key What it does Identifies each row of its own table Points at a row of another table Unique? Yes, and never NULL No: many books can share one author_id Example authors.id books.author_id

Try it

Try to give Dune (book 8) an author that does not exist, 42.

Answer 
UPDATE books SET author_id = 42 WHERE id = 8;

Runtime error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed (19)

docs.title: Step 4: Three kinds of relationship
docs.text:
Every link between two tables is one of three kinds:

One-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many One-to-one: each member has at most one library card, because library_cards uses member_id as its primary key. One-to-many: one author has many books, because each book stores one author_id. Many-to-many: members and books are linked through the loans table: one member has many loans, one book has many loans, and each loan holds one member_id and one book_id. ONE-TO-ONEONE-TO-MANYMANY-TO-MANY membersid PK library_cardsmember_id PK, FK authorsid PK booksauthor_id FK membersid PK loansmember_id FKbook_id FK booksid PK 10..1 1many 1many many1 a member has at mostone card an author has many books,a book has one author a junction table linksmany members to many books
  • One-to-one. A member has at most one library card. library_cards uses member_id as its own primary key, so the same member cannot appear twice. Lea has no card yet, which is allowed: "zero or one".
  • One-to-many. One author has many books; each book has one author. The foreign key always goes on the many side: books.author_id.
  • Many-to-many. A member borrows many books, and a book is borrowed by many members. One column cannot hold "many", so a third table sits in the middle, the junction table: each row of loans links one member to one book, and adds facts about that link, the dates.

book_tags is a junction table too, between books and tags, but a pure one: just two foreign keys. Its primary key is the pair (book_id, tag_id), a composite key, so the same tag cannot be put on the same book twice.

docs.title: Step 5: Combine tables with JOIN
docs.text:
JOIN puts two tables side by side, and ON says which rows belong together. Each book with its author's name:

SELECT books.title, authors.name
FROM books
JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id;

┌───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│               title               │       name       │
├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                    │ Ismail Kadare    │
│ Prilli i thyer                    │ Ismail Kadare    │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ Ismail Kadare    │
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ Dritëro Agolli   │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four              │ George Orwell    │
│ Animal Farm                       │ George Orwell    │
│ Pride and Prejudice               │ Jane Austen      │
│ Dune                              │ Frank Herbert    │
│ The Hobbit                        │ J. R. R. Tolkien │
│ Things Fall Apart                 │ Chinua Achebe    │
└───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

For every book, SQLite finds the author whose id equals the book's author_id, and makes one result row from the pair. This is an inner join: only pairs that match appear. JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN.

Long table names get tiring, so give each table a short alias with AS, and use it everywhere. After a join, you can filter and sort on columns from either table. The Albanian books, oldest first:

SELECT b.title, a.name AS author, a.country
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE a.country = 'Albania'
ORDER BY b.year;

┌───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┬─────────┐
│               title               │     author     │ country │
├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼─────────┤
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ Ismail Kadare  │ Albania │
│ Kronikë në gur                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ Albania │
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ Dritëro Agolli │ Albania │
│ Prilli i thyer                    │ Ismail Kadare  │ Albania │
└───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────┘

When two tables have a column with the same name, such as id, you must say which one you mean:

SELECT id, title, name FROM books JOIN authors ON author_id = authors.id;

Parse error: ambiguous column name: id
  SELECT id, title, name FROM books JOIN authors ON author_id = authors.id;
         ^--- error here

Join as many tables as you need, one JOIN ... ON at a time. Who has a book out right now? That needs loans, members and books:

SELECT l.loaned_on, m.name AS member, b.title
FROM loans AS l
JOIN members AS m ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
ORDER BY l.loaned_on;

┌────────────┬─────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│ loaned_on  │   member    │        title        │
├────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ 2026-09-25 │ Erion Shehu │ Pride and Prejudice │
│ 2026-10-03 │ Arta Hoxha  │ Prilli i thyer      │
│ 2026-10-10 │ Drita Leka  │ Dune                │
│ 2026-10-22 │ Arta Hoxha  │ The Hobbit          │
└────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────────────┘

Try it

List every book Arta Hoxha has borrowed, with its author and the date, oldest loan first.

Answer

Four tables: the loan links the member to the book, and the book links to its author.

SELECT l.loaned_on, b.title, a.name AS author
FROM loans AS l
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
JOIN members AS m ON l.member_id = m.id
WHERE m.name = 'Arta Hoxha'
ORDER BY l.loaned_on;

┌────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ loaned_on  │        title         │      author      │
├────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ 2026-09-02 │ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ George Orwell    │
│ 2026-09-18 │ Kronikë në gur       │ Ismail Kadare    │
│ 2026-10-03 │ Prilli i thyer       │ Ismail Kadare    │
│ 2026-10-22 │ The Hobbit           │ J. R. R. Tolkien │
└────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 6: Keep unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN
docs.text:
An inner join drops every row without a partner. Sometimes that is exactly the row you are looking for.

INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows, LEFT JOIN keeps them Three authors: Frank Herbert matches Dune, George Orwell matches Nineteen Eighty-Four and Animal Farm, and Ursula K. Le Guin matches no book. The inner join returns three rows and leaves Le Guin out. The left join returns four rows, keeping Le Guin with NULL as the title. AUTHORSBOOKS INNER JOIN · 3 rowsLEFT JOIN · 4 rows Frank Herbert Ursula K. Le Guin George Orwell Dune Nineteen Eighty-Four Animal Farm no match Frank HerbertDuneGeorge OrwellNineteen Eig…George OrwellAnimal Farm Frank HerbertDune Ursula K. Le GuinNULL George OrwellNineteen Eig…George OrwellAnimal Farm

With an inner join, Le Guin, who has no books in the library, vanishes:

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors AS a
JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE a.country = 'United States';

┌───────────────┬───────┐
│     name      │ title │
├───────────────┼───────┤
│ Frank Herbert │ Dune  │
└───────────────┴───────┘

LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, the one before the word JOIN. When there is no partner, the right side's columns are NULL:

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE a.country = 'United States';

┌───────────────────┬───────┐
│       name        │ title │
├───────────────────┼───────┤
│ Frank Herbert     │ Dune  │
│ Ursula K. Le Guin │       │
└───────────────────┴───────┘

The same works for the one-to-one link. Every member, with a card number if they have one:

SELECT m.name, c.card_number
FROM members AS m
LEFT JOIN library_cards AS c ON c.member_id = m.id;

┌─────────────────┬─────────────┐
│      name       │ card_number │
├─────────────────┼─────────────┤
│ Arta Hoxha      │ LIB-0001    │
│ Besnik Krasniqi │ LIB-0002    │
│ Drita Leka      │ LIB-0003    │
│ Erion Shehu     │ LIB-0004    │
│ Lea Marku       │             │
└─────────────────┴─────────────┘

Add WHERE ... IS NULL on the right table, and you keep only the rows without a partner. This is the standard way to ask "who is missing?":

SELECT m.name
FROM members AS m
LEFT JOIN library_cards AS c ON c.member_id = m.id
WHERE c.member_id IS NULL;

┌───────────┐
│   name    │
├───────────┤
│ Lea Marku │
└───────────┘

Test a column that can never be NULL in a real row, such as the primary key or the foreign key. Then NULL can only mean "no partner".

Try it

Which books have never been borrowed?

Answer 
SELECT b.title
FROM books AS b
LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.book_id = b.id
WHERE l.id IS NULL;

┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│               title               │
├───────────────────────────────────┤
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │
│ Things Fall Apart                 │
└───────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 7: RIGHT and FULL joins
docs.text:
RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: it keeps every row of the right table. This query gives exactly the result of the LEFT JOIN of authors and books in Step 6, with the tables written the other way round. Most people write the LEFT version, with the table they care about first:

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM books AS b
RIGHT JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE a.country = 'United States';

┌───────────────────┬───────┐
│       name        │ title │
├───────────────────┼───────┤
│ Frank Herbert     │ Dune  │
│ Ursula K. Le Guin │       │
└───────────────────┴───────┘

FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. Here it finds the loose ends of the tags in one query: a book with no tags, and a tag on no book:

SELECT b.title, t.name AS tag
FROM books AS b
LEFT JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = b.id
FULL JOIN tags AS t ON t.id = bt.tag_id
WHERE b.id IS NULL OR t.id IS NULL;

┌───────────────────┬────────┐
│       title       │  tag   │
├───────────────────┼────────┤
│ Things Fall Apart │        │
│                   │ poetry │
└───────────────────┴────────┘

SQLite version

RIGHT JOIN and FULL JOIN need SQLite 3.39 or later. Ubuntu 24.04 ships 3.45; check yours with sqlite3 --version. On an older version, rewrite a RIGHT JOIN as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.

docs.title: Step 8: Many-to-many through a junction table
docs.text:
To get from a book to its tags, go through the junction table: books to book_tags, then book_tags to tags. Three books and their tags:

SELECT b.title, t.name AS tag
FROM books AS b
JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = b.id
JOIN tags AS t ON t.id = bt.tag_id
WHERE b.id IN (3, 5, 8)
ORDER BY b.id, t.name;

┌────────────────────────────────┬──────────┐
│             title              │   tag    │
├────────────────────────────────┼──────────┤
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ albanian │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │ classic  │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four           │ classic  │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four           │ dystopia │
│ Dune                           │ classic  │
│ Dune                           │ sci-fi   │
└────────────────────────────────┴──────────┘

A book with two tags appears twice: one row per pair. To get one row per book, group the rows and glue the tags together with GROUP_CONCAT. LEFT JOIN keeps the untagged book:

SELECT b.title, GROUP_CONCAT(t.name, ', ') AS tags
FROM books AS b
LEFT JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = b.id
LEFT JOIN tags AS t ON t.id = bt.tag_id
GROUP BY b.id
ORDER BY b.id;

┌───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┐
│               title               │       tags        │
├───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                    │ albanian          │
│ Prilli i thyer                    │ albanian          │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │ classic, albanian │
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │ albanian          │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four              │ classic, dystopia │
│ Animal Farm                       │ classic, dystopia │
│ Pride and Prejudice               │ classic           │
│ Dune                              │ classic, sci-fi   │
│ The Hobbit                        │ classic, fantasy  │
│ Things Fall Apart                 │                   │
└───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────┘

GROUP_CONCAT does not promise any order for the values it glues together.

Try it

List the titles of every book tagged classic, alphabetically.

Answer 
SELECT b.title
FROM books AS b
JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = b.id
JOIN tags AS t ON t.id = bt.tag_id
WHERE t.name = 'classic'
ORDER BY b.title;

┌────────────────────────────────┐
│             title              │
├────────────────────────────────┤
│ Animal Farm                    │
│ Dune                           │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four           │
│ Pride and Prejudice            │
│ The Hobbit                     │
└────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 9: Count across tables
docs.text:
Joins and GROUP BY work together. Loans per member, including members with none:

SELECT m.name, COUNT(l.id) AS loans
FROM members AS m
LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id
ORDER BY loans DESC, m.name;

┌─────────────────┬───────┐
│      name       │ loans │
├─────────────────┼───────┤
│ Arta Hoxha      │ 4     │
│ Besnik Krasniqi │ 3     │
│ Drita Leka      │ 3     │
│ Erion Shehu     │ 2     │
│ Lea Marku       │ 0     │
└─────────────────┴───────┘

Look closely at COUNT(l.id). With COUNT(*), Lea gets 1:

SELECT m.name, COUNT(*) AS loans
FROM members AS m
LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id
ORDER BY loans DESC, m.name;

┌─────────────────┬───────┐
│      name       │ loans │
├─────────────────┼───────┤
│ Arta Hoxha      │ 4     │
│ Besnik Krasniqi │ 3     │
│ Drita Leka      │ 3     │
│ Erion Shehu     │ 2     │
│ Lea Marku       │ 1     │
└─────────────────┴───────┘

The LEFT JOIN produced one row for Lea, with NULLs on the loan side. COUNT(*) counts that row; COUNT(l.id) skips the NULL. After a LEFT JOIN, count a column of the right table.

Books borrowed more than once:

SELECT b.title, COUNT(*) AS times
FROM loans AS l
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY b.id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY times DESC, b.title;

┌──────────────────────┬───────┐
│        title         │ times │
├──────────────────────┼───────┤
│ Dune                 │ 2     │
│ Kronikë në gur       │ 2     │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ 2     │
│ The Hobbit           │ 2     │
└──────────────────────┴───────┘

And how many books carry each tag, including the unused one:

SELECT t.name AS tag, COUNT(bt.book_id) AS books
FROM tags AS t
LEFT JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.tag_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id
ORDER BY books DESC, t.name;

┌──────────┬───────┐
│   tag    │ books │
├──────────┼───────┤
│ classic  │ 6     │
│ albanian │ 4     │
│ dystopia │ 2     │
│ fantasy  │ 1     │
│ sci-fi   │ 1     │
│ poetry   │ 0     │
└──────────┴───────┘

Try it

Count the loans by the author's country.

Answer 
SELECT a.country, COUNT(l.id) AS loans
FROM loans AS l
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.country
ORDER BY loans DESC;

┌────────────────┬───────┐
│    country     │ loans │
├────────────────┼───────┤
│ United Kingdom │ 6     │
│ Albania        │ 4     │
│ United States  │ 2     │
└────────────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Step 10: Subqueries
docs.text:
A subquery is a query inside another query, in brackets. The inner query runs first, and the outer one uses its answer.

IN with a list from a subquery. The books by Albanian authors, without a join:

SELECT title FROM books
WHERE author_id IN (SELECT id FROM authors WHERE country = 'Albania');

┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│               title               │
├───────────────────────────────────┤
│ Kronikë në gur                    │
│ Prilli i thyer                    │
│ Gjenerali i ushtrisë së vdekur    │
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │
└───────────────────────────────────┘

NOT IN. The books that never appear in loans:

SELECT title FROM books
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT book_id FROM loans);

┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│               title               │
├───────────────────────────────────┤
│ Shkëlqimi dhe rënia e shokut Zylo │
│ Things Fall Apart                 │
└───────────────────────────────────┘

NOT EXISTS. EXISTS asks "does the inner query return at least one row?". The inner query can use the outer row, here m.id, so it runs once per member. The members who never borrowed anything:

SELECT name FROM members AS m
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l WHERE l.member_id = m.id
);

┌───────────┐
│   name    │
├───────────┤
│ Lea Marku │
└───────────┘

A single value. A subquery that returns one value can stand where a number would. The books older than the average:

SELECT title, year FROM books
WHERE year < (SELECT AVG(year) FROM books)
ORDER BY year;

┌─────────────────────┬──────┐
│        title        │ year │
├─────────────────────┼──────┤
│ Pride and Prejudice │ 1813 │
│ The Hobbit          │ 1937 │
│ Animal Farm         │ 1945 │
└─────────────────────┴──────┘

SELECT AVG(year) AS average_year FROM books;

┌──────────────┐
│ average_year │
├──────────────┤
│ 1945.2       │
└──────────────┘

NOT IN and NULL

If the list contains a NULL, NOT IN matches nothing at all:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS books FROM books WHERE id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);

┌───────┐
│ books │
├───────┤
│ 0     │
└───────┘

"Is 5 not in (1, 2, unknown)?" The answer is "unknown", so no row passes. If the subquery's column can be NULL, use NOT EXISTS, which does not have this problem.

Joins and subqueries often answer the same question. Use whichever reads more clearly to you; LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS are both standard for "what is missing".

Try it

Who has borrowed Dune? Use subqueries only, no JOIN.

Answer

The innermost query finds Dune's id, the middle one the members who borrowed it:

SELECT name FROM members
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT member_id FROM loans
    WHERE book_id = (SELECT id FROM books WHERE title = 'Dune')
);

┌─────────────────┐
│      name       │
├─────────────────┤
│ Besnik Krasniqi │
│ Drita Leka      │
└─────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 11: CROSS JOIN
docs.text:
CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, with no ON. Five members and six tags make thirty pairs:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS pairs FROM members CROSS JOIN tags;

┌───────┐
│ pairs │
├───────┤
│ 30    │
└───────┘

All six for Arta:

SELECT m.name, t.name AS tag
FROM members AS m
CROSS JOIN tags AS t
WHERE m.id = 1;

┌────────────┬──────────┐
│    name    │   tag    │
├────────────┼──────────┤
│ Arta Hoxha │ classic  │
│ Arta Hoxha │ albanian │
│ Arta Hoxha │ dystopia │
│ Arta Hoxha │ sci-fi   │
│ Arta Hoxha │ fantasy  │
│ Arta Hoxha │ poetry   │
└────────────┴──────────┘

On its own, that is rarely useful. It shines when you need every combination, and then check which ones are missing. A reading challenge: which members have not yet read a fantasy or a sci-fi book?

SELECT m.name, t.name AS tag
FROM members AS m
CROSS JOIN tags AS t
WHERE t.name IN ('fantasy', 'sci-fi')
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM loans AS l
      JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = l.book_id
      WHERE l.member_id = m.id AND bt.tag_id = t.id
  )
ORDER BY t.name, m.name;

┌─────────────────┬─────────┐
│      name       │   tag   │
├─────────────────┼─────────┤
│ Besnik Krasniqi │ fantasy │
│ Erion Shehu     │ fantasy │
│ Lea Marku       │ fantasy │
│ Arta Hoxha      │ sci-fi  │
│ Erion Shehu     │ sci-fi  │
│ Lea Marku       │ sci-fi  │
└─────────────────┴─────────┘

A join without a condition is a cross join

Forget the ON, or list tables with commas and no WHERE, and you get every combination, silently:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows FROM books, authors;

┌──────┐
│ rows │
├──────┤
│ 80   │
└──────┘

Ten books times eight authors: 80 rows, 70 of them nonsense. If a join returns far more rows than you expected, look for a missing condition.

AI in the loop

Ask an assistant for a join and check two things before you trust the result. The kind of join: does the question need unmatched rows, such as members with no loans? Then an inner join is wrong. The row count: predict roughly how many rows the answer should have. A join on the wrong column runs without error and returns plausible-looking nonsense; the count is usually what gives it away.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Parse error: ambiguous column name: id

Two joined tables have a column with that name. Prefix it with the table or its alias: b.id, a.id.

Runtime error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

The row points at something that does not exist, or you are deleting a row that others still point at. Check the ids, or delete or update the rows that point at it first.

A bad foreign key went in without an error

Foreign keys are off. Run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;, and add it to ~/.sqliterc.

The join returns far too many rows

A missing or wrong ON condition, or a join through a one-to-many link you did not expect, such as a book with two tags appearing twice. Check the ON of every join, and count rows as you add each table.

Rows disappear after I join

An inner join drops rows with no partner. If you need them, use LEFT JOIN. A condition on the right table in WHERE can also drop them; put it in the ON instead.

Parse error: RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOINs are not currently supported

Your SQLite is older than 3.39. Swap the tables and use LEFT JOIN.

docs.title: Practice set
docs.text:
Eight exercises on library.db, from easy to harder. Reload library.sql first for exactly these results.

1. One author's books. List George Orwell's books, oldest first, using a join.

Answer 
SELECT b.title, b.year
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE a.name = 'George Orwell'
ORDER BY b.year;

┌──────────────────────┬──────┐
│        title         │ year │
├──────────────────────┼──────┤
│ Animal Farm          │ 1945 │
│ Nineteen Eighty-Four │ 1949 │
└──────────────────────┴──────┘

2. One-to-one. Show each member with their card number and expiry date, the card that expires soonest first.

Answer 
SELECT m.name, c.card_number, c.expires_on
FROM members AS m
JOIN library_cards AS c ON c.member_id = m.id
ORDER BY c.expires_on;

┌─────────────────┬─────────────┬────────────┐
│      name       │ card_number │ expires_on │
├─────────────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
│ Arta Hoxha      │ LIB-0001    │ 2027-01-15 │
│ Besnik Krasniqi │ LIB-0002    │ 2027-02-03 │
│ Drita Leka      │ LIB-0003    │ 2027-03-10 │
│ Erion Shehu     │ LIB-0004    │ 2027-05-22 │
└─────────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┘

3. Missing partners. Which authors have no books in the library? Use NOT EXISTS.

Answer 
SELECT a.name
FROM authors AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM books AS b WHERE b.author_id = a.id
);

┌───────────────────┐
│       name        │
├───────────────────┤
│ Ursula K. Le Guin │
└───────────────────┘

4. Overdue. Which loans started before October and are still not returned? Show the member, the title and the date.

Answer 
SELECT m.name, b.title, l.loaned_on
FROM loans AS l
JOIN members AS m ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books AS b ON l.book_id = b.id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND l.loaned_on < '2026-10-01';

┌─────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────┐
│    name     │        title        │ loaned_on  │
├─────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────┤
│ Erion Shehu │ Pride and Prejudice │ 2026-09-25 │
└─────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────┘

5. Popular authors. Count the loans of each author's books, including authors with none, most borrowed first.

Answer 
SELECT a.name, COUNT(l.id) AS loans
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN loans AS l ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY a.id
ORDER BY loans DESC, a.name;

┌───────────────────┬───────┐
│       name        │ loans │
├───────────────────┼───────┤
│ Ismail Kadare     │ 4     │
│ George Orwell     │ 3     │
│ Frank Herbert     │ 2     │
│ J. R. R. Tolkien  │ 2     │
│ Jane Austen       │ 1     │
│ Chinua Achebe     │ 0     │
│ Dritëro Agolli    │ 0     │
│ Ursula K. Le Guin │ 0     │
└───────────────────┴───────┘

Two LEFT JOINs in a row keep the authors without books and the books without loans, and COUNT(l.id) counts zero for both.

6. Unused tags. Which tags are on no book? Use NOT IN.

Answer 
SELECT t.name
FROM tags AS t
WHERE t.id NOT IN (SELECT tag_id FROM book_tags);

┌────────┐
│  name  │
├────────┤
│ poetry │
└────────┘

NOT IN is safe here, because book_tags.tag_id can never be NULL.

7. Through a junction. Which members have borrowed at least one book tagged albanian? Each name once.

Answer

DISTINCT removes the repeats from members who borrowed several:

SELECT DISTINCT m.name
FROM members AS m
JOIN loans AS l ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN book_tags AS bt ON bt.book_id = l.book_id
JOIN tags AS t ON t.id = bt.tag_id
WHERE t.name = 'albanian'
ORDER BY m.name;

┌─────────────┐
│    name     │
├─────────────┤
│ Arta Hoxha  │
│ Drita Leka  │
│ Erion Shehu │
└─────────────┘

8. In or out. List every book with the status out if it has a loan that is not returned yet, and in otherwise.

Answer

CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END picks a value, and EXISTS asks whether an open loan exists:

SELECT b.title,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM loans AS l
           WHERE l.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL
       ) THEN 'out' ELSE 'in' END AS status
FROM books AS b
ORDER BY b.id;
